slides.title: let vs var
slides.body: Swift uses `let` to declare a constant -- a binding whose value cannot change after it is first set -- and `var` to declare a variable, whose value can be reassigned. Preferring `let` by default makes code easier to reason about because you know a value won't change underneath you, and the compiler will flag any attempt to mutate it.

slides.title: Type inference
slides.body: Swift's compiler infers the type of a constant or variable from its initial value, so you rarely need to write types explicitly. This keeps code concise while remaining fully statically typed -- the inferred type is fixed at compile time, just as if you had written it yourself.
slides.example:
let age = 27        // inferred as Int
var name = "Ada"     // inferred as String
let pi = 3.14159     // inferred as Double

slides.title: Explicit type annotations
slides.body: Sometimes you need to state a type explicitly: when there's no initial value to infer from, when you want a wider or different type than the literal would produce (like Double instead of Int), or simply to document intent for readers. You write the annotation after a colon following the name.

slides.title: Type safety and literal defaults
slides.body: Swift never performs implicit type conversions. An integer literal assigned to a Double-typed variable is converted at compile time, but mixing an Int and a Double in an expression requires an explicit conversion. This strictness catches a whole category of bugs before your code ever runs.
slides.example:
let score: Double = 5   // Int literal, Double type -- OK
let count = 5            // Int
let ratio = 2.5
// count + ratio          // compile error: Int + Double
let fixed = Double(count) + ratio  // 7.5

quiz.prompt: Which declaration should you prefer when a value will never need to change after it's set?

options.text: Either works identically in all cases
static var
var, because it's more flexible
let, because it documents that the value is immutable

quiz.explanation: `let` creates an immutable binding, which communicates intent and lets the compiler catch accidental reassignment.

quiz.prompt: What type does Swift infer for `let temperature = 98.6`?

options.text: Float
NSNumber
Int
Double

quiz.explanation: Swift infers floating-point literals as Double by default unless another type is specified.

quiz.prompt: Why does `let total = count + ratio` fail to compile if count is Int and ratio is Double?

options.text: The + operator only works with String in Swift
count and ratio must be declared with var
Swift never performs implicit type conversions between numeric types, even Int and Double
Swift doesn't support addition between numeric types at all

quiz.explanation: Swift's strict static typing means mixed-type arithmetic requires an explicit conversion, such as Double(count) + ratio.

quiz.prompt: Which of these correctly declares a variable with an explicit type when there's no initial value?

options.text: var score = Int
var score: Int
var score = Int()
let score: Int = nil

quiz.explanation: A colon followed by the type name is the correct syntax for an explicit type annotation without an initial value.

quiz.prompt: What happens if you try to reassign a value to a constant declared with let after initialization?

options.text: It's a compile-time error
It throws a runtime exception
The new value silently overwrites the old one
It works only inside a function

quiz.explanation: The Swift compiler statically enforces immutability for let bindings and reports an error if you attempt to reassign one.

slides.title: What optionals represent
slides.body: An optional in Swift is a type that can hold either a value or the absence of one, written as Type?. It's Swift's built-in, type-safe replacement for null references -- the compiler forces you to explicitly handle the 'no value' case before you can use what might be inside.

slides.title: if let and guard let
slides.body: if let and guard let safely unwrap an optional by binding its contents to a new, non-optional constant only if a value is present. guard let additionally requires the enclosing scope to exit (return, break, continue, or throw) in the else branch, making it ideal for early-exit validation at the top of a function.

slides.title: Force unwrapping and its dangers
slides.body: The ! operator force-unwraps an optional, assuming it has a value. If the optional is actually nil, this crashes the app at runtime with a fatal error. Force unwrapping should be reserved for cases where nil is logically impossible and proven by the surrounding code, never as a shortcut to silence the compiler.

slides.title: Nil-coalescing and optional chaining
slides.body: The ?? operator supplies a default value when an optional is nil, letting you unwrap and provide a fallback in one expression. Optional chaining (?.) lets you call a method or access a property on an optional and automatically produces nil if any link in the chain is nil, instead of crashing.
slides.example:
let nickname: String? = nil
let displayName = nickname ?? "Anonymous"

let user: User? = fetchUser()
let cityLength = user?.address?.city?.count

quiz.prompt: What does declaring a variable as String? mean?

options.text: It's a String that can be empty
It's a String or nil
It's always a non-nil String
It's an array of Strings

quiz.explanation: The ? suffix makes a type optional, meaning the variable can hold either a value of that type or nil.

quiz.prompt: What's the key difference between if let and guard let for unwrapping an optional?

options.text: if let works everywhere but guard let requires the else branch to exit the current scope
guard let can only be used with String values
if let is only valid inside classes
There is no difference

quiz.explanation: guard let's else clause must transfer control out of the enclosing scope, which makes it well suited to early-exit validation, while if let simply scopes the unwrapped value to its own block.

quiz.prompt: What happens at runtime when you force-unwrap (!) an optional that is nil?

options.text: It returns the type's default value
It silently becomes an empty optional
It's caught automatically as a thrown error
The app crashes with a fatal error

quiz.explanation: Force unwrapping asserts a value is present; if it's actually nil, the program terminates immediately with a fatal error.

quiz.prompt: What does `let name = nickname ?? "Guest"` do if nickname is nil?

options.text: It fails to compile
name becomes "Guest"
name becomes nil
It crashes

quiz.explanation: The nil-coalescing operator ?? supplies the right-hand value whenever the left-hand optional is nil.

quiz.prompt: Given `let count = user?.profile?.friends?.count`, if user.profile is nil, what is count?

options.text: nil
A compile error
A runtime crash

quiz.explanation: Optional chaining short-circuits to nil as soon as any link in the chain is nil, rather than crashing or throwing.

slides.title: if, else if, and else
slides.body: Swift's if statement evaluates a Boolean condition and executes a block of code when it's true, with optional else if and else branches for alternatives. Unlike some languages, Swift requires the condition itself to be a Bool -- there's no implicit truthiness for numbers or optionals.

slides.title: switch and exhaustiveness
slides.body: Swift's switch statement must be exhaustive: it has to cover every possible value of the type being switched on, either with explicit cases or a default case. Cases don't fall through to the next one automatically, and switch can match ranges, tuples, and pattern-bind associated values from enums.

slides.title: guard for early exit
slides.body: guard checks a condition and requires the else branch to exit the current scope if it's false, which lets you handle invalid states up front and keep the main logic of a function unindented. This reads naturally as 'this must be true to continue' rather than nesting the happy path inside an if block.

slides.title: where clauses and pattern matching
slides.body: Both switch cases and for loops can be refined with a where clause that adds an extra condition to a pattern match. This lets you combine matching a case's shape with an additional runtime check in a single, readable line instead of nesting an if inside the case.

quiz.prompt: Why won't `if user { ... }` compile in Swift when user is an Int?

options.text: Swift requires if conditions to be Bool, with no implicit truthiness for other types
Int values are always treated as true
Swift doesn't support if statements with variables
user needs to be declared with var instead of let

quiz.explanation: Unlike C or JavaScript, Swift does not coerce non-Bool types to Bool, so the condition must itself evaluate to Bool.

quiz.prompt: What must a switch statement over a non-enum type like Int include if it doesn't list every possible value?

options.text: Nothing -- switch statements are optional to complete
An if/else fallback outside the switch
A guard statement
A default case

quiz.explanation: Swift's switch must be exhaustive; a default case covers any values not explicitly listed.

quiz.prompt: In Swift, does a matched switch case automatically fall through to the next case?

options.text: Only for enum switches
No, unless you explicitly write fallthrough
Only if there's no default case
Yes, always, like C

quiz.explanation: Swift's switch cases do not fall through by default; you must use the fallthrough keyword to opt into that behavior explicitly.

quiz.prompt: What must happen in the else branch of a guard statement?

options.text: It must call fatalError()
It must print an error message
It must exit the current scope, e.g. via return, break, continue, or throw
Nothing in particular

quiz.explanation: guard's else block is required to transfer control out of the enclosing scope; the compiler enforces this.

quiz.prompt: What does `for number in 1...10 where number % 2 == 0` do?

options.text: Iterates only odd numbers from 1 to 10
Fails to compile because where can't be used with ranges
Iterates only even numbers from 1 to 10, skipping the rest without executing the loop body for them
Iterates all numbers 1 to 10, then filters afterward

quiz.explanation: The where clause adds a condition to the loop's pattern match, so the body only executes for elements that satisfy it.

slides.title: Function basics and parameter labels
slides.body: Swift functions can have distinct argument labels and parameter names, letting call sites read like natural language while the function body uses a shorter internal name. Parameters can also have default values, and functions are full types that can be passed around and stored in variables.

slides.title: Closures as first-class values
slides.body: A closure is a self-contained block of functionality that can be passed around and executed later, similar to a function but able to be written inline without a name. Closures capture variables and constants from their surrounding context by reference, which is what lets a completion handler still see the state that existed when it was created.

slides.title: Trailing closure syntax
slides.body: When a function's last parameter is a closure, Swift lets you move it outside the parentheses as a trailing closure, and if it's the only argument you can omit the parentheses entirely. This is why UIKit and SwiftUI APIs that take a completion handler or view builder read so cleanly.

slides.title: Escaping closures
slides.body: A closure passed as a function parameter is non-escaping by default, meaning it's guaranteed to be called before the function returns. When a closure needs to be stored or called later -- like a network completion handler -- it must be marked @escaping, which also means it can capture self strongly unless you explicitly capture it weakly.

quiz.prompt: In `func move(from start: Int, to end: Int)`, what is start inside the function body?

options.text: The internal parameter name used within the function
The external argument label
An invalid identifier
A closure

quiz.explanation: from is the external argument label used at the call site (move(from: 0, to: 10)), while start is the internal name used inside the function body.

quiz.prompt: What does `numbers.sorted { $0 < $1 }` do?

options.text: Sorts numbers in ascending order using a trailing closure
Mutates numbers in place with no return value
Filters out numbers less than 1
Fails to compile because closures can't be passed to sorted

quiz.explanation: sorted(by:) takes a closure describing the ordering; { $0 < $1 } is trailing closure syntax for an ascending comparator, returning a new sorted array.

quiz.prompt: Why must a closure stored for later use, such as a network completion handler, be marked @escaping?

options.text: Because it may be called after the function that received it has already returned
It's only needed for closures with no parameters
It makes the closure run synchronously
It's required for all closures in Swift

quiz.explanation: By default Swift assumes a closure parameter is called before the function returns; @escaping documents and enables the case where the closure outlives that call, such as being stored or invoked asynchronously.

quiz.prompt: What do closures capture from their surrounding context by default?

options.text: Nothing -- closures are isolated
Only constants, never variables
A copy of every variable in the enclosing file
References to the variables and constants they use from the enclosing scope

quiz.explanation: Closures capture the variables and constants they reference from their defining scope, by reference, so later changes to a captured var are visible inside the closure.

quiz.prompt: Which call correctly uses trailing closure syntax for `func fetchData(completion: (Data?) -> Void)`?

options.text: fetchData(completion: { data in ... })
fetchData.completion { data in ... }
fetchData { data in ... }
fetchData(() { data in ... })

quiz.explanation: When a closure is the only argument, Swift allows dropping the parentheses entirely and writing the closure directly after the function name.

slides.title: Array, Dictionary, and Set
slides.body: Array stores an ordered, possibly-duplicate collection of elements; Dictionary stores unordered key-value pairs with unique keys; Set stores an unordered collection of unique elements with fast membership testing. Choosing the right one communicates intent and often changes an algorithm's performance characteristics.

slides.title: Value semantics of collections
slides.body: Array, Dictionary, and Set are all value types in Swift: assigning one to a new variable or passing it to a function creates a logically independent copy, so mutating the copy never affects the original. Under the hood Swift uses copy-on-write, so the actual buffer is only duplicated the moment one of the copies is mutated, keeping simple assignment cheap.
slides.example:
var original = [1, 2, 3]
var copy = original
copy.append(4)
print(original) // [1, 2, 3] -- unaffected
print(copy)     // [1, 2, 3, 4]

slides.title: Common operations and complexity
slides.body: Dictionary and Set lookups, insertions, and deletions are average O(1) thanks to hashing, which is why they're preferred over Array for membership checks on large collections. Array offers O(1) access by index and O(1) append at the end, but inserting or removing at the front or middle is O(n) because later elements must shift.

slides.title: Iterating and transforming with higher-order functions
slides.body: map, filter, and reduce let you transform collections without writing manual loops: map produces a new collection by applying a closure to every element, filter keeps only elements matching a predicate, and reduce combines all elements into a single value. Chaining them reads declaratively but each call allocates an intermediate collection.

quiz.prompt: Which collection type should you choose to guarantee no duplicate elements and fast membership testing?

options.text: Array
Tuple
Dictionary
Set

quiz.explanation: Set enforces uniqueness of its elements and offers average O(1) membership testing via hashing, unlike Array which allows duplicates and requires O(n) linear search.

quiz.prompt: After `var copy = original` where original is an Array, what happens if you append to copy?

options.text: Both original and copy become nil
It's a compile error -- arrays can't be copied
original is also modified, since arrays are reference types
Only copy changes; original remains as it was, because Array has value semantics

quiz.explanation: Swift's Array has value semantics: assignment creates an independent logical copy, so mutating one doesn't affect the other, even though copy-on-write defers the actual memory copy until a mutation occurs.

quiz.prompt: What is the average time complexity of looking up a value by key in a Dictionary?

options.text: O(n)
O(log n)

quiz.explanation: Dictionary is backed by a hash table, giving average O(1) lookup, insertion, and deletion.

quiz.prompt: What does `numbers.filter { $0 > 10 }` return?

options.text: The count of elements greater than 10
It mutates numbers in place, removing elements <= 10
A new array containing only the elements greater than 10
A Bool indicating whether any element is greater than 10

quiz.explanation: filter returns a new collection containing only the elements that satisfy the predicate closure; it doesn't mutate the original.

quiz.prompt: Why is inserting an element at index 0 of a large Array slower than appending at the end?

options.text: Inserting at the front requires shifting every subsequent element, making it O(n), while append at the end is typically O(1)
Array elements are stored in a hash table, so position doesn't matter
Both operations are always O(1)
Array doesn't support insertion at index 0

quiz.explanation: Arrays are stored contiguously, so inserting at the front requires shifting all later elements over by one, which takes time proportional to the array's length.

slides.title: Throwing functions
slides.body: A function marked throws can propagate an error to its caller instead of returning normally. To call it you use try, and the surrounding code must either handle the error with a do/catch block or itself be marked throws to pass the error further up the call stack.

slides.title: do, try, and catch
slides.body: A do block wraps one or more try expressions; if any of them throws, execution jumps immediately to a matching catch clause. You can write multiple catch clauses to handle specific error cases differently, similar to how switch matches patterns, with a catch-all clause to handle anything else.

slides.title: try?, try!, and when to use each
slides.body: try? converts a throwing call into an optional, returning nil if it throws and discarding the error's details -- useful when you only care whether it succeeded. try! asserts the call will never throw and crashes at runtime if it does, so it should be used as rarely as force unwrapping, only when failure is truly impossible.

slides.title: Result as an alternative to throwing
slides.body: Result<Success, Failure> is an enum with .success and .failure cases that packages an outcome as a value you can store, pass around, or return from an async completion handler -- situations where throws doesn't apply directly. You extract the value with a switch or by calling .get(), which itself is a throwing function that bridges back to do/try/catch.

quiz.prompt: What must a function declaration include if it can throw an error?

options.text: throws
async
Nothing -- any function can throw
@escaping

quiz.explanation: Only functions explicitly marked with throws in their declaration are allowed to propagate errors to their caller.

quiz.prompt: What happens when a try expression inside a do block throws an error?

options.text: The error is silently ignored
The do block returns nil automatically
The program crashes immediately
Execution jumps to a matching catch clause in the same do block

quiz.explanation: Control transfers to the first catch clause whose pattern matches the thrown error, letting you handle it there.

quiz.prompt: What does `try? someThrowingCall()` produce if the call throws?

options.text: It re-throws the error to the caller
nil, wrapping the result as an optional and discarding the specific error
It returns the error itself as the result
It crashes the app

quiz.explanation: try? converts a throwing expression's result into an optional: a value on success, or nil on failure, discarding details of the actual error.

quiz.prompt: When is it appropriate to use try!?

options.text: It's the recommended default for all throwing calls
Whenever you want to avoid writing a do/catch block
Only when you can prove the call cannot fail in that context, since it crashes on failure
Any time performance matters

quiz.explanation: try! asserts success and crashes at runtime if the call throws, so it's appropriate only when failure is provably impossible, much like force unwrapping.

quiz.prompt: Why might an API use Result<Success, Failure> in a completion handler instead of a throwing function?

options.text: Result is faster than throws in all cases
Result types are required for all enums
Throwing functions can't be called at all from closures
A completion handler is called asynchronously after the original function has returned, and Swift's throws only propagates synchronously up the call stack

quiz.explanation: Swift's throws/try mechanism only works within the synchronous call stack, so an outcome delivered later via a closure is instead modeled as a value using Result (or, in modern Swift, an async throwing function).

quiz.prompt: Which keyword should be your default choice for declaring a value in Swift, unless you know it needs to change?

options.text: let
const
var
final

quiz.explanation: let is preferred by default because immutable bindings are easier to reason about and prevent accidental mutation.

quiz.prompt: What does force-unwrapping a nil optional with ! do?

options.text: Throws a catchable error
Returns the type's default value
Crashes with a fatal error at runtime
Returns nil safely

quiz.explanation: Force unwrapping asserts a value is present; if the optional is actually nil, the app crashes immediately.

options.text: Only inside a function
No, switch must be exhaustive, so a default case (or full coverage) is required
Only if you add @unknown
Yes, switch never needs to be exhaustive

quiz.explanation: Swift's switch statements must cover every possible case, which for a broad type like Int requires a default clause.

quiz.prompt: What must the else branch of a guard statement do?

options.text: Exit the current scope
Return an optional
Nothing special

quiz.explanation: guard's else clause is required to transfer control out of the enclosing scope.

The closure may be called after the function that received it returns
The closure can't capture any variables
The closure is automatically retried on failure

quiz.explanation: @escaping documents that a closure may be stored and invoked after its enclosing function has already returned.

quiz.prompt: Why does mutating a copy of a Swift Array not affect the original?

options.text: Arrays are reference types
Only Dictionary has this behavior
Arrays have value semantics, so assignment creates a logically independent copy
Arrays are always immutable

quiz.explanation: Array is a value type; assignment produces an independent logical copy, with copy-on-write deferring the actual buffer duplication until a mutation happens.

quiz.prompt: What is the average complexity of inserting a key-value pair into a Dictionary?

options.text: O(log n)
O(n)

quiz.explanation: Dictionary's hash-table backing gives average O(1) insertion.

quiz.prompt: What is required to call a function declared with throws?

options.text: The call must be wrapped in an if let
The call must be prefixed with try, and the error handled or propagated
The function must return an optional
Nothing special

quiz.explanation: Calling a throwing function requires try, and the calling context must either catch the error or itself be marked throws.

options.text: Int
Int?
Never
Result<Int, Error>

quiz.explanation: try? wraps the throwing call's result as an optional of the original return type.

quiz.prompt: In `func send(to recipient: String)`, what is `to` used for?

options.text: A closure marker
The internal parameter name
A default value
The external argument label used at the call site

quiz.explanation: to is the external argument label shown at the call site, e.g. send(to: "Ada"), distinct from the internal name recipient used in the function body.

slides.title: Structs are value types, classes are reference types
slides.body: A struct instance is copied whenever it's assigned to a new variable, passed to a function, or stored in a collection, so each copy is independent. A class instance is a reference: assigning it just copies a pointer to the same underlying object, so mutating it through one reference is visible through every other reference to that same instance.

slides.title: Identity vs equality
slides.body: Classes have identity -- two class references can point to the exact same object, checkable with the === operator -- while structs have no identity, only equality, checkable with == when the type conforms to Equatable. Asking 'is this the same instance?' only makes sense for reference types.

slides.title: Why Swift defaults to structs
slides.body: Apple's own frameworks and Swift's standard library favor structs (String, Array, Dictionary, and most SwiftUI views are structs) because value semantics eliminate a whole class of bugs caused by unexpected shared mutable state. Use a class when you specifically need shared, mutable identity, reference counting for lifetime management, or interoperability with Objective-C/UIKit APIs that expect reference types.

slides.title: Mutating structs from methods
slides.body: Because a struct's own methods operate on a copy-like value, a method that changes its properties must be marked mutating, which is only callable on a variable (var) instance -- never on a let constant. Classes never need mutating because modifying a property through a reference doesn't require reassigning the reference itself.

quiz.prompt: If `let account2 = account1` where Account is a class, and you mutate a property through account2, what happens to account1?

options.text: It causes a compile error
account1 reflects the change too, since both reference the same object
account1 becomes nil
account1 is unaffected because classes are value types

quiz.explanation: Classes are reference types, so account1 and account2 point to the same underlying instance; mutating through either reference is visible through both.

quiz.prompt: What operator checks whether two class references point to the exact same instance?

options.text: is

quiz.explanation: === is Swift's identity operator, which compares whether two references point to the same object in memory; == compares value equality instead.

quiz.prompt: Why must a struct's method that modifies self's properties be marked mutating?

options.text: Because all struct methods are mutating by default
Because struct instances have value semantics, and mutating is required to signal and permit the implicit rewrite of self
It's only a stylistic convention with no real effect
mutating is only needed for class methods

quiz.explanation: Since structs are value types, modifying a property effectively produces a new value assigned back to self; mutating makes this explicit and is required by the compiler.

quiz.prompt: Which of these can call a mutating method?

options.text: A struct instance declared with var
A struct instance declared with let
Neither -- mutating methods can never be called
Only class instances

quiz.explanation: Because a mutating method effectively reassigns self, it can only be invoked on a variable (var) instance, not a constant (let) one.

quiz.prompt: Why does Swift's standard library favor structs for types like String and Array?

options.text: Structs support inheritance, which classes don't
Structs are always faster than classes in every situation
Classes can't store properties
Value semantics avoid unexpected shared mutable state, making copies behave independently and predictably

quiz.explanation: Value types copy on assignment, so passing them around doesn't risk one part of the program unexpectedly mutating state that another part still relies on.

slides.title: Designated and convenience initialisers
slides.body: A designated initialiser is a class's primary initialiser, responsible for fully initialising all of its stored properties and calling a superclass's designated initialiser. A convenience initialiser is a secondary, convenience-marked initialiser that must call another initialiser on the same class, ultimately funnelling through to a designated one.

slides.title: Two-phase initialisation and super.init
slides.body: Swift initialises objects in two phases: first every stored property in the class and its superclasses gets an initial value (subclass properties before calling super.init), then each class in the hierarchy has a chance to customise properties further. A subclass must call super.init(...) before it can read self or access inherited properties.

slides.title: Overriding methods and properties
slides.body: A subclass overrides an inherited method or computed property by marking it override, which the compiler requires so accidental overrides (and typos that fail to override anything) are caught. Overridden methods can still call the superclass's original implementation via super.methodName() before or after adding their own behavior.

slides.title: final to prevent overriding
slides.body: Marking a class, method, or property final prevents further subclassing or overriding, which documents that the implementation is not meant to be extended and lets the compiler perform certain optimisations since dynamic dispatch is no longer possible for that member. It's good practice to mark classes final unless you deliberately designed them to be subclassed.

quiz.prompt: What must a subclass's designated initialiser do before it can access self or inherited properties?

options.text: Mark itself as convenience
Call super.init(...)
Nothing special
Override viewDidLoad

quiz.explanation: Two-phase initialisation requires that inherited properties be set up by the superclass's initialiser (via super.init) before the subclass can use self.

quiz.prompt: What must a convenience initialiser ultimately do?

options.text: Call super.init() directly
Be marked final
Call another initialiser on the same class, which eventually reaches a designated initialiser
Directly set every stored property itself

quiz.explanation: Convenience initialisers delegate across (to another initialiser in the same class), never straight to the superclass, and that chain must terminate at a designated initialiser.

quiz.prompt: What keyword is required when a subclass overrides an inherited method?

options.text: override
super
mutating
final

quiz.explanation: Swift requires the override keyword on any member that overrides a superclass implementation, which also prevents accidental unintended overrides from compiling silently.

quiz.prompt: What does marking a class final do?

options.text: Makes the class a struct
Makes all of its properties constants
Requires the class to conform to Codable
Prevents the class from being subclassed

quiz.explanation: final disallows further subclassing (or overriding, at the member level), which also enables the compiler to use static dispatch instead of dynamic dispatch.

quiz.prompt: How can an overriding method still invoke the superclass's original implementation?

options.text: By calling self.methodName() again
By calling super.methodName()
It's impossible once overridden
By marking itself convenience

quiz.explanation: super.methodName() explicitly calls the superclass's implementation, which an override can call before, after, or instead of adding its own logic.

slides.title: Defining a protocol
slides.body: A protocol defines a blueprint of methods, properties, and other requirements without providing an implementation -- any type (class, struct, or enum) can then conform to it by supplying that implementation. This is Swift's core mechanism for defining an interface or contract independent of a specific type hierarchy.

slides.title: Conforming to a protocol
slides.body: A type declares conformance by listing the protocol name after a colon in its declaration, and must implement every requirement the protocol specifies, or the compiler reports an error. Protocol requirements can include instance methods, static methods, instance and static properties (with required get or get/set), and initialisers.

slides.title: Protocols as types
slides.body: A protocol can be used as a type itself -- a function parameter, variable, or array element typed as any Drawable can hold any concrete instance that conforms, letting you write code against the abstraction rather than a specific concrete type. This is what enables polymorphism without inheritance.

slides.title: Protocol inheritance and composition
slides.body: A protocol can inherit requirements from one or more other protocols, and a type can be required to conform to several protocols at once by combining them with &, such as some Codable & Equatable. This lets you compose small, focused protocols into exactly the capability a given function needs.

quiz.prompt: What must a type do to conform to a protocol?

options.text: Mark itself final
Only implement the requirements it wants
Subclass the protocol
Implement every requirement the protocol declares

quiz.explanation: Protocol conformance is all-or-nothing: the compiler requires the conforming type to implement every method, property, and initialiser the protocol declares.

slides.title: Protocol extensions and default implementations
slides.body: An extension on a protocol can provide a default implementation for one or more of its requirements, which every conforming type automatically gets for free unless it chooses to override that implementation itself. This lets you share behavior across unrelated types without needing a common base class.

slides.title: Retroactively extending existing types
slides.body: You can make an existing type -- even one from a library or the standard library that you didn't author, like Int or Array -- conform to a protocol you defined, by writing an extension on that type. This is how protocol-oriented programming lets you add capabilities to types you don't own, something class inheritance can't do.

slides.title: Protocol-oriented vs object-oriented thinking
slides.body: Where object-oriented design often starts by asking 'what class should this inherit from,' protocol-oriented design asks 'what capabilities does this type need,' and composes those capabilities from small, focused protocols. This avoids the fragile, deep inheritance hierarchies that make later changes risky and encourages reusable, independently testable pieces.

slides.title: Default implementations with constraints
slides.body: A protocol extension's default implementation can be constrained with a where clause so it only applies when a conforming type also satisfies extra requirements, like conforming to Equatable or having a particular associated type. This lets a protocol offer smarter defaults for types that happen to have more capability, without forcing every conformer to have it.

quiz.explanation: Protocol extensions let you supply a default implementation that conforming types inherit for free, while still allowing any specific type to override it with its own.

quiz.prompt: How can you add new functionality to a type you don't own, like Int or Array?

quiz.explanation: Swift extensions let you retroactively add conformances and methods to any existing type, including ones you don't own the source of, which class inheritance cannot do for structs like Array.

quiz.explanation: A conforming type's own implementation overrides the protocol extension's default; the default only applies when the type doesn't supply its own.

slides.title: Why generics exist
slides.body: Generics let you write a function or type that works with any type satisfying certain constraints, instead of duplicating the same logic for Int, String, and every other type separately. A generic function like func swapValues<T>(_ a: inout T, _ b: inout T) works identically for any T, with the concrete type filled in at each call site.

slides.title: Type parameters and constraints
slides.body: A generic type parameter can be constrained to require conformance to a protocol, such as <T: Equatable>, which lets the generic code use operations that protocol guarantees, like ==, while still working with any concrete type that conforms. Without a constraint, only operations common to every possible type -- like assignment -- are available.

slides.title: Associated types in protocols
slides.body: A protocol can declare an associated type as a placeholder for a type that's only decided when a concrete type conforms, written with associatedtype. Swift's own Collection and Sequence protocols use this heavily -- Element is an associated type, so Array<Int>'s Element is Int while Array<String>'s Element is String, without Collection itself needing to know.

slides.title: Generic types and opaque types
slides.body: A generic type like Stack<Element> can hold any single Element type consistently across an instance, giving compile-time type safety without runtime overhead from type-erasure. some Protocol (an opaque return type) lets a function return 'a specific but unspecified type that conforms to a protocol,' preserving type information the caller can use, unlike returning the protocol as any Protocol.

quiz.explanation: Generics abstract over the concrete type, so a single function or type definition can serve Int, String, or any other type that satisfies its constraints.

quiz.explanation: Without the Equatable constraint, the compiler wouldn't know that == is available for an arbitrary T, since not every type supports equality comparison.

slides.title: The problem with deep inheritance
slides.body: Deep class hierarchies tend to become fragile: a change to a base class can ripple unpredictably through every subclass, and a subclass often ends up inheriting methods or properties it doesn't actually want, just because they happened to live on a shared ancestor. This is sometimes called the 'fragile base class' problem.

slides.title: Composing behavior instead of inheriting it
slides.body: Composition means building a type out of smaller, independent pieces -- either as stored properties that are themselves objects with their own responsibility, or as protocol conformances providing focused capabilities -- rather than inheriting a large, general-purpose base class. Each piece can be developed, tested, and reused independently of the whole.

slides.title: Has-a vs is-a relationships
slides.body: Inheritance models an 'is-a' relationship (a Car is a Vehicle), which is appropriate when the subtype really is a more specific version of the supertype and should be substitutable everywhere the supertype is used. Composition models a 'has-a' relationship (a Car has an Engine), which is usually the better fit when you just want to reuse a piece of behavior without inheriting its full identity.

slides.title: Using protocols to compose capabilities
slides.body: Rather than a UserProfile class inheriting from a big Persistable base class, it can instead conform to a small Persistable protocol alongside other focused protocols like Cacheable, mixing in exactly the capabilities it needs. Because protocol conformance isn't limited to a single 'parent,' a type can compose as many independent capabilities as it needs without the single-inheritance ceiling classes impose.

quiz.explanation: Deep inheritance hierarchies couple subclasses tightly to their ancestors' implementation details, so a seemingly safe change to the base class can ripple into subtle breakage in far-away subclasses.

quiz.explanation: Inheritance fits best when the Liskov substitution principle holds -- the subclass genuinely is a specialized version of the base class and can stand in for it everywhere.

slides.title: Custom Error types
slides.body: Any type conforming to the Error protocol can be thrown; in practice this is almost always an enum, since its cases naturally enumerate the distinct failure modes a function can produce, optionally with associated values carrying extra context like an underlying error or a failing value.

slides.title: Propagating and handling errors across calls
slides.body: A function that calls a throwing function with try and doesn't handle the error itself must be marked throws too, letting the error propagate up the call stack until something catches it with do/catch. This makes error propagation explicit and visible in every function signature along the chain, unlike unchecked exceptions in some other languages.

slides.title: Typed throws
slides.body: Since Swift 6, a function can declare exactly which error type it throws with throws(SpecificError) instead of the general throws (which is really throws(any Error)). This lets callers exhaustively switch over the specific error cases in a catch block without needing a catch-all, and documents the failure surface precisely in the function's signature.

slides.title: Choosing between throws, Result, and optionals
slides.body: Use throws for operations that can fail for one of several distinct reasons and where the caller needs to react differently to each; use Result when the outcome needs to be stored as a value or delivered asynchronously via a closure; use a plain optional when the only information needed is whether something succeeded, with no detail about why it failed.

slides.title: Model-View-Controller in UIKit
slides.body: MVC splits an app into Models (data and business logic), Views (UI elements), and Controllers (which mediate between them, responding to user input and updating the view). In practice, UIKit view controllers often end up doing far more than mediation -- networking, formatting, layout, and state -- earning the nickname 'Massive View Controller.'

slides.title: Model-View-ViewModel
slides.body: MVVM introduces a ViewModel between the Model and the View: the ViewModel holds presentation state and logic (like formatting a date for display, or exposing a loading flag) and the View binds to it, observing changes and rendering accordingly, without the View needing to know how that state was derived. The Model stays unaware of both the View and ViewModel.

slides.title: Why MVVM fits SwiftUI naturally
slides.body: SwiftUI views are already declarative descriptions of UI given some state, so pairing them with an Observable ViewModel that publishes that state is a very natural fit: the view simply re-renders whenever the ViewModel's observed properties change, with no manual update calls needed. This is a big part of why MVVM (or similar state-driven patterns) has become the default pattern for SwiftUI apps.

slides.title: Where responsibilities live in each pattern
slides.body: In MVC, formatting logic and UI update calls are often written directly in the controller alongside networking and layout code, making the controller hard to unit test in isolation. In MVVM, that same formatting and state logic moves into the ViewModel, which has no dependency on UIKit or SwiftUI types, so it can be unit tested directly without instantiating any UI at all.

quiz.explanation: Because MVC doesn't provide a clear home for presentation logic, that logic tends to pile up in the controller, growing it far beyond its intended mediating role.

quiz.explanation: SwiftUI's declarative, state-driven rendering model maps naturally onto an Observable ViewModel exposing the state a view needs, though other patterns are technically possible too.

slides.title: What separation of concerns means
slides.body: Separation of concerns means dividing a program into distinct sections, each responsible for one specific aspect of the functionality -- such as networking, persistence, business rules, or presentation -- so that a change to one concern doesn't ripple into unrelated ones. It's a foundational design principle behind most architecture patterns, including MVC and MVVM.

slides.title: Symptoms of poor separation
slides.body: Warning signs include a single type that parses JSON, makes network calls, formats dates for display, and updates UI state all in one place; changing how data is displayed forcing you to touch networking code; or being unable to test business logic without mocking an entire UI framework.

slides.title: Extracting a networking layer
slides.body: A dedicated networking type (or a small set of them) is responsible only for making requests and decoding raw responses into model types -- it shouldn't know anything about how that data will be displayed, cached, or formatted. Other parts of the app depend on this layer through a narrow, protocol-defined interface rather than reaching into its implementation details.

slides.title: Layering: data, domain, and presentation
slides.body: A common layering splits an app into a data layer (networking, persistence), a domain layer (business rules and models, independent of how data is fetched or displayed), and a presentation layer (view models and views). Each layer only talks to the layer directly below it, typically through protocols, which lets you swap an implementation -- like replacing a REST API with a local cache -- without touching the layers above it.

quiz.explanation: Separation of concerns groups related responsibilities together and keeps unrelated ones apart, so a change to one aspect doesn't require touching unrelated code.

quiz.explanation: Mixing unrelated responsibilities like networking, parsing, and UI formatting into one type is a classic sign that concerns haven't been separated.

quiz.explanation: When concerns are separated, logic that doesn't depend on the UI or network can be exercised directly in a unit test, without setting up the rest of the system.

slides.title: What dependency injection is
slides.body: Dependency injection (DI) means a type receives the objects it depends on from the outside -- typically through its initialiser or a property -- rather than creating them itself internally. Instead of a ViewModel doing let service = NetworkService() inside itself, it accepts a NetworkService (or a protocol) as an initialiser parameter.

slides.title: Why DI improves testability
slides.body: When a dependency is injected as a protocol, a test can pass in a fake or mock implementation instead of the real one -- letting you simulate a network failure, a slow response, or specific data, without making an actual network call. Without DI, a type's dependencies are hard-coded and effectively untestable in isolation.

slides.title: Initialiser injection vs property injection
slides.body: Initialiser injection passes dependencies as parameters to init, guaranteeing the object is never in an invalid state without them -- this is generally preferred. Property injection sets a dependency after construction via a settable property, which is sometimes necessary but leaves a window where the object exists without its dependency set.

slides.title: Composition root
slides.body: A composition root is the single place in an app -- often near the app's entry point -- where concrete dependencies are actually constructed and wired together into the object graph, such as creating the real NetworkService and passing it into a ViewModel's initialiser. Keeping this wiring in one place means the rest of the app's code only ever depends on protocols, never on concrete construction.

slides.title: The role of a view model
slides.body: A view model exposes the state a view needs to render, in a form the view can consume directly, and the logic to update that state in response to user actions or new data -- without knowing anything about SwiftUI or UIKit itself. It sits between the view and the domain/data layer, translating raw model data into presentation-ready state.

slides.title: Keeping view models UI-framework-agnostic
slides.body: A well-designed view model doesn't import SwiftUI or UIKit and has no reference to a specific View instance; it exposes plain Swift properties (Strings, Bools, Ints, arrays of simple structs) that a view binds to. This separation is what makes a view model reusable across different view implementations and directly unit-testable.

slides.title: View models and single responsibility
slides.body: A view model should correspond to a single screen or a cohesive piece of one, exposing exactly the state and actions that screen needs -- not a shared 'god' view model reused across unrelated screens. When a view model starts accumulating unrelated state for multiple screens, it's usually a sign it should be split.

slides.title: Actions and one-way data flow
slides.body: A view calls methods on its view model (like viewModel.search() or viewModel.toggleFavorite(item)) in response to user interaction; the view model updates its state; the view re-renders. Data flows in one direction -- from state down to the view, and from user actions up as method calls -- which keeps the relationship predictable compared to two systems mutating shared state from multiple directions.

quiz.prompt: What should a well-designed view model expose to its view?

options.text: Direct references to UIKit or SwiftUI view instances
Raw, unparsed network responses
Presentation-ready state and actions, in plain Swift types the view can consume directly
Nothing -- views should read the model directly

quiz.explanation: A view model translates domain/model data into state a view can render directly (Strings, Bools, simple structs) and exposes methods for the view to call in response to user actions.

quiz.prompt: Why does a view model typically avoid importing SwiftUI or UIKit?

options.text: To stay reusable and directly unit-testable without needing to instantiate any UI framework types
Because Swift doesn't allow importing UI frameworks outside of Views
It's a hard technical requirement, not a design choice
Because view models can't have properties

quiz.explanation: Keeping the view model UI-framework-agnostic means its logic can be tested and reused without any dependency on how it's eventually rendered.

quiz.prompt: What's a sign that a view model has taken on too much responsibility?

options.text: It's marked @Observable
It has an isLoading property
It exposes state for exactly one screen
It has grown to hold unrelated state and logic for multiple, unrelated screens

quiz.explanation: A 'god' view model juggling unrelated screens' concerns violates single responsibility and should typically be split into one view model per cohesive screen.

quiz.prompt: In the typical view/view-model relationship, how does the view trigger a change in state?

options.text: It mutates the view model's private storage directly
State changes happen automatically with no code
It calls a method (an action) on the view model, which updates its own state
The view model polls the view for changes

quiz.explanation: The view calls an action method exposed by the view model in response to user interaction; the view model then updates its own published state, which the view observes and re-renders from.

quiz.prompt: Why is one-way data flow (state down, actions up) considered easier to reason about than having multiple objects mutate shared state directly?

options.text: One-way data flow means the UI never updates
It isn't -- two-way binding is always simpler
It only applies to UIKit, not SwiftUI
It creates a single, predictable path for how state changes, instead of state being modified unpredictably from many places

quiz.explanation: When updates only flow one direction, you can reason about a state change by looking at the single action that triggered it, rather than tracking multiple places that might be mutating the same state.

slides.title: Imperative vs declarative navigation
slides.body: UIKit navigation is imperative: you call navigationController?.pushViewController(_:animated:) to move forward and popViewController to go back, directly commanding a transition to happen. SwiftUI's NavigationStack is declarative: navigation is driven by state -- a path (an array of values) that describes what should be on the stack -- and the framework figures out which transitions to animate.

slides.title: NavigationStack and path-based navigation
slides.body: NavigationStack(path:) binds to a collection (commonly an array or a NavigationPath) representing the current navigation stack; appending a value pushes a new screen, and removing values pops. Because the stack is just state, you can programmatically pop to the root by clearing the array, or restore a deep multi-screen stack by setting it all at once -- for example after a deep link.

slides.title: Modal presentation: sheets and full-screen covers
slides.body: Sheets (.sheet(isPresented:) or .sheet(item:)) and full-screen covers present content on top of the current view rather than pushing it onto a navigation stack, and are typically used for self-contained tasks like composing a new item or onboarding, rather than for drilling deeper into a hierarchy of related content.

slides.title: Coordinators and centralizing navigation logic
slides.body: As an app grows, deciding 'which screen comes next' directly inside view code tends to scatter navigation logic across many views and couples them tightly to specific destinations. A coordinator (or a router/navigation view model) centralizes that decision-making in one place, exposing a navigation path or similar state that views update by calling methods, keeping the views themselves simpler and more reusable.

quiz.prompt: What's the key difference between UIKit's navigation approach and SwiftUI's NavigationStack?

options.text: UIKit navigation is imperative (you command pushes/pops); SwiftUI's is declarative, driven by a state value representing the stack
UIKit navigation doesn't support back buttons
They are functionally identical
SwiftUI navigation can't be programmatic

quiz.explanation: UIKit requires explicitly calling push/pop methods, while NavigationStack derives its displayed stack from a bound state value, so changing that state changes the navigation.

quiz.prompt: How do you programmatically pop a NavigationStack all the way back to its root?

options.text: Call navigationController?.popToRootViewController()
Clear (remove all elements from) the array or NavigationPath bound to the stack's path
It's not possible in SwiftUI
Restart the app

quiz.explanation: Since the stack is driven by its bound path state, emptying that collection removes every pushed screen, returning to the root.

quiz.prompt: When is a sheet typically preferred over pushing onto a NavigationStack?

options.text: For a self-contained task, like composing a new item, that isn't part of the current navigational hierarchy
For drilling deeper into a hierarchy of closely related content
Sheets and pushes are interchangeable with no difference
Sheets can only show a single line of text

quiz.explanation: Sheets present content as a distinct, often temporary task layered on top of the current context, whereas pushes represent moving deeper into a related hierarchy of screens.

quiz.prompt: What problem does a coordinator (or router) pattern address?

options.text: It centralizes 'what screen comes next' logic in one place instead of scattering it across many views
It makes every view responsible for deciding all possible navigation destinations
It removes the need for any navigation state
It only works with UIKit, not SwiftUI

quiz.explanation: Without a coordinator, decisions about which destination to navigate to tend to get embedded directly in view code across the app; a coordinator centralizes that logic, keeping views simpler.

quiz.prompt: In NavigationStack(path: $path) with .navigationDestination(for: Destination.self), what triggers pushing a new screen?

options.text: Setting isPresented to true
Nothing -- screens push automatically on a timer
Appending a matching Destination value to the path array
Calling a UIKit push method

quiz.explanation: navigationDestination maps values of a given type appearing in the path to the view that should be pushed for them, so appending a Destination to path pushes its corresponding screen.

slides.title: Organizing by feature vs by type
slides.body: Organizing 'by type' groups files into folders like Views, ViewModels, and Models across the whole app, while organizing 'by feature' groups everything related to one feature -- its view, view model, and models -- together in a single folder. Feature-based organization tends to scale better because working on a feature touches one folder instead of jumping between several parallel type-based folders.

slides.title: A typical feature folder
slides.body: A feature folder for, say, 'Profile' might contain ProfileView.swift, ProfileViewModel.swift, and any Profile-specific model or subview files, all colocated. Code shared across many features -- common UI components, networking utilities, extensions -- lives in a separate shared location instead of being duplicated per feature.
slides.example:
Profile/
  ProfileView.swift
  ProfileViewModel.swift
  ProfileHeaderView.swift
Search/
  SearchView.swift
  SearchViewModel.swift
Shared/
  NetworkService.swift
  DateFormatting.swift

slides.title: Why modularity matters as an app grows
slides.body: Modularity means keeping the boundaries between parts of a codebase explicit and minimizing how much one part needs to know about another's internals. This keeps build times more manageable (changing one module doesn't necessarily force a full rebuild of unrelated ones), makes ownership clearer on a team, and reduces the chance that unrelated features accidentally become tangled together.

slides.title: Access control as a modularity tool
slides.body: Within a single app target, Swift's access control (private, fileprivate, internal, public) lets you deliberately hide implementation details, exposing only the interface a feature's consumers actually need. Marking a ViewModel's internal helper methods private prevents other code from accidentally depending on details that might change, even before you've split anything into separate Swift packages or frameworks.

quiz.prompt: What's the main advantage of organizing project files by feature rather than by type?

options.text: Working on a feature stays contained to one folder, rather than jumping across several parallel type-based folders
It's required by Xcode
It removes the need for a Models layer
It requires fewer files overall

quiz.explanation: Feature-based folders colocate everything related to one piece of functionality, so changes to that feature don't require navigating scattered, parallel folders like Views/, ViewModels/, and Models/.

quiz.prompt: Where should code shared across many features, like a NetworkService, typically live?

options.text: Deleted, since sharing code isn't possible in Swift
Inside the AppDelegate only
Duplicated inside every feature folder that uses it
In a separate shared location, referenced by the features that need it

quiz.explanation: Truly shared utilities belong in a common location so there's a single source of truth, rather than being copy-pasted into each feature that needs them.

quiz.prompt: What does 'modularity' primarily refer to in app architecture?

options.text: Using as many third-party libraries as possible
Keeping boundaries between parts of a codebase explicit, minimizing how much one part depends on another's internals
Avoiding the use of protocols
Writing all code in a single file

quiz.explanation: Modularity is about clear, minimal-coupling boundaries between components, which improves build times, ownership clarity, and reduces accidental entanglement.

quiz.prompt: How does marking a ViewModel's helper method private support modularity, even within a single app target?

options.text: It's required for all methods in Swift
It hides an implementation detail so other code can't accidentally depend on it, keeping the type's public interface intentional
It prevents the method from ever being called
It has no effect -- private is purely stylistic

quiz.explanation: Access control lets you deliberately narrow what's visible outside a type, so consumers only see and depend on the interface you intend to expose, not incidental internal details.

quiz.prompt: As an app grows, what's a practical benefit of modular boundaries between components?

options.text: It automatically improves UI performance
It guarantees zero bugs
It removes the need for tests
Build times can be more manageable since changing one module doesn't necessarily require rebuilding unrelated ones, and team ownership is clearer

quiz.explanation: Clear module boundaries can limit the scope of rebuilds triggered by a change and make it clearer which team or person owns which part of the codebase.

quiz.prompt: What is the 'Massive View Controller' problem?

options.text: A bug specific to storyboards
A SwiftUI-only issue
A view controller in MVC accumulating responsibilities beyond simple mediation, like networking and formatting
Too many separate view controllers in a project

quiz.explanation: MVC provides no clear home for presentation logic, so it tends to accumulate directly in the view controller.

ViewModels can't have properties otherwise
It's a hard technical restriction

quiz.prompt: What does separation of concerns aim to prevent?

options.text: Having more than one file in a project
Unrelated responsibilities (like networking and UI formatting) being tangled together in one place
Writing tests
Using protocols

quiz.explanation: It keeps each part of a program responsible for one aspect of functionality, avoiding tangled, hard-to-change code.

quiz.prompt: What is dependency injection?

options.text: Storing dependencies in global mutable state only
A SwiftUI-specific concept with no other uses
A type receiving its dependencies from outside, often via its initialiser
A type constructing all its own dependencies

quiz.explanation: DI hands a type its collaborators from outside rather than having it construct them internally.

quiz.prompt: Why does injecting a protocol-typed dependency help with testing?

options.text: Protocols can't be used as parameter types
It removes the need to write any test code
It doesn't; concrete types are always required for tests

quiz.prompt: What state does NavigationStack use to determine what's currently pushed?

options.text: A hidden internal counter with no way to observe it
A bound path value (like an array or NavigationPath) that the app can read and modify
UIKit's navigation controller stack
It always mirrors the app's launch screen

options.text: It's required for every SwiftUI app
It centralizes 'what screen comes next' decisions instead of scattering that logic across many views
It removes all navigation from the app
