quiz.prompt: In one-way data flow (state down, actions up), how does a view typically change application state?

options.text: By calling an action method on the view model, which then updates its own state
By mutating the view model's private storage directly from the view
State can't be changed from the view
By modifying the Model layer directly

quiz.explanation: The view calls an action method on the view model in response to user interaction, and the view model updates its own state accordingly.

slides.title: What ARC tracks
slides.body: Automatic Reference Counting (ARC) manages the memory of class instances by keeping a count of how many strong references currently point to each instance. Every time a strong reference is assigned, the count increments; every time one goes out of scope or is set to nil, the count decrements.

slides.title: Deallocation when the count hits zero
slides.body: When an instance's strong reference count drops to zero -- meaning nothing strongly references it anymore -- ARC immediately deallocates it, freeing its memory and calling its deinit if one is defined. This happens deterministically and synchronously, unlike garbage collection, which runs periodically and asynchronously.

slides.title: ARC only applies to reference types
slides.body: ARC manages the memory of class instances (and closures, which are reference types under the hood) because they live on the heap and can be shared across multiple owners. Struct and enum instances are value types stored directly wherever they're used and don't participate in reference counting at all -- copying one copies its data, not a reference count.

slides.title: Compile-time insertion, not a runtime scanner
slides.body: ARC's retain and release calls are inserted by the compiler at build time based on static analysis of your code's ownership, not computed by a scanning garbage collector at runtime. This is why ARC has predictable, low overhead compared to tracing garbage collectors, but also why it can't detect cycles automatically -- it only counts references, it doesn't reason about whether those references form a cycle nothing external can reach.

quiz.prompt: What does ARC's reference count for a class instance represent?

options.text: The number of methods the class defines
The number of strong references currently pointing to that instance
The instance's memory address
The number of times the instance has been mutated

quiz.explanation: ARC increments the count each time a new strong reference is made to an instance and decrements it when a strong reference is removed or goes out of scope.

quiz.prompt: When does ARC deallocate a class instance?

options.text: At a fixed interval, like a garbage collector
Only when the app terminates
Only when deinit is explicitly called by the developer
Immediately when its strong reference count drops to zero

quiz.explanation: ARC deallocates an instance as soon as no strong references to it remain, deterministically and synchronously, calling its deinit if defined.

quiz.prompt: Why don't struct instances participate in ARC's reference counting?

options.text: Structs always live only inside classes
ARC applies equally to structs and classes
Structs are value types; they're copied rather than referenced, so there's no shared instance to count references to
Structs can't be stored in memory

quiz.explanation: ARC tracks references to a single shared instance; because assigning a struct copies its value instead of sharing a reference, there's nothing for a reference count to track.

quiz.prompt: How does ARC insert its retain/release calls?

options.text: ARC only runs when the app receives a memory warning
A background garbage collector scans memory periodically at runtime
The developer must call retain() and release() manually
The compiler inserts them at build time based on static analysis of ownership

quiz.explanation: Unlike tracing garbage collection, ARC's retain/release logic is determined and inserted by the compiler ahead of time, giving predictable overhead at the cost of not being able to detect reference cycles automatically.

quiz.prompt: Why can't ARC automatically detect and break a reference cycle (two objects strongly referencing each other)?

options.text: ARC always breaks cycles automatically using weak references
ARC only counts references; it doesn't analyze whether those references form an unreachable cycle
Reference cycles are impossible in Swift
Cycles are only a problem for structs

quiz.explanation: ARC's model is purely counting: as long as each object in a cycle has a nonzero strong reference count from the other, neither will ever be deallocated, even though nothing outside the cycle can reach them.

slides.title: Strong references: the default
slides.body: A regular reference to a class instance -- a plain var or let of that class type -- is a strong reference by default, meaning it contributes to keeping that instance alive by incrementing its reference count. Most references in a well-structured app are, and should be, strong; the exceptions are deliberate.

slides.title: weak references
slides.body: A weak reference doesn't increment the reference count, and it's automatically set to nil by the runtime when the instance it points to is deallocated -- which is why a weak reference must always be declared as an optional (weak var delegate: SomeDelegate?). This makes it the safe choice whenever the referenced instance might be deallocated while you're still holding a reference to it.

slides.title: unowned references
slides.body: An unowned reference also doesn't increment the reference count, but unlike weak it's not optional and isn't automatically nilled out -- if you access an unowned reference after its instance has been deallocated, the app crashes. Use unowned only when you can guarantee the referenced instance will always outlive (or have exactly the same lifetime as) the reference itself.

slides.title: Choosing between weak and unowned
slides.body: Choose weak when the reference could legitimately become nil during the referencing object's lifetime (like a delegate that might be deallocated first, or an optional back-reference) -- it's the safer default. Choose unowned only when you're certain, by the design of the relationship, that the referenced object can never be deallocated before the reference is used, since getting this wrong crashes the app rather than producing a safe nil.

quiz.prompt: What kind of reference is created by default when you write `var delegate: SomeClass`?

options.text: None -- you must specify a reference type
strong
unowned
weak

quiz.explanation: A plain reference to a class instance is strong by default in Swift, contributing to the instance's reference count unless explicitly marked weak or unowned.

quiz.prompt: Why must a weak reference always be declared as an optional?

options.text: Weak references can't be initialized with a value
Because the runtime automatically sets a weak reference to nil once its instance is deallocated
Swift requires all class references to be optional
It's just a stylistic convention with no technical reason

quiz.explanation: Since a weak reference can become nil at any point (when the instance it points to is deallocated), it must be an optional type to represent that possibility.

quiz.prompt: What happens if you access an unowned reference after the instance it pointed to has already been deallocated?

options.text: It returns the last known value
It safely returns nil
The app crashes with a runtime error
Nothing -- unowned references can't be invalidated

quiz.explanation: Unlike weak, unowned doesn't automatically become nil and isn't optional, so accessing it after deallocation is undefined and typically crashes.

quiz.prompt: When is unowned an appropriate choice over weak?

options.text: When you can guarantee the referenced instance will never be deallocated before the reference is used
Whenever you want to avoid using optionals
Whenever the referenced object might already be gone
unowned should always be preferred over weak for performance

quiz.explanation: unowned trades the safety of an automatic nil for the convenience of a non-optional value, which is only appropriate when the relationship guarantees the referenced instance outlives the reference.

quiz.prompt: Does a weak reference increment the reference count of the instance it refers to?

options.text: Only during debug builds
Only if the instance conforms to Codable
Yes, exactly like a strong reference
No -- weak references don't contribute to the reference count at all

quiz.explanation: Both weak and unowned references are non-owning: they don't increase the strong reference count, so they don't keep the referenced instance alive by themselves.

slides.title: How a closure can retain self
slides.body: A closure captures the variables and objects it references from its surrounding scope, and by default those captures are strong. If a class stores a closure as a property, and that closure references self (say, to call one of its methods), the closure holds a strong reference to self -- and if self also strongly holds the closure, you get a cycle.

slides.title: A classic cycle: a stored completion handler
slides.body: A common source of retain cycles is a class storing a closure property that captures self strongly, especially completion handlers or callbacks kept around for later use. Here, self owns onComplete, and onComplete captures self strongly, so neither can ever be deallocated even after both should logically be gone.

slides.title: Breaking the cycle with a capture list
slides.body: A capture list at the start of a closure -- { [weak self] in ... } -- tells the closure to capture self weakly instead of strongly, breaking the strong reference in that direction. Because self is now optional inside the closure, you typically unwrap it with guard let self else { return } or self?.method().

slides.title: When weak self isn't actually necessary
slides.body: Not every closure that references self needs [weak self] -- a short-lived, non-escaping closure passed directly to something like Array.map or DispatchQueue.main.async doesn't create a lasting cycle, because the closure itself is discarded once it runs and isn't retained as a stored property. The cycle only matters when the closure is stored somewhere that keeps it alive alongside self.

quiz.prompt: Why can a class storing a closure that captures self strongly create a retain cycle?

options.text: Closures are always weak by default
Retain cycles only happen with structs
The closure holds self strongly, and if self also holds the closure (e.g. as a stored property), each keeps the other alive
Closures can never capture self

quiz.explanation: If self owns the closure and the closure captures self strongly, neither's reference count can ever reach zero, since each is kept alive by the other.

quiz.prompt: What does adding [weak self] to a closure's capture list do?

options.text: It prevents the closure from ever accessing self
It converts the closure into a non-escaping closure
It makes self immutable inside the closure
It captures self as a weak reference, so it doesn't increment self's reference count and becomes nil if self is deallocated

quiz.explanation: [weak self] breaks the strong capture, letting self be deallocated even while the closure exists, at the cost of self being optional inside the closure body.

quiz.prompt: After using [weak self], why is `guard let self else { return }` commonly used at the top of the closure?

options.text: It's required syntax with no functional purpose
Because self is now optional inside the closure, and this safely unwraps it (or exits if it's already been deallocated)
It converts self back into a strong reference permanently
It prevents the closure from capturing any other variables

quiz.explanation: Since weak self can become nil, guard-unwrapping it gives you a non-optional self to work with for the rest of the closure, safely bailing out if the instance is already gone.

quiz.prompt: Does every closure that references self need [weak self] to avoid a retain cycle?

options.text: No -- only closures that are stored (e.g. as a property) alongside self, creating a genuine cycle, need it; short-lived closures that aren't retained don't
Only closures passed to network calls need it
No closure ever needs it
Yes, always, with no exceptions

quiz.explanation: A cycle requires both directions of strong reference to persist; a closure that runs and is discarded (not stored as a property that self also owns) doesn't create a lasting cycle even if it references self.

quiz.prompt: In the Downloader example, which two objects hold strong references to each other before the fix?

options.text: Two separate Downloader instances
The Downloader instance (via its onComplete property) and the closure (via its capture of self)
The closure and DispatchQueue.main
The Downloader and its deinit method

quiz.explanation: self.onComplete strongly holds the closure, and the closure's capture of self is strong by default, forming a cycle between the instance and the closure it stores.

slides.title: The delegate pattern's reference shape
slides.body: In the delegate pattern, one object (say, a custom view) holds a reference to another object (its delegate) that it calls back to report events. If that reference were strong, and the delegate also holds a strong reference back to the view (which it very often does, since it typically owns the view), you'd get a two-object retain cycle.

slides.title: Why delegate properties are conventionally weak
slides.body: By convention, a delegate property is declared weak var delegate: SomeDelegate?, so the delegating object doesn't keep its delegate alive. This matches the typical ownership direction in UIKit and custom component design: the delegate (often a view controller) owns the component, not the other way around, so the component shouldn't extend the delegate's lifetime.

slides.title: AnyObject-constrained protocols
slides.body: A delegate protocol is typically constrained to AnyObject (protocol ChatViewDelegate: AnyObject), which restricts conformance to class types. This is required because weak can only apply to reference types -- you can't have a weak reference to a struct, since structs don't have the notion of a shared instance to grow stale.

slides.title: What happens if delegate is accidentally strong
slides.body: If a delegate property is declared as a plain strong reference instead of weak, and the owning object (say, a view controller) also strongly holds the component whose delegate it is, the two objects keep each other alive indefinitely, leaking both even after the view controller should have been dismissed and deallocated. This is one of the most common real-world retain cycle bugs, and is exactly why the weak convention exists.

quiz.prompt: Why is a delegate property conventionally declared weak?

options.text: To prevent the delegating object from keeping its delegate (which often owns it) alive, avoiding a retain cycle
It's required by Swift syntax for all protocol-typed properties
Delegates are always structs, so weak is required
weak properties are faster to access

quiz.explanation: Since the delegate (e.g. a view controller) commonly owns the object it delegates for, a strong delegate reference in the other direction would create a cycle keeping both alive indefinitely.

quiz.prompt: Why must a delegate protocol be constrained to AnyObject for its property to be declared weak?

options.text: weak works with structs too, so this isn't actually necessary
weak only works with reference types (classes), and AnyObject restricts conformance to class types
It's unrelated to weak; it's just a style convention
AnyObject makes the protocol faster

quiz.explanation: weak references rely on a reference-counted instance that can be deallocated and observed becoming nil, which only applies to class instances, hence the AnyObject constraint.

quiz.prompt: What happens if a delegate property is mistakenly declared as a strong reference in a scenario where the owning object also strongly holds the delegating component?

options.text: Nothing -- Swift automatically converts it to weak
Only the delegate gets deallocated correctly
Both objects keep each other alive, leaking memory since neither can be deallocated
It causes a compile-time error

quiz.explanation: A strong reference in both directions forms a retain cycle: each object's reference count never reaches zero because the other keeps holding it, so neither is ever deallocated.

quiz.prompt: In a typical UIKit-style delegate relationship, which object usually owns which?

options.text: The delegate (e.g. a view controller) usually owns the component it delegates for
Neither owns the other; delegates are always global singletons
The component always owns its delegate
Ownership is irrelevant to the delegate pattern

quiz.explanation: The owning direction typically runs from the view controller (delegate) to the component (like a custom view or table view), which is why the component's reference back to its delegate should be weak.

quiz.prompt: What is the delegate pattern used for?

options.text: Replacing the need for protocols
Storing an object's value-type data
Letting one object report events or ask for information from another object it holds a reference to, without owning that logic itself
Managing Swift's memory allocation directly

quiz.explanation: The delegate pattern lets an object (like a custom view) notify or query another object (its delegate) about events, without the delegating object needing to know the delegate's concrete type or implementation.

slides.title: Where value and reference types typically live
slides.body: Instances of value types (structs, enums) are typically stored inline wherever they're used -- inside a containing struct, on the stack for local variables, or inline within an array's buffer -- though the Swift compiler ultimately decides based on optimization. Class instances always live on the heap, with variables and properties holding a reference to that heap allocation.

slides.title: Copying costs: value vs reference types
slides.body: Copying a reference type is cheap regardless of the underlying object's size -- it just copies a pointer and bumps a reference count. Copying a value type copies its actual data, so a large struct could in principle be expensive to copy -- but Swift's copy-on-write optimization for Array, Dictionary, Set, and String means most everyday value type copies remain cheap until a mutation actually occurs.

slides.title: No ARC overhead for value types
slides.body: Because value types don't have shared identity, they aren't reference-counted by ARC at all -- there's no retain/release overhead for passing a plain Int, Double, or a struct composed purely of value types around. However, if a struct contains a class-typed property, that property itself is still ARC-managed, even though the struct as a whole is a value type.

slides.title: Practical implications for app memory
slides.body: Preferring value types for simple data models avoids retain-cycle risk entirely (there's no shared reference to hold onto in a cycle) and can reduce ARC's retain/release traffic in hot paths like collection iteration. Reference types remain necessary when you specifically need shared, mutable identity across multiple owners -- such as a shared cache, a delegate, or a long-lived service.

quiz.prompt: Where does an instance of a class type live in memory?

options.text: Inline wherever it's declared, like a struct
Always on the stack
In a special reference-only memory region inaccessible to ARC
On the heap, with variables holding a reference to it

quiz.explanation: Class instances are heap-allocated, and every variable or property referencing one holds a pointer to that heap allocation rather than the data itself.

quiz.prompt: Why does copying a large struct not necessarily copy its entire underlying buffer immediately?

options.text: Large structs are automatically converted to classes
Structs can't be copied in Swift
Swift ignores struct copies for performance reasons
Copy-on-write defers the actual buffer copy until one of the copies is mutated

quiz.explanation: Types like Array, Dictionary, Set, and String use copy-on-write, so assignment shares the underlying storage until a mutation forces an actual copy, keeping simple copies cheap.

quiz.prompt: Do plain value types (structs and enums composed only of other value types) incur ARC retain/release overhead?

options.text: Only during debug builds
Yes, exactly like class instances
Only if they conform to Codable
No -- ARC only manages reference-counted (class) instances, so pure value types have no retain/release overhead

quiz.explanation: ARC's job is tracking references to shared heap instances; a value type with no class-typed properties has nothing for ARC to track.

quiz.prompt: If a struct contains a property that is a class instance, does ARC still manage that property?

options.text: It depends on whether the struct is declared with let or var
Yes -- the class-typed property is still reference-counted by ARC, even though the struct itself has value semantics
Only if the struct conforms to AnyObject
No, being inside a struct exempts it from ARC

quiz.explanation: Value semantics apply to the struct's own identity, but any class instance it holds a reference to is still an independent, heap-allocated, ARC-managed object.

quiz.prompt: What's a practical benefit of preferring value types for simple data models, from a memory-management perspective?

options.text: They carry no shared reference for a retain cycle to form around, eliminating that entire class of bug
They eliminate the need for any memory management concepts
They guarantee better UI performance in every case
They automatically become weak references

quiz.explanation: Since value types don't have shared, reference-counted identity, there's no possibility of two value-type instances forming a strong reference cycle the way two class instances can.

slides.title: The Leaks and Allocations instruments
slides.body: Xcode's Instruments app includes the Leaks instrument, which detects memory that's become unreachable but was never deallocated (a true leak, usually from a retain cycle), and the Allocations instrument, which tracks every live allocation over time so you can watch an object count grow when it shouldn't. Allocations is often more useful day-to-day since it catches 'retained too long' bugs that aren't technically unreachable leaks.

slides.title: The Debug Memory Graph in Xcode
slides.body: Xcode's built-in Debug Memory Graph (the icon in the debug bar while running) pauses your app and shows every live object and the reference relationships between them, highlighting objects it suspects are leaked with a purple exclamation mark. Selecting a suspected leak shows exactly which references are keeping it alive, which is often enough to spot the cycle directly without launching Instruments.

slides.title: A practical technique: deinit logging
slides.body: Adding a deinit { print("X deallocated") } to a suspect class during development is a simple, direct way to confirm whether an instance is actually being deallocated when you expect it to be -- if you navigate away from a screen and never see its deinit log, something is still holding a strong reference to it.

slides.title: Common places to look first
slides.body: When investigating a suspected leak, check stored closures that capture self without [weak self], delegate properties that were accidentally declared strong instead of weak, and Timers or NotificationCenter observers that were never invalidated or removed -- a repeating Timer in particular strongly retains its target until explicitly invalidated, and is a very common leak source.

quiz.prompt: What does the Leaks instrument in Xcode's Instruments detect?

options.text: Network request failures
Memory that has become unreachable from your program but was never deallocated
CPU usage spikes
Every object ever allocated during the run

quiz.explanation: Leaks specifically flags memory that's no longer reachable by anything in the running app (typically due to a reference cycle) yet still hasn't been freed.

quiz.prompt: Why is the Allocations instrument often more useful day-to-day than Leaks?

options.text: Allocations is faster to run
It's the only instrument that works with Swift
Leaks only works with Objective-C code
It tracks every live allocation over time, catching objects that are technically reachable but retained far longer than expected, which Leaks wouldn't flag

quiz.explanation: A bug where an object is kept alive too long (but is still technically reachable, e.g. through a growing cache) isn't a 'leak' in the strict sense Leaks detects, but Allocations reveals it as an object count that keeps climbing.

quiz.prompt: What does Xcode's Debug Memory Graph show when you pause a running app?

options.text: Every live object and the reference relationships between them, flagging suspected leaks
Only CPU and battery usage
A list of all functions called so far
Network traffic only

quiz.explanation: The memory graph visualizes the live object graph and its references, marking objects it suspects are leaked so you can inspect exactly what's still referencing them.

quiz.prompt: Why is adding a `deinit { print(...) }` to a suspect class a useful debugging technique?

options.text: deinit runs on a timer regardless of deallocation
It directly confirms whether the instance is actually deallocated when expected -- if the log never appears, something still holds a strong reference to it
deinit only works in Instruments, not in normal runs
It automatically fixes any retain cycle

quiz.explanation: deinit is only called when ARC actually deallocates the instance, so seeing (or not seeing) the log is direct, immediate evidence about whether a suspected leak is real.

quiz.prompt: Why is a repeating Timer a common source of leaks?

options.text: A Timer strongly retains its target until it's explicitly invalidated, so a Timer referencing self keeps self alive indefinitely if never invalidated
Timers automatically create weak references
Timers are structs and can't be deallocated
Timers can only run once per app launch

quiz.explanation: A scheduled Timer holds a strong reference to its target (or captures self in its closure) and keeps firing and retaining it until invalidate() is called, which is easy to forget, especially when a screen is dismissed.

quiz.prompt: What does ARC's reference count for a class instance track?

options.text: Its memory address
The number of strong references currently pointing to it
The number of methods it defines
The number of protocols it conforms to

quiz.explanation: ARC increments the count on each strong reference and decrements it when one goes away, deallocating the instance once it reaches zero.

quiz.prompt: Why don't structs participate in ARC's reference counting?

options.text: They're too small
They're value types, copied rather than shared by reference
Structs can't be stored in variables
ARC applies equally to structs and classes

quiz.explanation: Since structs are copied on assignment rather than shared, there's no single shared instance for ARC to count references to.

quiz.prompt: What must a weak reference always be declared as?

options.text: A computed property
A static property
An optional
A non-optional constant

quiz.explanation: Because a weak reference can become nil when its instance is deallocated, it must be optional.

quiz.prompt: What happens when you access an unowned reference after its instance has been deallocated?

options.text: The app crashes
It automatically re-allocates the instance
It returns nil safely
It returns a default value

quiz.explanation: unowned doesn't automatically nil out and isn't optional, so accessing it after deallocation crashes the app.

quiz.prompt: How does [weak self] in a closure's capture list help prevent retain cycles?

options.text: It converts self into a struct
It prevents the closure from ever running
It captures self without incrementing its reference count, so self can be deallocated even while the closure exists
It deletes self entirely

quiz.explanation: Weak captures break the strong reference direction that would otherwise keep self alive as long as the closure exists.

quiz.prompt: Why is a delegate property conventionally declared weak?

options.text: Because Swift requires all protocol properties to be weak
weak is faster to access at runtime
To prevent the delegating object from keeping its (often owning) delegate alive, avoiding a cycle
Because delegates are always structs

quiz.explanation: Since the delegate commonly owns the delegating object, a strong reference back to it would create a retain cycle.

quiz.prompt: Copying a reference type is cheap because...

options.text: It copies the full object's data every time
It triggers copy-on-write like value types
It only copies a pointer and increments a reference count
Reference types can't be copied

quiz.explanation: Copying a class reference just duplicates the pointer and bumps the reference count, regardless of the underlying object's size.

quiz.prompt: What does Xcode's Debug Memory Graph show?

options.text: CPU temperature
Live objects and their reference relationships, flagging suspected leaks
Source code coverage
Only network requests

quiz.explanation: It visualizes the live object graph and highlights objects it suspects are leaked.

quiz.prompt: Why is a repeating Timer a common leak source?

options.text: Timers are automatically weak
A Timer strongly retains its target until explicitly invalidated
Timers are value types
Timers can only be created once

quiz.explanation: A Timer keeps a strong reference to its target (or captured closure state) until invalidate() is called, which is easy to forget.

quiz.prompt: What is a practical way to confirm whether an object is actually being deallocated when expected?

options.text: Mark it final
Check its access control level
Convert it to a struct
Add a deinit with a print statement and see if it fires

quiz.explanation: deinit only runs when ARC deallocates the instance, so a print inside it directly confirms whether deallocation actually happened.

slides.title: What @State is for
slides.body: @State marks a piece of value-type state that a SwiftUI view owns and manages internally -- like whether a toggle is on, or the text in a text field. SwiftUI stores the actual value outside the view struct itself, in storage tied to the view's identity, so the value survives across the view struct being recreated on every re-render.

slides.title: Why @State works with structs
slides.body: SwiftUI views are structs, which are recreated frequently (every time their body is re-evaluated), so a plain stored property would reset to its initial value every time. @State is a property wrapper that keeps the actual value in separate, persistent storage managed by SwiftUI, and the view struct just holds a lightweight reference to that storage.

slides.title: @State should be private and local
slides.body: Convention (and good practice) is to mark @State properties private, since this state is meant to belong to, and be managed entirely within, the view that declares it. If a child view needs to read or modify that same state, you pass a Binding to it rather than making the @State property itself accessible from outside.

slides.title: @State with value types beyond simple primitives
slides.body: @State isn't limited to Bool, Int, or String -- it works with any value type, including a whole struct holding several related fields, and SwiftUI will re-render the view whenever any part of that struct changes. This is often simpler than several separate @State properties when the fields are logically related, like a form's multiple text fields grouped into one struct.

quiz.prompt: Why can't a plain stored property (without @State) hold a view's mutable state correctly?

options.text: Plain properties can only hold reference types
Plain stored properties aren't allowed in structs
SwiftUI doesn't support stored properties at all
SwiftUI views are structs recreated on every re-render, so a plain property would reset to its initial value each time

quiz.explanation: Because the view struct itself is recreated whenever its body re-evaluates, @State's job is to keep the actual value in persistent, SwiftUI-managed storage outside the struct so it survives that recreation.

quiz.prompt: Why is it conventional to mark @State properties private?

options.text: private properties are faster
@State represents state a view owns and manages internally; private signals it shouldn't be accessed directly from outside
It's required by the Swift compiler for all @State
It prevents the property from ever changing

quiz.explanation: @State is meant to be the view's own internal state; exposing it directly to other views breaks that encapsulation, which is why a Binding is passed instead when sharing is needed.

quiz.prompt: Can @State be used with a whole struct containing multiple fields, not just simple types like Bool or String?

options.text: Yes -- @State works with any value type, and the view re-renders when any part of that struct changes
Only if the struct conforms to Codable
No, @State only works with primitives
Only inside UIKit view controllers

quiz.explanation: @State can wrap any value type, including a custom struct grouping related fields, and SwiftUI observes and reacts to changes in the whole value.

quiz.prompt: Where does SwiftUI actually store the value behind an @State property?

options.text: It's recomputed from scratch on every access
In separate, persistent storage tied to the view's identity, managed by SwiftUI outside the struct
In UserDefaults automatically
Inside the view struct itself, exactly like a normal stored property

quiz.explanation: The @State property wrapper keeps its underlying value in storage that SwiftUI manages independently of the view struct, which is what lets the value persist across the struct's frequent recreation.

quiz.prompt: In `Button("Count: \(count)") { count += 1 }` with `@State private var count = 0`, what triggers the view to re-render after the button is tapped?

options.text: The button re-renders only the app is restarted
Nothing automatic -- you must manually call a redraw method
count must be marked @Published for this to work
Mutating the @State property triggers SwiftUI to invalidate and re-render the view

quiz.explanation: @State is an observed source of truth for the view; mutating it automatically tells SwiftUI the view's body needs to be re-evaluated.

slides.title: What a Binding represents
slides.body: A Binding<Value> is a two-way connection to a piece of state owned somewhere else -- it lets a child view read the current value and write a new one, without owning the underlying storage itself. It's how a child view can both display and mutate state that actually lives in a parent.

slides.title: Creating a Binding with $
slides.body: The $ prefix on a property wrapper (like @State) produces a Binding to that property's underlying value, which you pass down to a child view that expects a Binding parameter. The child view declares its parameter with @Binding, and reading or writing through it reads or writes the original @State value in the parent.

slides.title: Bindings don't own the value
slides.body: A Binding is just a getter/setter pair pointing at someone else's storage -- it has no storage of its own. Mutating a Binding's wrappedValue doesn't create a new independent copy; it writes through to and changes the original source of truth wherever that binding was created from.

slides.title: When to use @Binding vs passing a plain value
slides.body: Pass a plain value (not a Binding) when a child view only needs to display data and never modify it -- this keeps the child's contract simpler and prevents it from accidentally mutating state it shouldn't own. Use @Binding specifically when the child needs to both read and write back to the parent's state, like a custom toggle, stepper, or text field component.

quiz.prompt: What does a Binding<Value> represent?

options.text: A closure that returns a value
An independent copy of a value
A two-way connection to state owned elsewhere, letting you read and write it without owning the storage
A read-only snapshot of a value

quiz.explanation: A Binding exposes get and set access to a value whose actual storage lives somewhere else (often an @State property in a parent view), letting a child read and mutate that same source of truth.

quiz.prompt: How do you create a Binding to pass to a child view, given `@State private var isOn = false` in the parent?

options.text: Pass $isOn
Pass Binding(isOn)
Bindings can't be created from @State
Pass isOn directly

quiz.explanation: The $ prefix on a property wrapper like @State produces a Binding to its underlying value, which is what a child's @Binding parameter expects.

quiz.prompt: If a child view mutates a @Binding's value, what happens?

options.text: It causes a compile error
It creates a new independent copy that doesn't affect the parent
It writes through to and changes the original value in the parent (or wherever the binding's storage actually lives)
It has no effect until the parent view is recreated

quiz.explanation: A Binding has no storage of its own -- it's a getter/setter pointing at the original source, so mutating it changes that original value directly.

quiz.prompt: When should a child view receive a plain value instead of a Binding?

options.text: When the child only needs to display the data and never needs to write back to it
Bindings should always be used instead of plain values
Whenever the child needs to modify the value
Plain values can never be passed to SwiftUI views

quiz.explanation: Passing a plain (non-Binding) value keeps a read-only child's contract simple and prevents it from being able to mutate state it doesn't own.

quiz.prompt: What does @Binding declare on a child view's property?

options.text: That the property must be a class instance
That the property holds its own persistent storage, like @State
That the property is a two-way connection to state owned by another view
That the property is read-only and can never change

quiz.explanation: @Binding marks a property as a pass-through connection to externally-owned state, rather than state the view itself stores and manages.

slides.title: The @Observable macro
slides.body: The @Observable macro (from Swift's Observation framework, available from iOS 17) makes a class's stored properties observable, so any SwiftUI view that reads one of those properties inside its body automatically re-renders when that specific property changes. Unlike the older ObservableObject approach, you don't need @Published on each property, and only the properties actually read by a given view trigger its re-render, not every change to the object.

slides.title: Using an @Observable class in a view
slides.body: A view holds a reference to an @Observable class (often via a plain let or @State if the view creates and owns it), and simply reads its properties directly in body -- no special property wrapper is needed on the reading side for that to work, because SwiftUI's rendering automatically tracks which properties were accessed.

slides.title: @Bindable for creating bindings to an observable object's properties
slides.body: When you need a Binding to a specific property of an @Observable object -- for example to pass $model.name to a TextField -- you mark the property holding that object @Bindable, which enables the $ syntax on its properties. Without @Bindable, you can still read and mutate the object's properties directly, but you can't derive a Binding from one of them.

slides.title: Why @Observable improved on ObservableObject
slides.body: The older ObservableObject/@Published pattern (pre-iOS 17) re-rendered any observing view whenever any @Published property changed, even ones the view never actually read, because the whole object published a single 'something changed' signal. @Observable instead tracks field-level access during body's evaluation, so a view that only reads model.count won't re-render when an unrelated model.name changes -- significantly reducing unnecessary re-renders.

quiz.prompt: What does the @Observable macro do to a class's properties?

options.text: Requires each property to be marked @Published
Makes them individually trackable, so views automatically re-render only when a property they actually read changes
Converts the class into a struct
Makes them immutable

quiz.explanation: @Observable enables per-property change tracking: SwiftUI notices exactly which properties a view's body reads and only re-renders that view when one of those specific properties changes.

quiz.prompt: Do you need @Published on each property of an @Observable class, the way you did with ObservableObject?

options.text: Yes, it's still required
Only for String properties
Only for computed properties
No -- @Observable makes all stored properties observable automatically without needing @Published

quiz.explanation: One of the key improvements of the Observation framework is that @Observable applies to the whole class's stored properties without needing a per-property @Published wrapper.

quiz.prompt: When is @Bindable needed on a property holding an @Observable object?

options.text: Only when the object is a struct
Always, any time you reference the object at all
@Bindable is never needed with @Observable
Specifically when you need to create a Binding to one of the object's properties, e.g. to pass to a TextField

quiz.explanation: @Bindable enables the $property syntax to derive a Binding from a specific field of an @Observable object; without it you can still read/write the property directly, just not create a Binding to it.

quiz.prompt: What was a key limitation of the older ObservableObject/@Published pattern that @Observable improves on?

options.text: ObservableObject only worked with Int properties
Any @Published change re-rendered every observing view, even ones that only read unrelated properties
ObservableObject required SwiftUI views to be classes
ObservableObject couldn't be used with classes at all

quiz.explanation: ObservableObject published one combined objectWillChange signal for any @Published property changing, so observing views re-rendered even for properties they never actually used, unlike @Observable's field-level tracking.

quiz.prompt: In `struct CounterView: View { @State private var model = CounterModel() ... }`, why is @State used here even though CounterModel is a class?

options.text: It's a mistake -- @State can't be used with classes
@State is required by the @Observable macro to compile
@State ensures the view keeps the same CounterModel instance alive across re-renders, rather than creating a new one every time body runs
@State makes CounterModel into a value type

quiz.explanation: Since the view struct is recreated on every re-render, @State is used to persist which single CounterModel instance the view owns and keeps referring to, rather than instantiating a fresh one each time.

slides.title: What @Environment provides
slides.body: @Environment reads a value from the environment -- an implicit, ambient set of values that flows down through a view hierarchy from parent to child, without needing to be passed explicitly as a parameter at every level. It's used for both system-provided values (like color scheme or dismiss action) and custom app-specific values you define.

slides.title: Reading a system environment value
slides.body: SwiftUI provides many built-in environment keys out of the box, such as \.colorScheme, \.dismiss (a function to dismiss the current presentation), and \.locale, each read with @Environment(\.keyPath). A view automatically re-renders if the specific environment value it reads changes, just like with other observed state.

slides.title: Injecting a custom @Observable type via environment
slides.body: With the Observation framework, you can inject a custom @Observable object into the environment with .environment(myModel) on a parent view, and any descendant view can read it with @Environment(MyModelType.self), without it needing to be passed explicitly through every intermediate view in between.

slides.title: Environment vs explicit parameters
slides.body: Environment is best suited to values that are genuinely ambient and needed broadly across a subtree -- like the current user session, theme, or a dismiss action -- not for passing data that's specific to one particular view's role in a screen, which should be an explicit initialiser parameter or Binding instead. Overusing environment for everything makes a view's actual dependencies harder to see at a glance.

quiz.prompt: What does @Environment let a view do?

options.text: Read a value that flows implicitly down from an ancestor in the view hierarchy, without it being passed as an explicit parameter
Create new state local only to itself
Bypass SwiftUI's rendering system entirely
Directly modify a parent view's layout

quiz.explanation: Environment values are ambient: a parent can set them and any descendant can read them with @Environment, without every intermediate view needing to pass them along explicitly.

quiz.prompt: What does `@Environment(\.dismiss)` give you access to?

options.text: The device's locale
The app's launch arguments
The current color scheme
A function to dismiss the current presentation (like a sheet)

quiz.explanation: \.dismiss is a built-in SwiftUI environment value providing an action to dismiss the view that was presented modally, such as a sheet.

quiz.prompt: How do you inject a custom @Observable object into the environment for descendants to read?

options.text: Pass it as an initialiser parameter to every child view
Mark it @Binding
It's not possible with custom types, only system-provided ones
Call .environment(myModel) on a parent view, and read it in a descendant with @Environment(Type.self)

quiz.explanation: The .environment(_:) modifier injects an @Observable instance into the environment for the view subtree, and any descendant reads it by type with @Environment(Type.self).

quiz.prompt: When is @Environment generally a better fit than an explicit initialiser parameter?

options.text: For genuinely ambient values needed broadly across a subtree, like a session or theme, rather than data specific to one view's particular role
Never -- explicit parameters should always be preferred
Only for Bool values
For any and all data a view might need, regardless of scope

quiz.explanation: Environment fits values that many descendants need without caring about the specific path they took to get there; view-specific data is clearer as an explicit parameter so the view's dependencies are visible.

quiz.prompt: What happens to a view if the specific environment value it reads changes?

options.text: Only the root view re-renders
It automatically re-renders, the same way it would if an @State or @Observable property it read changed
The entire app restarts
Nothing automatic happens; you must manually trigger a refresh

quiz.explanation: Environment values participate in SwiftUI's observation system, so a view reading one automatically re-renders when that specific value changes.

slides.title: Structural (implicit) identity
slides.body: By default, SwiftUI assigns identity to views based on their type and position in the view hierarchy -- this is called structural identity. Two views of the same type in the same structural position across two renders of body are treated as 'the same view' whose state persists, even though a brand-new struct value was created each time.

slides.title: Explicit identity with .id()
slides.body: The .id(_:) modifier lets you explicitly assign identity to a view based on a value you provide, overriding structural identity. When that id value changes, SwiftUI treats it as an entirely new view instance -- discarding any @State it held -- rather than the same view whose content just updated, which is useful for deliberately resetting a view's internal state.
slides.example:
TextField("Search", text: $query)
    .id(selectedTab)   // new id -> resets internal @State when tab changes

slides.title: ForEach and identifiable data
slides.body: Inside a ForEach, each row's identity comes from the id parameter (or Identifiable conformance) of the data it loops over, not from its position in the list. This is why ForEach needs stable, unique ids: if a row's id doesn't change even though its content did, SwiftUI reuses that row's state and just re-renders its content; if the id itself changes, SwiftUI treats it as a different view entirely.

slides.title: Why identity matters for state and animation
slides.body: A view's identity determines whether its @State survives across a re-render (same identity -> state persists) or gets discarded and reinitialized (different identity -> fresh state). Identity also drives SwiftUI's animations: a view transitioning between different identities animates as one view disappearing and a new one appearing, while a view keeping the same identity animates its properties changing in place.

quiz.prompt: By default, how does SwiftUI determine a view's identity across re-renders?

options.text: Based on the view's type and its position in the view hierarchy (structural identity)
By comparing every stored property's value
By a randomly generated UUID each time
By comparing memory addresses

quiz.explanation: SwiftUI's default, structural identity treats a view at the same type and position in the hierarchy across renders as continuing to be 'the same view,' preserving its associated state.

quiz.prompt: What happens to a view's @State when you change the value passed to its .id(_:) modifier?

options.text: It causes a runtime crash
SwiftUI treats it as an entirely new view instance and discards its previous @State
Nothing -- .id() has no effect on state
The @State value is preserved and just relabeled

quiz.explanation: Explicit identity via .id() overrides structural identity; a changed id tells SwiftUI this is a different view, so any state tied to the old identity is discarded and the view starts fresh.

quiz.prompt: In `ForEach(items) { item in Text(item.title) }`, what determines each row's identity?

options.text: The id from the data itself, via Identifiable conformance or an explicit id parameter
The row's position (index) in the array
ForEach doesn't track identity at all
The Text view's content string

quiz.explanation: ForEach derives each element's identity from its Identifiable id (or an explicit id: keyPath), not from array index, so reordering or inserting items behaves correctly as long as ids are stable and unique.

quiz.prompt: If a view keeps the same identity across a state change but its properties differ, how does SwiftUI typically animate that change?

options.text: As the old view disappearing and an unrelated new view appearing
It always uses a cross-fade regardless of identity
SwiftUI never animates identity-preserving changes
As the same view's properties animating in place from the old values to the new ones

quiz.explanation: When identity is preserved, SwiftUI treats it as the same view whose properties are changing, so transitions/animations interpolate that view's own properties rather than swapping views.

quiz.prompt: Why does ForEach need stable, unique ids for the data it iterates over?

options.text: It doesn't -- any id scheme works equally well
ForEach automatically generates ids and ignores the ones you provide
IDs are only used for sorting, not identity
Unstable or duplicate ids can cause SwiftUI to misattribute state or animations between rows, since identity drives what 'the same row' means across updates

quiz.explanation: Because identity determines whether SwiftUI treats an item as continuing to exist (preserving its state and animating its changes) versus being a new or removed item, unstable or duplicate ids lead to incorrect state association and glitchy animations.

slides.title: What actually triggers a re-render
slides.body: A SwiftUI view's body is re-evaluated when a piece of state it reads during that evaluation changes -- this includes @State, @Binding, @Environment values, and properties of an @Observable object accessed in body. Simply having an @State property doesn't cause re-renders on its own; it's specifically reading that property inside body, combined with it later changing, that establishes the dependency.

slides.title: Only what body actually reads matters
slides.body: SwiftUI dynamically tracks exactly which properties were accessed the last time a view's body ran, and only triggers re-evaluation when one of those specific properties changes -- not simply any change anywhere in an object the view happens to hold a reference to. This is a big part of why @Observable's field-level tracking reduces unnecessary re-renders compared to the old ObservableObject pattern.

slides.title: Re-render of body is not the same as a UI redraw
slides.body: When a view's body re-evaluates, SwiftUI diffs the newly produced view value against the previous one and only actually updates the parts of the rendered UI that differ -- re-evaluating body is cheap by design, closer to recomputing a description than performing expensive UI work, so it's expected to happen often and isn't itself something to avoid at all costs.

slides.title: Common causes of excessive re-rendering
slides.body: Re-renders can become a real performance issue when a view's body does expensive work directly (rather than just describing UI), when @State is placed too high up a hierarchy so a small change re-evaluates a huge subtree's body, or, in the older ObservableObject pattern, when a view reads an entire object rather than the one property it actually needs, since it would recompute on every property change to that object regardless of relevance.

quiz.prompt: What specifically causes a SwiftUI view's body to be re-evaluated?

options.text: A fixed timer interval
Only changes to @State properties, never @Environment or @Observable
A piece of state the view's body actually read during its last evaluation (e.g. @State, @Binding, an @Observable property) changing value
Any change anywhere in the app

quiz.explanation: SwiftUI tracks which specific pieces of observed state a view's body accessed, and only re-evaluates that view when one of those specific values actually changes.

quiz.prompt: In `struct CountView: View { let model: Model; var body: some View { Text("\(model.count)") } }` with an @Observable Model that also has a `name` property, does CountView re-render when model.name changes?

options.text: Only if name is marked @Published
No -- since body only reads model.count, a change to an unrelated model.name property doesn't trigger a re-render
It re-renders, but only once per app session

slides.title: What async/await actually is
slides.body: async marks a function as capable of suspending its execution to wait for work without blocking the underlying thread, and await marks the point where that suspension can happen. Under the hood, Swift's concurrency runtime can park the current task at an await point and resume it later, potentially on a different thread, while the thread itself goes on to do other work. This is fundamentally different from a blocking call, which ties up a thread for the whole duration of the operation.

slides.title: Calling async functions
slides.body: You can only call an async function from another async context, or by bridging in with a Task. Marking a function async changes its type, so callers must either await it inside an async function or wrap the call in a Task to start a new asynchronous context from synchronous code such as a button action.

slides.title: Suspension points and thread reuse
slides.body: Each await is a potential suspension point: the task may pause there and the thread is freed to run other tasks in the cooperative thread pool. When the awaited work completes, the task resumes, but not necessarily on the same thread it started on, which is why async/await code should not assume thread identity across await boundaries.

slides.title: async/await vs completion handlers
slides.body: Completion-handler based APIs require manual callback nesting, make error propagation awkward, and provide no compiler help for forgetting to call the completion. async/await lets you write asynchronous code that reads top-to-bottom like synchronous code, with try/catch for errors and the compiler enforcing that a value is actually produced.

It forces the awaited function to run synchronously on the main thread

quiz.explanation: await marks a potential suspension point: the task can pause there, releasing the thread back to the cooperative pool, and resume later possibly on a different thread.

quiz.explanation: A synchronous function has no concept of suspension, so it cannot await; you need an async context (or a Task) that the runtime can pause and resume.

quiz.explanation: Swift's concurrency runtime schedules continuations onto the cooperative thread pool without guaranteeing thread affinity across suspension points, unless the code is isolated to a specific actor like MainActor.

quiz.explanation: The main ergonomic win is readability and structured error handling; async/await doesn't change the runtime cost model or automatically parallelize anything by itself.

quiz.explanation: `Task { }` creates a new unstructured top-level task that provides the asynchronous context needed to call and await async functions from synchronous code.

slides.title: What structured concurrency means
slides.body: Structured concurrency means every child task's lifetime is scoped to the function or task that created it, forming a tree of parent-child relationships. A parent cannot return until all of its child tasks have completed, been awaited, or been explicitly cancelled, which makes it far harder to accidentally leak a running task.

slides.title: async let for concurrent child tasks
slides.body: `async let` starts a child task immediately and lets it run concurrently with the rest of the function, and you `await` its value only when you actually need it. Because it's structured, if the enclosing function exits early (e.g. via an error), any unawaited `async let` tasks are automatically cancelled.
slides.example:
async let user = fetchUser()
async let posts = fetchPosts()
let (u, p) = try await (user, posts) // run concurrently, join here

slides.title: Cancellation propagates down the tree
slides.body: When a parent task is cancelled, cancellation propagates to all of its structured children automatically. Individual tasks must still cooperate by checking `Task.isCancelled` or calling `Task.checkCancellation()` at appropriate points, since cancellation in Swift concurrency is cooperative, not preemptive.

slides.title: Structured vs unstructured tasks
slides.body: `async let` and `TaskGroup` are structured: their lifetime is bound to their enclosing scope. A plain `Task { }` is unstructured: it outlives the function that created it and keeps running even if that function returns, so you're responsible for cancelling or tracking it yourself if you don't want it to keep running.

quiz.explanation: By tying child task lifetimes to their parent scope and propagating cancellation down the tree, structured concurrency reduces the chance of tasks running longer than intended or being forgotten.

slides.title: Why actors exist
slides.body: Actors are a reference type that protects its mutable state by ensuring only one task can access that state at a time, eliminating a whole class of data races at compile time. Instead of manually reaching for locks or serial dispatch queues to guard shared mutable state, you model the state as an actor and the compiler enforces safe access.

slides.title: Actor isolation and await
slides.body: Accessing an actor's mutable state or methods from outside the actor requires `await`, because the call has to wait its turn to enter the actor's isolated region. Code running inside the actor itself doesn't need await to touch its own state, since it's already isolated there.

slides.title: Actor reentrancy
slides.body: Actors are reentrant: while a task is suspended at an await inside an actor method, the actor can process other calls in the meantime. This means state you read before an await inside an actor method might have changed by the time execution resumes after the await, so you can't assume the actor's state is frozen across a suspension point.

slides.title: Actors vs classes for shared state
slides.body: A plain class with mutable properties accessed from multiple tasks is a classic data race waiting to happen, since Swift's concurrency checking can't verify safe access to it. Converting that class to an actor moves the safety check to compile time: the compiler refuses code that touches actor state without going through the isolated, serialized access path.

quiz.explanation: Actors serialize access to their isolated state, so concurrent tasks cannot read and write it simultaneously, preventing data races.

quiz.explanation: Entering an actor's isolated region from outside may require waiting if the actor is currently busy with another call, so the access point is a genuine suspension point.

quiz.prompt: What does actor 'reentrancy' mean in practice?

options.text: While a task is suspended at an await inside an actor method, the actor can service other incoming calls, so state may change across that suspension
An actor method can call itself recursively without limit

It means actor methods automatically retry if they throw an error

quiz.explanation: Reentrancy allows other work to run on the actor during a suspension, which means code after an await inside an actor method cannot assume the actor's state is unchanged from before the await.

options.text: Add `@MainActor` to every function in the app

quiz.explanation: Turning the type into an actor lets the compiler verify that all state access is properly isolated, which is the idiomatic Swift concurrency replacement for manual locking.

quiz.prompt: Which of the following can safely access an actor's stored property without using `await`?

quiz.explanation: Code executing inside the actor's own methods is already isolated to it, so it can touch the actor's state directly without needing to await; external access is what requires await.

slides.title: Creating unstructured work with Task
slides.body: `Task { }` creates a new unstructured top-level task that starts running immediately and inherits the priority and actor context of where it was created (e.g. it stays on MainActor if launched from a MainActor context). It's the standard bridge from synchronous code, like a SwiftUI button action or a delegate callback, into async/await.

slides.title: Task priority and cancellation
slides.body: A `Task` returns a handle you can use to `cancel()` it or check its result later, and you can inspect `Task.isCancelled` inside the task's own body to react to cancellation cooperatively. `Task.detached` is similar but does not inherit the current actor context or priority, which is rarely what you want and should be used deliberately.

slides.title: TaskGroup for dynamic concurrency
slides.body: `withTaskGroup` (or `withThrowingTaskGroup`) lets you spawn an arbitrary, dynamic number of child tasks and collect their results, which `async let` can't do since it requires a fixed number of bindings known at compile time. All child tasks in the group are structured: the group waits for them before it returns, and cancelling the group cancels every child.

slides.title: TaskGroup example
slides.body: Each child task added with `group.addTask` runs concurrently, and you collect results by iterating the group, which acts like an async sequence of completed child results. This pattern is ideal for something like downloading N images concurrently where N is only known at runtime.

quiz.explanation: `async let` bindings are declared individually in source, so the count is fixed at compile time; `withTaskGroup` lets you loop and add a task per element for a runtime-determined collection.

quiz.explanation: Because TaskGroup children are structured, cancelling the parent task propagates cancellation to every child in the group automatically.

slides.title: Why UI work needs MainActor
slides.body: UIKit and SwiftUI are not thread-safe: view and view-model state that drives the UI must be read and written from the main thread, or you risk crashes and visual glitches. `MainActor` is Swift concurrency's way of expressing 'this code must run on the main thread' as a type-system guarantee instead of a runtime convention you have to remember.

slides.title: Annotating types and methods with @MainActor
slides.body: Marking a class, or an `ObservableObject`/`@Observable` view model, with `@MainActor` isolates all of its stored properties and methods to the main actor, so the compiler rejects any attempt to touch them from a background context without awaiting. This is the standard pattern for view models that publish state consumed directly by SwiftUI views.

slides.title: Hopping to MainActor from a background task
slides.body: If you're in a non-isolated async context and need to touch main-actor state, awaiting a call into that MainActor-isolated code automatically performs the hop for you; there's no need for `DispatchQueue.main.async` anymore. This replaces the old GCD pattern of manually dispatching UI updates back to the main queue.

slides.title: MainActor.run and its costs
slides.body: `MainActor.run { }` lets you execute a block on the main actor from anywhere, which is handy for one-off UI updates inside otherwise non-isolated code. Overusing it as a substitute for properly isolating your view model, though, scatters main-actor hops throughout your code and makes it harder to reason about where isolation boundaries actually are.

quiz.explanation: Crossing from a non-isolated context into MainActor-isolated state requires an await, since it's a genuine actor hop that may need to wait its turn on the main actor.

slides.title: What Sendable represents
slides.body: `Sendable` is a marker protocol that says a type's values can be safely passed across concurrency domains (e.g. from one task or actor to another) without introducing a data race. Value types like structs and enums are often automatically Sendable when all their members are Sendable, since each copy is independent.

slides.title: Why classes are usually not Sendable
slides.body: A class is a reference type, so passing an instance across tasks means multiple tasks could hold the same reference and mutate its properties concurrently, which is exactly the data race Sendable is meant to prevent. A class can be made Sendable only if it's immutable (all stored properties are `let` and themselves Sendable) or if it manages its own synchronization, and even then you often mark it `@unchecked Sendable` and take on the responsibility yourself.
slides.example:
final class Config: Sendable { // ok: all properties are immutable
    let apiKey: String
    let baseURL: URL
}

slides.title: Strict concurrency checking
slides.body: With Swift's strict concurrency checking enabled (the default posture is moving toward this over recent Swift versions), the compiler flags places where a non-Sendable value crosses an isolation boundary, turning what used to be a silent runtime data race into a build-time error. This is why teams migrating older codebases to structured concurrency often see a wave of Sendable-related warnings.

slides.title: @unchecked Sendable and when it's appropriate
slides.body: `@unchecked Sendable` tells the compiler to trust you that a type is safe to share across concurrency domains, even though it can't verify that itself, typically because you're using a lock or other synchronization internally. It should be used sparingly and only when you can justify the safety manually, since it disables the compiler's protection for that type.

quiz.explanation: @unchecked Sendable is meant for cases where you can manually guarantee safety (like internal locking) that the compiler's static analysis can't see through, not as a blanket way to bypass warnings.
