quiz.explanation: async let ties the child task's lifetime to its enclosing scope, while a bare Task { } creates an independent top-level task that keeps running after the creating function returns.

quiz.prompt: Why must code outside an actor use `await` to call the actor's methods?

options.text: Because actor methods are always slower than normal methods
It's purely stylistic and enforced only by convention
Because actors run exclusively on background threads
Because entering the actor's isolated region may require waiting until the actor is free to service the call

quiz.explanation: Access to actor-isolated state from outside must go through a suspension point since the actor may currently be busy handling other isolated work.

quiz.prompt: What does it mean for actors to be 'reentrant'?

options.text: While suspended at an await inside an actor method, the actor may process other calls, so state can change across that suspension
An actor can be reinitialized multiple times
Reentrancy means actor methods cannot call other methods on the same actor
It refers to actors being able to inherit from other actors

quiz.explanation: Reentrancy means other work can interleave during a suspension inside an actor method, so you can't assume state is frozen from before an await to after it.

quiz.prompt: Why is cancellation in Swift concurrency described as 'cooperative'?

options.text: Because cancelling a task requires two different threads to agree
Because calling cancel() only sets a flag; the running task must itself check Task.isCancelled or use a cancellation-aware API to actually stop
Because only TaskGroups support cancellation, not individual Tasks
Because cancellation always requires explicit user confirmation via UI

quiz.explanation: Swift doesn't forcibly kill tasks; cancellation is a cooperative signal that well-behaved code must check for and respond to.

quiz.prompt: When would you reach for `withTaskGroup` instead of a handful of `async let` bindings?

options.text: When you need only one asynchronous operation total
async let and withTaskGroup are never interchangeable in any case
When the number of concurrent child tasks is only known at runtime, such as one task per element in a dynamically-sized array
TaskGroup is required for any function that returns a value

quiz.explanation: async let requires each binding to be written explicitly in source, so it can't express a variable, runtime-determined number of concurrent tasks the way withTaskGroup's loop-and-addTask pattern can.

quiz.prompt: What does marking a view model `@MainActor` guarantee?

options.text: Its methods run in a background thread pool for performance
It automatically becomes Codable
It disables Swift's strict concurrency checking for that type
All of its state and methods are isolated to the main actor, so the compiler enforces that they're only accessed from the main thread context

quiz.explanation: @MainActor isolation ties a type's state and methods to the main actor, letting the compiler catch any attempt to touch them from an unsafe context.

quiz.prompt: What is the risk of sharing a plain, mutable class instance across multiple concurrent tasks without any synchronization?

options.text: A data race: multiple tasks could read and write its properties simultaneously, leading to corrupted or unpredictable state
There is no risk as long as the class conforms to Codable
The class will automatically be deallocated early
Swift will silently convert it to a value type at runtime

quiz.explanation: Since a class is a reference type, uncoordinated concurrent access from multiple tasks can corrupt its state or crash the app, which is exactly what Sendable checking tries to catch at compile time.

quiz.prompt: When is `@unchecked Sendable` an appropriate choice?

options.text: As a default habit to silence any Sendable-related compiler warning
When a type manages its own internal synchronization (e.g. a lock) in a way the compiler can't verify, and you've manually confirmed it's safe
Only for enums with no associated values
It should never be used under any circumstances

quiz.explanation: @unchecked Sendable opts a type out of compiler-verified safety in cases where the developer has manually ensured thread safety through means the compiler can't statically analyze, like internal locking.

quiz.prompt: What's the key difference between `Task { }` and `Task.detached { }`?

options.text: Task.detached runs synchronously while Task { } runs asynchronously
Task.detached cannot be cancelled
Task { } inherits the current actor context and priority; Task.detached does not
They are identical; detached is just a naming alias

quiz.explanation: A plain Task inherits the surrounding actor isolation (e.g. MainActor) and priority, while Task.detached deliberately starts fresh without inheriting either.

quiz.prompt: In a function using `async let user = fetchUser()` followed later by `async let posts = fetchPosts()`, when do these two calls actually start executing concurrently?

options.text: Only once both are awaited together
They run sequentially, one after the other, regardless of async let
Only if they are wrapped in a TaskGroup
Each async let task begins running as soon as it is declared, so both run concurrently from their declaration points

quiz.explanation: async let starts the child task immediately at the point of declaration; awaiting it later just retrieves the already-in-progress result, which is what lets two async let calls overlap in time.

slides.title: The XCTest building blocks
slides.body: XCTest organizes tests into `XCTestCase` subclasses, where each method whose name starts with `test` is discovered and run automatically as an individual test. Assertions like `XCTAssertEqual` and `XCTAssertTrue` report failures with file and line information, and `setUp`/`tearDown` run before and after each test method to establish and clean up fixture state.

slides.title: A minimal XCTest example
slides.body: Each test method should be independent and runnable in isolation, since XCTest doesn't guarantee execution order across methods. Keeping setUp lightweight and resetting shared fixtures in tearDown avoids one test's leftover state silently affecting another.

slides.title: Swift Testing: the modern alternative
slides.body: Swift Testing (the `import Testing` framework introduced alongside Swift 5.9/6) replaces `XCTestCase` subclassing with plain `@Test` functions and replaces XCTAssert calls with a single `#expect` macro that captures rich failure diagnostics automatically. It also supports parameterized tests natively, running the same test body against multiple inputs without hand-written loops.

slides.title: Swift Testing example
slides.body: Because `@Test` functions are just top-level or type functions rather than XCTestCase overrides, they can be async and throwing directly without special XCTest expectation plumbing. `#expect` continues past a failed check to report more failures in the same test, while `#require` stops the test immediately if its condition isn't met.

quiz.prompt: In XCTest, how does the framework decide which methods in an XCTestCase subclass are actual tests?

options.text: Methods whose name begins with `test` and take no parameters are discovered and run automatically
Every method in the class is run as a test
You must register each test manually in an Info.plist
Only methods marked `@objc` are treated as tests

quiz.explanation: XCTest uses a naming convention: any no-argument method starting with `test` on an XCTestCase subclass is automatically discovered as a test case.

quiz.prompt: What is the main structural difference between a Swift Testing `@Test` function and an XCTest test method?

options.text: Swift Testing tests must be written in Objective-C
@Test functions don't require subclassing XCTestCase and can be plain functions, including async/throwing ones, without special expectation APIs
Swift Testing tests cannot use assertions at all
@Test functions can only be run from the command line, never from Xcode's UI

quiz.explanation: Swift Testing drops the XCTestCase subclassing requirement in favor of freestanding @Test-annotated functions, which can naturally be async or throws.

quiz.prompt: What does `#expect` do differently from a failed `XCTAssertEqual` call when a check fails?

options.text: #expect crashes the test process immediately
#expect silently ignores the failure
#expect records the failure but lets the test continue running so later checks in the same test can also report
#expect can only be used for Boolean conditions, never equality checks

quiz.explanation: Like XCTAssert calls, #expect records a failure and continues, letting a single test surface multiple independent failures instead of stopping at the first one — use #require when you need to stop immediately.

quiz.prompt: Why should test methods generally avoid depending on the execution order of other test methods?

options.text: XCTest always runs tests in strict alphabetical order, so order dependence is actually safe
Order dependence is only a problem for UI tests, never unit tests
Swift Testing enforces a fixed run order that makes this a non-issue
XCTest does not guarantee execution order, and order-dependent tests become flaky or fail when run individually or in parallel

quiz.explanation: Tests that rely on shared mutable state or a specific run order can pass or fail inconsistently depending on how the test runner schedules them, especially under parallel execution.

quiz.prompt: What is Swift Testing's built-in feature for running the same test logic against multiple input values without writing a manual loop?

options.text: Parameterized tests via arguments passed to @Test
XCTestExpectation
setUpWithError()
@available annotations

quiz.explanation: Swift Testing supports parameterized @Test functions that take arguments, automatically generating a separate test run for each provided input.

slides.title: The Arrange-Act-Assert shape
slides.body: Arrange-Act-Assert (AAA) is a convention for structuring a test into three clear sections: set up the objects and state under test (Arrange), perform the one behavior being tested (Act), then verify the outcome (Assert). Keeping these sections visually distinct, even with blank lines or comments, makes a test's intent obvious at a glance months later.

slides.title: AAA in practice
slides.body: A test that mixes setup, action, and assertions together is harder to read and harder to debug when it fails, because it's unclear which part of the test caused the failure. Following AAA consistently also nudges you toward testing one behavior per test method, since cramming multiple 'acts' into one test blurs what's actually being verified.

slides.title: One logical assertion per test
slides.body: A good unit test verifies one logical behavior, even if that requires more than one assertion call to fully check the outcome (e.g. checking both a status code and a decoded body). Testing multiple unrelated behaviors in a single test method makes failures ambiguous: you can't tell which behavior broke just from the test name.

slides.title: Naming tests for readability
slides.body: A test name should describe the scenario and expected outcome, such as `testAppliesDiscount_whenCartTotalExceedsThreshold`, so that a failing test's name alone tells you roughly what broke without opening the test body. This is especially valuable in CI logs where you're scanning a list of failures quickly.

quiz.prompt: What do the three parts of Arrange-Act-Assert represent?

options.text: Allocate memory, run the app, then attach the debugger
Set up test state, perform the behavior under test, then verify the outcome
Write the test, run it, then delete it if it fails
Assert the answer first, then arrange the code to match

quiz.explanation: AAA structures a test as: arrange the preconditions, act by invoking the behavior under test, then assert on the resulting outcome.

quiz.prompt: Why is it good practice to keep a test method focused on one logical behavior, even if that needs multiple assertion calls?

options.text: XCTest silently ignores any assertion after the first one
Multiple assertions in one test always cause a compiler error
A focused test gives a failure that clearly points to which behavior broke, rather than an ambiguous failure covering many unrelated behaviors
It's required because Swift Testing does not allow more than one #expect per test

quiz.explanation: Testing one behavior per method keeps failures diagnostic: when the test fails, its name and scope tell you exactly what broke, instead of forcing you to dig through a test that covers several unrelated scenarios.

quiz.prompt: What's a downside of writing a test method that mixes setup, the action under test, and assertions without clear separation?

options.text: XCTest will refuse to compile the file
It makes the test run slower at runtime
It prevents the test from being run in CI
It becomes harder to tell at a glance which part of the test is responsible for a failure

quiz.explanation: Blending the sections together obscures the test's structure, making it harder for a reader (including future you) to quickly understand what's being set up versus what's actually being verified.

quiz.prompt: Why does a descriptive test name like `testReturnsError_whenNetworkRequestTimesOut` matter?

options.text: A descriptive name communicates the scenario and expected outcome, so a failure list in CI is scannable without opening each test body
XCTest requires exactly this naming format to compile
It has no practical benefit over `test1`, `test2`, etc.
It's only useful for UI tests, not unit tests

quiz.explanation: Good test names act as documentation: when a test fails in a CI log, a descriptive name lets you understand roughly what broke before even opening the file.

quiz.prompt: A test sets up a cart, applies a discount, asserts the discounted total, and then ALSO asserts an unrelated inventory count changed. What's the concern with this test?

options.text: There is no concern; more assertions always make a test stronger
It's testing two different behaviors in one test, making it unclear which one broke on failure and coupling unrelated concerns
XCTest limits tests to a single assertion, so this test would fail to compile
This is the correct way to write AAA-style tests

quiz.explanation: Bundling unrelated behaviors into one test reduces the diagnostic value of a failure and often signals the test should be split into two focused tests.

slides.title: Why hardcoded dependencies resist testing
slides.body: A type that directly instantiates its dependencies, like calling `URLSession.shared` inline inside a view model, can't be tested without making a real network request. Dependency injection breaks that coupling by passing dependencies in from outside (via initializer or property), so tests can substitute a fake in place of the real implementation.

slides.title: Injecting a protocol dependency
slides.body: Defining a small protocol for the dependency's interface lets the production code depend on the abstraction rather than a concrete type, and lets tests inject a lightweight fake that conforms to the same protocol. This is the core technique that makes network calls, persistence, and other side effects testable in isolation.

slides.title: Stubs, fakes, and mocks
slides.body: A stub returns canned data with no real logic, a fake is a lightweight working implementation (like an in-memory dictionary standing in for a database), and a mock additionally records how it was called so the test can verify interactions (e.g. 'fetchUser was called exactly once with id X'). Choosing the simplest one that answers the test's question keeps tests readable and avoids over-specifying implementation details.

slides.title: A test using an injected fake
slides.body: Because the view model depends on the `UserService` protocol rather than a concrete networking type, the test can inject a fake that returns a fixed user synchronously and deterministically, with no network access required. This makes the test fast, reliable, and independent of external state.

quiz.prompt: Why does a view model that directly calls `URLSession.shared.data(from:)` internally resist unit testing?

options.text: URLSession cannot be called from async functions
URLSession.shared is deprecated and can't be used at all
The test would need a real network connection and a live server, making it slow, flaky, and dependent on external state
Unit tests cannot call any async function

quiz.explanation: Hardcoding a concrete networking dependency ties the test to real network conditions, which is slow and unreliable; the fix is to inject an abstraction that can be swapped for a test double.

quiz.prompt: What is the core technique that lets tests substitute a fake implementation in place of a real dependency?

options.text: Marking the class `final` so it can't be subclassed
Using `#if DEBUG` to conditionally compile different networking code
Always using singletons so tests can override the shared instance
Depending on a protocol abstraction and injecting the concrete implementation from outside (dependency injection)

quiz.explanation: Defining a protocol for the dependency and injecting an implementation (via initializer, typically) decouples the consumer from a specific concrete type, letting tests provide a fake conforming to the same protocol.

quiz.prompt: What distinguishes a 'mock' from a simple 'stub' in test terminology?

options.text: A mock also records how it was called so the test can assert on interactions, whereas a stub just returns canned data
A mock is always slower than a stub
Stubs can only be used in UI tests
There is no meaningful difference; the terms are interchangeable in every context

quiz.explanation: A stub simply returns predetermined data, while a mock additionally tracks invocation details (call count, arguments) so tests can verify specific interactions occurred.

quiz.prompt: In the example `ProfileViewModel(service: FakeUserService())`, why is the fake service passed through the initializer rather than the view model creating its own service internally?

options.text: Because ObservableObject requires all properties to be injected
So the test can control exactly what the dependency returns, without needing a real network call
Because Swift does not allow types to create their own dependencies
It has no real benefit; it's just a style preference

quiz.explanation: Constructor injection lets the test supply a deterministic fake in place of the real service, isolating the view model's logic from actual network behavior.

quiz.prompt: What's a risk of over-using mocks that assert on exact call counts and arguments for every dependency?

options.text: Mocks are not supported by XCTest, only by Swift Testing
Overusing mocks always makes tests run slower
Tests become tightly coupled to implementation details, breaking on harmless refactors even when behavior is unchanged
There is no downside; asserting on every call is always the best practice

quiz.explanation: Over-specifying interactions makes tests brittle to internal refactors that don't change observable behavior, which increases maintenance cost without a proportional safety benefit.

slides.title: Async test methods
slides.body: Both XCTest and Swift Testing support `async` (and `throws`) test functions directly: mark the test method `async`, and `await` the async code under test just like you would anywhere else. The test runner suspends and resumes the test the same way any async caller would, so there's no special ceremony needed for straightforward async/await code.

slides.title: A basic async test
slides.body: Because the view model's `load()` method is itself async, the test can simply await it and then assert on the resulting state, with no callbacks or expectations involved. This is one of the clearest ergonomic wins of async/await over completion-handler-based testing.

slides.title: Testing older completion-handler APIs with XCTestExpectation
slides.body: For legacy code that still uses completion handlers rather than async/await, XCTest provides `XCTestExpectation`: you create an expectation, fulfill it inside the completion handler, and call `wait(for:timeout:)` to pause the test until it's fulfilled or the timeout elapses. This bridges the gap for code that hasn't been migrated to structured concurrency yet.

slides.title: XCTestExpectation example
slides.body: The timeout in `wait(for:timeout:)` should be generous enough to avoid flaky failures on slower CI machines but short enough that a genuinely hung test fails quickly rather than stalling the whole suite. Once code is migrated to async/await, these expectation-based tests can usually be simplified to a plain `await`.

quiz.prompt: How do you write a test for an `async throws` function using either XCTest or Swift Testing?

options.text: Wrap the call in DispatchQueue.main.async and poll a boolean flag
Async functions cannot be unit tested; they require UI testing instead
Use XCTestExpectation exclusively, since async test functions are not supported
Mark the test function itself async (and throws if needed), then await the call directly

quiz.explanation: Both frameworks support async (and throwing) test functions natively, so you can simply await the async code under test just like any other async caller.

quiz.prompt: What is `XCTestExpectation` primarily used for?

options.text: Bridging tests to legacy completion-handler-based asynchronous APIs that haven't been migrated to async/await
Testing SwiftUI view layout
Measuring code coverage percentage
Replacing the need for any assertions in a test

quiz.explanation: XCTestExpectation lets a test wait for a completion handler to fire before asserting, which is the standard tool for testing pre-async/await asynchronous code.

quiz.prompt: Why is it important to choose a reasonable (not excessively long) timeout when using `wait(for:timeout:)`?

options.text: Timeouts have no effect on test behavior
Too short a timeout causes flaky failures on slower machines, while too long a timeout lets a genuinely hung test stall the whole suite
XCTest ignores the timeout value entirely
The timeout only affects UI tests, not unit tests

quiz.explanation: The timeout balances tolerance for normal variance in execution speed against not wasting excessive time when a test is truly stuck, which matters especially for CI reliability and speed.

quiz.prompt: Once code that used to rely on completion handlers is migrated to async/await, what typically happens to its XCTestExpectation-based tests?

options.text: They must be deleted since async functions cannot be tested
They need to be converted into UI tests
They can usually be simplified to a plain await call instead of the expectation/wait dance
They become slower and require longer timeouts

quiz.explanation: Async/await removes the need for the expectation-fulfill-wait pattern, since the test can simply await the now-async function directly.

quiz.prompt: A test needs to verify that a view model's `@Published` property updates correctly after an async `load()` call completes. What's the simplest correct approach?

options.text: Poll the property in a busy-wait loop with Thread.sleep
Use XCTestExpectation even though load() is already async
It cannot be tested without launching the full app in a UI test
Mark the test async, `await vm.load()`, then assert on the property immediately afterward

quiz.explanation: Since load() is async, awaiting it in an async test guarantees it has fully completed before the assertion runs, making a direct assertion both correct and simplest.

slides.title: What UI tests actually exercise
slides.body: XCUITest drives the app as a black box: it launches a real instance of the app in a separate process and interacts with it through the accessibility tree, the same way VoiceOver or a real user would. This means UI tests validate the full integration, from taps and gestures through to what's actually rendered on screen, but they're slower and more brittle than unit tests.

slides.title: Querying elements with XCUIApplication
slides.body: You locate on-screen elements through `XCUIApplication()` and its element queries (buttons, staticTexts, textFields, etc.), which rely on accessibility identifiers or labels to find the right element. Giving views a stable `accessibilityIdentifier` in the app code, rather than matching on visible text, makes UI tests resilient to copy changes and localization.
slides.example:
let app = XCUIApplication()
app.launch()
app.textFields["emailField"].tap()
app.textFields["emailField"].typeText("ada@example.com")
app.buttons["loginButton"].tap()

slides.title: Waiting for asynchronous UI state
slides.body: Because UI tests interact with a live, asynchronously updating app, asserting immediately after an action can race against network calls or animations still in flight. `XCTestCase.wait(for:timeout:)` combined with `NSPredicate` expectations, or simpler helpers like checking `element.waitForExistence(timeout:)`, let the test wait for the expected state instead of asserting too early.

slides.title: Keeping UI tests focused and few
slides.body: UI tests are valuable for critical end-to-end flows (login, checkout, core navigation) but are expensive to run and maintain, so most test coverage should live at the unit level where feedback is fast and failures are precise. A good rule of thumb is a small number of UI tests covering the highest-value user journeys, layered on top of a much larger base of unit tests.

quiz.prompt: How does XCUITest interact with the app under test?

It calls internal Swift functions directly inside the same process as the test
It reads the app's source code statically without ever running it
It only works with SwiftUI apps, not UIKit apps

quiz.explanation: XCUITest treats the app as a black box running in its own process, interacting with on-screen elements via the accessibility hierarchy rather than calling internal code.

accessibilityIdentifier automatically generates snapshot tests

quiz.explanation: Text content changes often (copy edits, localization), but a stable identifier set explicitly in code doesn't, so tests built on identifiers are far less brittle.

quiz.prompt: Why might a UI test that asserts immediately after tapping a login button flake intermittently?

options.text: XCUITest cannot tap buttons reliably
UI tests always run assertions before the tap actually happens
The assertion may run before an in-flight network call or animation finishes updating the UI, racing against asynchronous state
Flaky UI tests are unrelated to timing and are usually a Swift compiler bug

quiz.explanation: Since the app under test updates asynchronously, asserting too early can catch the UI mid-transition; waiting for the expected element (e.g. via waitForExistence) avoids this race.

quiz.prompt: Why do most teams keep the number of UI tests relatively small compared to unit tests?

options.text: UI tests are prohibited by Apple's App Store guidelines

UI tests are slower to run and more brittle, so they're best reserved for a handful of critical end-to-end user journeys

quiz.explanation: UI tests carry a much higher execution and maintenance cost than unit tests, so teams typically use them sparingly for the highest-value flows and rely on unit tests for detailed coverage.

quiz.prompt: What does `element.waitForExistence(timeout:)` help avoid in a UI test?

options.text: It avoids asserting on an element before the asynchronous UI update that produces it has actually completed
It avoids the need to launch the app at all
It replaces the need for accessibility identifiers

quiz.explanation: waitForExistence polls for the element to appear up to the timeout, letting the test tolerate the natural delay of asynchronous UI updates instead of asserting prematurely.

slides.title: What code coverage measures (and doesn't)
slides.body: Code coverage reports what percentage of lines or branches were executed by the test suite, but it says nothing about whether the right things were actually verified. A test that calls a function without meaningfully asserting on its behavior inflates coverage without providing real protection against regressions.

slides.title: Chasing 100% coverage as a trap
slides.body: Chasing a specific coverage number as a target encourages writing low-value tests just to touch lines of code, including trivial getters/setters or SwiftUI view bodies that are better validated visually. Coverage is a useful diagnostic for finding completely untested areas, but it's a poor primary goal.

slides.title: What's actually worth testing
slides.body: Business logic with real branching (discount rules, validation, parsing, state machines) gives the highest return on testing investment because it's where subtle bugs hide and where regressions are costly. Pure UI layout code, thin wrappers around system APIs, and generated boilerplate are usually lower priority since they're simple, visually verifiable, or already covered by the framework's own tests.

slides.title: Testing edge cases and boundaries
slides.body: The most valuable tests target edge cases: empty collections, zero/negative values, boundary conditions (exactly at a threshold), and error paths, since these are where implementations most often diverge from intent. A discount engine test suite, for example, should cover the exact threshold value, not just a value comfortably above it.
slides.example:
func testNoDiscountBelowThreshold() { XCTAssertEqual(engine.apply(to: Cart(total: 49)), 49) }
func testDiscountAppliesExactlyAtThreshold() { XCTAssertEqual(engine.apply(to: Cart(total: 50)), 45) }

High coverage is mathematically impossible above 80%
Coverage percentage only applies to UI tests

quiz.explanation: A line can be 'covered' just by being executed, even if no assertion actually checks the outcome, so coverage numbers don't guarantee tests catch real bugs.

quiz.explanation: Optimizing for the coverage number itself, rather than for catching real regressions, leads to tests that exist to satisfy a metric rather than to validate meaningful behavior.

quiz.prompt: Which kind of code typically gives the highest return on investment for unit testing?

options.text: Simple property getters and setters with no logic
SwiftUI view body declarations

Business logic with real branching, like discount calculation or input validation rules

quiz.explanation: Code with actual conditional logic and edge cases is where bugs are most likely to hide and where a regression is most costly, making it the highest-value target for tests.

quiz.prompt: Why should a discount engine's test suite include a case exactly at the discount threshold, not just a case comfortably above it?

options.text: Boundary values are where off-by-one and comparison-operator bugs (like using > instead of >=) most commonly surface
XCTest requires at least one boundary test per function
Testing the exact threshold is slower and therefore more thorough
There's no real benefit; any value above the minimum works equally well

quiz.explanation: Boundary conditions are a classic source of subtle bugs (off-by-one errors, wrong comparison operators), so explicitly testing the exact threshold catches mistakes that a mid-range value wouldn't reveal.

quiz.prompt: A pull request adds a test that instantiates a view model and asserts nothing beyond `XCTAssertNotNil(vm)`. What's the concern with this test?

options.text: XCTAssertNotNil cannot be used on class instances

It will fail to compile because view models cannot be tested

quiz.explanation: A test like this inflates coverage metrics but doesn't verify any real behavior, so it gives a false sense of safety without actually catching future bugs.

quiz.prompt: How does XCTest discover which methods in an XCTestCase subclass to run as tests?

options.text: Every public method in the class
Only methods explicitly listed in a plist
Any no-argument method whose name starts with `test`
Methods annotated with @Test

quiz.explanation: XCTest relies on the naming convention: a parameterless method beginning with 'test' on an XCTestCase subclass is automatically treated as a test.

quiz.prompt: In Swift Testing, what does `#expect` do when its condition is false?

quiz.prompt: What does the Arrange-Act-Assert pattern primarily improve about a test's structure?

options.text: It separates setup, the behavior under test, and verification into clear, readable sections

quiz.explanation: AAA is about organizing a test's internal structure for readability and debuggability, clearly separating what's set up, what's exercised, and what's checked.

quiz.prompt: Why does injecting a protocol-typed dependency (rather than a concrete networking type) make a view model easier to test?

It lets tests substitute a fake or stub conforming to the same protocol, avoiding real network calls

quiz.explanation: Depending on an abstraction decouples the view model from a specific implementation, so a test can inject a deterministic fake instead of hitting the real network.

quiz.prompt: What distinguishes a mock from a stub?

options.text: A stub can only be used for synchronous code
