A mock additionally records how it was invoked, enabling assertions on interactions; a stub just returns fixed data
There's no real difference between the two terms

quiz.explanation: Stubs are the simpler test double that just returns canned values; mocks add call-tracking so the test can verify specific interactions happened.

quiz.prompt: What is `XCTestExpectation` primarily used for today?

options.text: Replacing all XCTAssert calls
Measuring test coverage percentage
Running UI tests instead of XCUITest
Bridging tests to legacy completion-handler-based async APIs that haven't adopted async/await

quiz.explanation: XCTestExpectation lets a synchronous test wait for a completion handler to fire, which is mainly needed for asynchronous APIs that predate or haven't adopted async/await.

quiz.prompt: Why should UI tests locate elements via `accessibilityIdentifier` rather than matching on visible label text?

options.text: Identifiers are stable across copy changes and localization, while text matching breaks whenever wording changes
accessibilityIdentifier is required for App Store submission
Text-based matching runs significantly faster
SwiftUI does not support accessibilityIdentifier

quiz.explanation: A stable identifier set in code survives copy edits and localization, making identifier-based UI tests far less brittle than text-based ones.

quiz.prompt: Why are UI tests typically kept to a small number of critical flows rather than covering everything?

options.text: Xcode enforces a hard cap on UI test count
UI tests are slow and comparatively brittle, so unit tests provide faster, more precise feedback for most logic
UI tests cannot assert on text content
UI tests are deprecated in favor of snapshot testing

quiz.explanation: Because UI tests run a full app instance and are more prone to flakiness, teams typically reserve them for the highest-value end-to-end journeys and push detailed coverage down to unit tests.

quiz.prompt: Why is 100% code coverage a poor primary testing goal?

options.text: Coverage percentage is a legally regulated metric for App Store apps
It is mathematically impossible to exceed 90% in any Swift project
It can be inflated by tests that execute code without meaningfully asserting on behavior, giving a false sense of safety
Code coverage tools are not available for Swift projects

quiz.explanation: Coverage measures execution, not verification, so optimizing purely for the number rewards low-value tests rather than tests that actually catch regressions.

quiz.prompt: Why should a test suite for a threshold-based rule (like 'apply a discount when total is at least $50') explicitly test the value exactly at the threshold?

options.text: XCTest requires at least one test per numeric literal in the code
Threshold values always run faster than other test inputs
It has no particular value over testing any other valid input
Boundary values are a common source of off-by-one or wrong-comparison-operator bugs that mid-range values wouldn't reveal

quiz.explanation: Exact-boundary tests catch subtle logic errors, like using > instead of >=, that a comfortably-above-threshold value would never expose.

slides.title: URLSession and its configurations
slides.body: `URLSession` is the foundation for all network requests on Apple platforms, and it's built around a session configuration that controls caching, cookie storage, and timeout behavior. `.shared` is a convenient default session for simple one-off requests, while a custom session with its own `URLSessionConfiguration` gives you control over things like request timeouts or whether to use the disk cache.

slides.title: Session types: default, ephemeral, background
slides.body: A default session persists cookies and caches to disk like a normal browsing session; an ephemeral session keeps everything in memory only, useful for private or sensitive requests that shouldn't leave traces on disk. A background session lets uploads and downloads continue even after the app is suspended or terminated, handled by the system outside the app's process.

slides.title: URLRequest and HTTP methods
slides.body: A `URLRequest` wraps a URL along with HTTP method, headers, and body data, giving you full control beyond a simple GET. Building requests explicitly (rather than only ever using the default GET convenience methods) is necessary for POST/PUT/DELETE calls and for attaching headers like `Content-Type` or `Authorization`.

slides.title: Inspecting the HTTP response
slides.body: The response from a URLSession data task should be cast to `HTTPURLResponse` to inspect the status code, since a successful callback with no thrown error doesn't by itself mean the server returned a 2xx status; a 404 or 500 still delivers a valid response with a body. Checking `response.statusCode` explicitly is necessary to correctly detect server-side failures.

quiz.prompt: What is the key difference between an ephemeral URLSession and a default URLSession?

options.text: Ephemeral sessions keep cookies and cache in memory only with nothing persisted to disk, unlike the default session
Ephemeral sessions are faster because they skip TLS handshakes
Ephemeral sessions can only make GET requests
There is no functional difference; ephemeral is just a naming alias

quiz.explanation: An ephemeral session avoids writing cookies, cache, and credentials to disk, which is useful for private or sensitive requests, whereas the default session persists this data like a normal session.

quiz.prompt: Why would you use a background URLSession configuration instead of the default one?

options.text: Background sessions are required for all GET requests
To let uploads or downloads continue even after the app is suspended or terminated, managed by the system outside the app process
Background sessions automatically retry failed requests up to 10 times
Background sessions bypass the need for HTTPS

quiz.explanation: Background sessions hand off long-running transfers to the OS, so they can keep progressing even when the app itself isn't actively running, which the default configuration doesn't do.

quiz.prompt: After awaiting `URLSession.shared.data(for:)` with no error thrown, is it safe to assume the request succeeded?

options.text: Yes, absence of a thrown error always means a 2xx response
No, because data(for:) never throws under any circumstances
No; a completed request can still carry a non-2xx status code (like 404 or 500) that must be checked explicitly via the HTTPURLResponse
Yes, but only for POST requests

quiz.explanation: URLSession only throws for transport-level failures (like no connectivity); a server responding with an error status code still returns normally, so the status code has to be checked separately.

quiz.prompt: Why would you build a `URLRequest` explicitly instead of just passing a URL to a convenience GET method?

options.text: URLRequest is required for any request that isn't over HTTPS
URLRequest is deprecated and should be avoided
It has no functional benefit; it's purely stylistic
To set the HTTP method, custom headers, or a request body, none of which a bare URL convenience call supports

quiz.explanation: A plain URL only supports a default GET; URLRequest gives you control over method, headers (like Authorization or Content-Type), and body data needed for POST/PUT/DELETE calls.

quiz.prompt: What does casting the response from a data task to `HTTPURLResponse` let you do?

options.text: Inspect the HTTP status code and headers to determine whether the server considered the request successful
Automatically decode the response body as JSON
Force the request to use HTTP/2
Cache the response indefinitely regardless of server headers

quiz.explanation: URLResponse alone doesn't expose the status code; casting to HTTPURLResponse gives access to statusCode and header fields needed to correctly interpret the server's result.

slides.title: Codable as encode+decode
slides.body: `Codable` is a type alias for `Encodable & Decodable`, and the compiler can synthesize conformance automatically for structs and enums whose stored properties are themselves Codable. This removes most of the boilerplate that used to be needed to manually parse JSON dictionaries into typed Swift models.

slides.title: Mapping JSON keys with CodingKeys
slides.body: When a JSON payload's key names don't match your Swift property names (a very common case with snake_case APIs), a `CodingKeys` enum lets you map each property to its corresponding JSON key. This keeps your Swift model idiomatic (camelCase) while still decoding the API's actual wire format correctly.

slides.title: Handling optional and missing fields
slides.body: A property typed as optional (`String?`) will decode to `nil` if the key is entirely missing from the JSON or explicitly `null`, without throwing an error, whereas a non-optional property will throw a `DecodingError.keyNotFound` if the API omits that key. Real-world APIs frequently add or omit optional fields, so being deliberate about which properties are optional versus required avoids brittle decoding failures.

slides.title: Custom decoding with an initializer
slides.body: For cases the automatic synthesis can't handle, like a field that's sometimes a String and sometimes a number, or converting an ISO date string into a `Date`, you implement `init(from decoder:)` manually and pull values out of a `KeyedDecodingContainer` with full control over fallbacks and type coercion.

quiz.prompt: What does the compiler need in order to automatically synthesize Codable conformance for a struct?

options.text: The struct must be marked `final`
Every stored property must itself already conform to Codable (or be a standard Codable-conforming type)
The struct must have a custom init(from:)
Automatic synthesis never works and manual conformance is always required

quiz.explanation: Swift can generate Codable conformance automatically as long as every stored property's type is itself Codable; anything else requires a manual implementation.

quiz.prompt: An API returns JSON keys in snake_case (like `full_name`), but your Swift property is `fullName`. What's the idiomatic way to bridge this without abandoning automatic synthesis?

options.text: Rename the Swift property to `full_name` to match exactly
Manually parse the raw JSON as a dictionary and skip Codable entirely
Define a `CodingKeys` enum mapping `fullName` to the `"full_name"` JSON key
Use JSONSerialization instead of JSONDecoder

quiz.explanation: CodingKeys lets you keep idiomatic Swift naming while still telling the decoder which JSON key each property corresponds to, preserving automatic synthesis for everything else.

quiz.prompt: If an API response omits a JSON key entirely, what happens when decoding into a struct where that property is declared as `String` (non-optional)?

options.text: The property is silently set to an empty string
The property is set to nil regardless of being non-optional
JSONDecoder automatically substitutes the type's default value
Decoding throws a DecodingError.keyNotFound, failing the whole decode

quiz.explanation: A non-optional property requires its key to be present in the JSON; if it's missing, JSONDecoder throws keyNotFound rather than silently defaulting.

quiz.prompt: When is a custom `init(from decoder:)` implementation necessary instead of relying on automatic Codable synthesis?

options.text: When the decoding logic needs custom handling, such as a field with an inconsistent type or converting a raw string into a richer type with fallback behavior
Whenever the struct has more than three properties
Custom init(from:) is never necessary; synthesis always works
Only when the struct also conforms to Equatable

quiz.explanation: Automatic synthesis handles the straightforward one-to-one property mapping case; anything requiring conditional logic, type coercion, or fallback values needs a hand-written decoder implementation.

quiz.prompt: Why might making a property optional (`String?`) instead of required (`String`) be a deliberate, useful decision when modeling an API response?

options.text: Optional properties decode faster than required ones
It allows the type to still decode successfully even if the API omits or nulls that field, rather than failing the entire decode
Optional properties are required for Codable to work at all
It has no functional effect on decoding, only on Swift's type checker

quiz.explanation: Marking a field optional tells the decoder that its absence or null value is acceptable, preventing one missing field from causing the whole object to fail to decode.

slides.title: data(for:) and data(from:)
slides.body: URLSession's async APIs, `data(for:)` (taking a URLRequest) and `data(from:)` (taking a URL), replace the old completion-handler-based `dataTask` methods with a single awaited call that returns the data and response together, or throws. This removes the need for manual completion-handler plumbing and lets network calls compose naturally with other async code.

slides.title: A full async fetch-and-decode
slides.body: A typical async networking call combines `data(for:)` with `JSONDecoder`, wrapped in a single throwing async function that the caller can await; both the network error and the decoding error surface through the same `throws` mechanism. This is significantly more linear to read than the old pattern of nested completion handlers with a Result type.

slides.title: AsyncBytes for streaming responses
slides.body: `bytes(for:)` returns an `AsyncSequence` of bytes that you can iterate as they arrive, which is useful for large downloads or streaming APIs where you want to process data incrementally rather than waiting for the entire response to buffer in memory. This is a case where the async APIs offer capability the old completion-handler API didn't expose as naturally.

slides.title: Cancellation and async networking
slides.body: Because `data(for:)` is a proper async function, wrapping a network call in a `Task` gives you cancellation for free: cancelling the task propagates to the underlying URLSession task, aborting the in-flight request. This is much cleaner than the old pattern of manually holding onto a `URLSessionDataTask` reference just to call `.cancel()` on it later.

quiz.prompt: What do URLSession's `data(for:)` and `data(from:)` async methods return?

options.text: Only the response status code
A Combine publisher that must be subscribed to separately
The response Data along with the URLResponse, or they throw if the request fails
A completion handler closure that must still be provided

quiz.explanation: These async methods return a tuple of (Data, URLResponse), replacing the old completion-handler callback with a single awaited return value or a thrown error.

quiz.prompt: How do both network failures and JSON decoding failures typically surface in an async networking function like `fetchUser(id:) async throws -> User`?

options.text: Decoding failures use a separate delegate callback, network failures throw
Decoding errors are silently ignored and return a default value
Network failures must be handled with a completion handler even in async code
Both surface through the same `throws` mechanism, letting the caller catch either kind of error with one do/catch

quiz.explanation: Since both URLSession's async methods and JSONDecoder's decode method are throwing, a single throws function combining them lets callers handle any failure uniformly with try/catch.

quiz.prompt: When would you reach for `bytes(for:)` instead of `data(for:)`?

options.text: When you want to process a large or streaming response incrementally instead of buffering the entire body in memory first
bytes(for:) is required for all POST requests
When you need synchronous, blocking network access
bytes(for:) is only usable with background URLSession configurations

quiz.explanation: bytes(for:) exposes the response as an AsyncSequence you can iterate as data arrives, which is valuable for large downloads where you don't want to hold the whole response in memory at once.

quiz.prompt: If you wrap `try await fetchUser(id:)` inside a `Task` and later call `task.cancel()` before it completes, what happens?

options.text: Nothing; cancellation has no effect on network requests
Cancellation propagates down to the underlying URLSession request, aborting the in-flight network call
The task keeps running to completion but discards its result
The app crashes because network tasks cannot be cancelled

quiz.explanation: Structured task cancellation is honored by URLSession's async APIs: cancelling the Task cancels the underlying network request, unlike the old pattern where you had to manually track and cancel a URLSessionDataTask.

quiz.prompt: Compared to the old completion-handler-based `dataTask(with:completionHandler:)`, what's a key ergonomic advantage of `data(for:)`?

options.text: It automatically retries failed requests three times
It skips SSL/TLS validation for faster requests
It lets the network call be awaited directly within a linear async function, with errors propagated via throws instead of a Result passed to a closure
It eliminates the need to ever check the HTTP status code

quiz.explanation: The async API lets networking code read top-to-bottom like synchronous code and unifies error handling under throws, avoiding the nested-closure structure of the old completion-handler API.

slides.title: Modeling network errors as a typed enum
slides.body: Wrapping the various failure modes, transport errors, bad status codes, decoding failures, into a single custom `Error` enum gives callers a consistent, exhaustive way to handle failures with a switch statement, rather than inspecting loosely-typed NSError codes. This also lets you attach useful context, like the actual status code, to each case.

slides.title: A typed network error enum
slides.body: Distinguishing between different failure categories, like connectivity loss versus a 4xx client error versus a 5xx server error, lets calling code make smarter decisions, such as showing an offline banner for connectivity failures but a generic error message for server failures. This is much more actionable than a single generic 'something went wrong' error.

slides.title: Which failures are worth retrying
slides.body: Not every failure should be retried: a 401 Unauthorized or 404 Not Found will fail identically on retry and just wastes time and battery, while a timeout, a 503 Service Unavailable, or a transient connectivity drop often succeeds on a second attempt. A good retry strategy checks the failure category before deciding whether to retry at all.

slides.title: Exponential backoff
slides.body: Retrying immediately and repeatedly on failure can hammer a struggling server and make things worse; exponential backoff increases the delay between attempts (e.g. 1s, 2s, 4s) so retries space themselves out and give the server room to recover. Adding a small random jitter to each delay also avoids many clients retrying in lockstep after an outage.

quiz.prompt: What's the benefit of modeling network failures as a custom `Error` enum with specific cases, instead of propagating raw NSError/URLError values?

options.text: It makes the app compile faster
Custom error enums are required for async throws functions to compile
It automatically retries the request on any failure
It gives callers an exhaustive, switchable set of known failure categories, and lets you attach relevant context like a status code

quiz.explanation: A typed error enum documents the possible failure modes explicitly and lets calling code handle each category deliberately, rather than parsing loosely-typed system error codes.

quiz.prompt: Why is it usually pointless to retry a request that failed with a 401 Unauthorized status?

options.text: The failure is due to invalid or missing credentials, which won't change on a simple retry without first re-authenticating
401 errors are automatically retried by URLSession itself
401 only occurs for GET requests, so retrying is unnecessary
Retrying a 401 always succeeds on the second attempt due to server-side caching

quiz.explanation: A 401 reflects an authorization problem, not a transient issue, so retrying the exact same request will fail again; the real fix is refreshing credentials before retrying.

quiz.prompt: Which of these failures is generally the best candidate for an automatic retry?

options.text: A 404 Not Found response
A request timeout or 503 Service Unavailable, which often reflect transient conditions
A 400 Bad Request due to malformed input
A JSON decoding failure due to a permanently malformed response schema

quiz.explanation: Timeouts and 503s often indicate temporary conditions (network hiccups, server overload) that can resolve themselves, unlike client errors like 404/400 or a persistent schema mismatch, which will fail identically every time.

quiz.prompt: What problem does exponential backoff solve compared to retrying immediately after every failure?

options.text: It reduces the total number of retries to exactly one
It guarantees the request will never fail again
It spaces out retry attempts with increasing delay, avoiding hammering a struggling server and giving it time to recover
It eliminates the need for a maximum retry count

quiz.explanation: By increasing the wait time between attempts, exponential backoff reduces load on a recovering server and avoids clients retrying so aggressively that they make an outage worse.

quiz.prompt: Why is adding random 'jitter' to a backoff delay useful when many clients might be retrying the same failing endpoint?

options.text: Jitter has no practical effect and is purely cosmetic
Jitter guarantees each client gets a unique server response
Jitter is required by URLSession's API and cannot be disabled
It prevents many clients from retrying at the exact same moment in lockstep, which could cause a synchronized thundering-herd spike

quiz.explanation: Without jitter, many clients that failed at the same time would also retry at the same time, creating repeated synchronized load spikes; randomizing the delay spreads retries out.

slides.title: Bearer tokens and the Authorization header
slides.body: Most modern APIs authenticate requests using a bearer token sent in the `Authorization: Bearer <token>` HTTP header, obtained once via a login or OAuth flow and then attached to every subsequent request. The token proves the request comes from an authenticated session without re-sending credentials on every call.

slides.title: Attaching an auth header to a request
slides.body: Rather than duplicating header-setting logic at every call site, it's common to centralize it, for example in a URLRequest builder or a URLSession delegate, so every outgoing request automatically carries the current token. This also makes it a single place to update when the token refreshes.
slides.example:
var request = URLRequest(url: url)
request.setValue("Bearer \(token)", forHTTPHeaderField: "Authorization")

slides.title: Access tokens, refresh tokens, and expiry
slides.body: Access tokens are typically short-lived for security, so APIs pair them with a longer-lived refresh token that can be exchanged for a new access token without asking the user to log in again. A well-designed client detects a 401 caused by an expired access token, silently refreshes it, and retries the original request rather than surfacing an error to the user.

slides.title: Handling token refresh around concurrent requests
slides.body: If multiple requests are in flight when the token expires, naively refreshing the token separately for each failed request can trigger redundant refresh calls or even invalidate tokens mid-flight. A common pattern is to funnel refresh attempts through a single actor or task that in-flight requests await, so only one refresh happens and everyone waiting gets the new token.

quiz.prompt: What is the standard HTTP header used to send a bearer token with a request?

options.text: Authorization: Bearer <token>
X-Auth-Password
Cookie: token=<token>
Content-Type: application/auth

quiz.explanation: Bearer token authentication conventionally uses the Authorization header with the 'Bearer' scheme, which most modern APIs expect for authenticated requests.

quiz.prompt: Why do many APIs pair a short-lived access token with a longer-lived refresh token?

options.text: To reduce the number of HTTP headers sent per request
So the client can silently obtain a new access token when it expires, without requiring the user to log in again
Refresh tokens are only used for encrypting the request body
Access tokens expire only when the app is force-quit

quiz.explanation: Short-lived access tokens limit the damage if one is compromised, while a longer-lived refresh token lets the client re-establish a valid session automatically, preserving a good user experience.

quiz.prompt: What problem can arise if several concurrent requests each independently trigger a token refresh when they all receive a 401 at the same time?

options.text: No problem; independent refreshes are the recommended approach
The app will crash immediately
Redundant or overlapping refresh calls can occur, potentially invalidating tokens mid-flight or wasting a limited number of refresh attempts
URLSession automatically deduplicates refresh calls, so this is a non-issue

quiz.explanation: Without coordination, multiple requests can each kick off their own refresh, which is wasteful and can race, sometimes invalidating a token another request just started using.

quiz.prompt: What is the purpose of routing token refresh through a single actor (or similarly serialized mechanism) that other in-flight requests await?

options.text: To make refresh calls run in parallel for speed
To permanently cache the token so it never needs to be refreshed again
Actors are required by URLSession for any authenticated request
To ensure only one refresh happens at a time and all waiting requests receive the same freshly refreshed token

quiz.explanation: Serializing refresh through an actor means concurrent callers all await the same in-progress refresh task instead of each triggering their own, avoiding duplicate or conflicting refresh attempts.

quiz.prompt: A request fails with a 401 and the client silently refreshes the access token and retries the original request once. What's the benefit of this pattern over immediately surfacing the error to the user?

options.text: It avoids showing a disruptive error for what is often just a normal, expected token expiry, keeping the user logged in transparently
It removes the need for the app to ever handle authentication errors
It guarantees the retry will always succeed
It reduces the number of HTTP requests sent overall

quiz.explanation: Token expiry is a routine, expected event, not a real error condition; refreshing and retrying transparently avoids interrupting the user for something the app can usually recover from on its own.

slides.title: HTTP caching and URLCache
slides.body: URLSession has a built-in `URLCache` that can automatically cache responses on disk and in memory based on the HTTP caching headers the server sends, like `Cache-Control` and `ETag`. The `URLRequest.CachePolicy` on each request controls how aggressively that cache is used, from always preferring the network to only using the cache and never hitting the network.

slides.title: Choosing a cache policy
slides.body: `.useProtocolCachePolicy` (the default) respects the server's caching headers, `.reloadIgnoringLocalCacheData` always hits the network, and `.returnCacheDataElseLoad` prefers a cached response if one exists and only falls back to the network if there's nothing cached. Choosing the right policy per request matters: a settings screen might want fresh data, while a rarely-changing content feed might be fine serving a cached copy first.
slides.example:
var request = URLRequest(url: url)
request.cachePolicy = .returnCacheDataElseLoad

slides.title: Application-level caching beyond URLCache
slides.body: For data that needs to be available even when there's no cached HTTP response, or that you want to shape and query more richly than raw response bodies allow, it's common to persist decoded model data explicitly, e.g. into SwiftData or a file, rather than relying solely on URLCache. This is what makes true offline read access possible, since URLCache alone doesn't guarantee a response will still be cached when you need it.

slides.title: A stale-while-revalidate style pattern
slides.body: A common offline-friendly pattern is to immediately show data from local persistence (which might be stale) while kicking off a network refresh in the background, then update the UI when fresh data arrives. This gives users an instantly responsive UI even on a slow or absent connection, while still keeping data reasonably current.

quiz.prompt: What does URLSession's built-in URLCache use to decide whether and how long to cache a response?

options.text: The response body's file size only
HTTP caching headers sent by the server, such as Cache-Control and ETag
A fixed 24-hour timer applied to every response
The device's current battery level

quiz.explanation: URLCache respects standard HTTP caching semantics driven by response headers like Cache-Control and ETag, rather than an arbitrary fixed timer.

quiz.prompt: What does the `.returnCacheDataElseLoad` cache policy do?

options.text: Always ignores the cache and hits the network
Deletes the cache after every request
Returns cached data if available, and only falls back to a network request if nothing is cached
Only works for POST requests

quiz.explanation: This policy prioritizes speed and offline availability by preferring a cached response when one exists, falling back to the network only when there's no cached data to return.

quiz.prompt: Why might an app persist decoded model data explicitly (e.g. in SwiftData or a file) instead of relying solely on URLCache for offline support?

options.text: URLCache is deprecated and no longer functions on iOS 17+
SwiftData is required for any network request to succeed
URLCache only works for requests using HTTP/1.0
URLCache doesn't guarantee a specific response stays cached, and it stores raw response data rather than queryable, structured model objects

quiz.explanation: URLCache's retention isn't guaranteed and it caches raw HTTP payloads, not structured queryable data, so genuine offline read access and richer querying typically needs explicit application-level persistence.

quiz.prompt: In a stale-while-revalidate pattern, what's shown to the user first?

options.text: Locally cached data immediately (even if potentially stale), followed by an update once a background network refresh completes
A blank loading screen until the network request completes
An error message until connectivity is confirmed
Only data explicitly marked as 'fresh' by the server

quiz.explanation: The pattern favors immediate responsiveness by showing what's already stored locally right away, then reconciling with fresh data from the network as soon as it arrives.

quiz.prompt: What is the tradeoff of using `.reloadIgnoringLocalCacheData` for every request in an app?

options.text: It has no tradeoff and should always be used
It guarantees the freshest data but forfeits any offline availability and increases network usage even when a valid cached copy exists
It causes the app to store more data on disk than necessary
It disables HTTPS for that request

quiz.explanation: Always bypassing the cache ensures freshness but means the app can't serve anything when offline and re-fetches data over the network even when a perfectly valid cached response was available.

quiz.prompt: What does an ephemeral URLSession configuration avoid doing compared to the default configuration?

options.text: Sending any HTTP headers
Supporting HTTPS connections
Persisting cookies and cached responses to disk
Making POST requests

quiz.explanation: Ephemeral sessions keep cookies and cache in memory only, with nothing written to disk, unlike the default session which persists this data.

quiz.prompt: After a successful (non-throwing) URLSession data call, why must you still check the HTTP status code?

options.text: Because URLSession never throws even for connectivity failures
Because status codes are unrelated to whether the request succeeded
Because HTTPURLResponse cannot represent error codes
Because the call only throws for transport-level failures; a server error like 404 or 500 still returns normally with its own status code

quiz.explanation: A completed request with no thrown error just means the transport succeeded; the server's actual outcome (success or failure) is conveyed via the status code, which must be checked separately.

quiz.prompt: What is the purpose of a `CodingKeys` enum on a Codable struct?

options.text: To map Swift property names to differently-named JSON keys while keeping automatic Codable synthesis
To make a struct conform to Equatable
To disable Codable synthesis entirely
To specify the network endpoint the struct is fetched from

quiz.explanation: CodingKeys bridges a mismatch between Swift property naming conventions and the JSON's actual key names, without giving up the convenience of automatic Codable synthesis.

quiz.prompt: What do URLSession's async methods like `data(for:)` return when awaited successfully?

options.text: Only a Bool indicating success
A tuple containing the response Data and the URLResponse
A Combine publisher
The decoded model object directly

quiz.explanation: data(for:) returns the raw response body and the URLResponse together; decoding into a model type is a separate step performed with JSONDecoder.

quiz.prompt: Which type of failure is generally NOT worth automatically retrying?

options.text: A request timeout
A 503 Service Unavailable
A 401 Unauthorized caused by an expired or invalid token
A transient dropped connection

quiz.explanation: A 401 reflects an authentication problem that a plain retry won't fix; it needs a token refresh (or re-login) first, unlike transient failures like timeouts or 503s which may resolve on their own.

quiz.prompt: What does exponential backoff change about how a client retries a failing request?

options.text: It retries immediately and repeatedly with no delay
It guarantees exactly one retry attempt
It disables retries entirely after the first failure
It increases the delay between successive retry attempts, easing load on a potentially struggling server

quiz.explanation: Backoff spaces retries further apart on each attempt, reducing pressure on the server and improving the odds that a transient issue has resolved by the time the next attempt happens.

quiz.prompt: What is the standard way to send a bearer token to authenticate an HTTP request?

options.text: Via the Authorization header using the Bearer scheme
In the URL's query string as ?token=
As a custom User-Agent string
Bearer tokens cannot be sent over HTTPS

quiz.explanation: The Authorization: Bearer <token> header is the conventional mechanism most modern APIs expect for token-based authentication.

quiz.prompt: Why is it problematic for multiple concurrent requests to each independently trigger their own token refresh after receiving a 401?

options.text: It's not problematic; independent refreshes are best practice
It can cause redundant or racing refresh calls that may invalidate tokens or waste limited refresh attempts
URLSession blocks more than one refresh call per app lifetime
It causes the access token to never expire

quiz.explanation: Uncoordinated refresh attempts can race and interfere with each other; centralizing refresh logic (e.g. via an actor) avoids duplicate, potentially conflicting refresh calls.

quiz.prompt: What does the `.returnCacheDataElseLoad` cache policy prioritize?

options.text: Always fetching fresh data over the network, ignoring any cache
Deleting the cache after every launch
Serving a cached response if one exists, falling back to the network only when nothing is cached
Only working for image downloads

quiz.explanation: This policy favors availability and speed by using cached data when present, hitting the network only as a fallback when there's no cached copy.

quiz.prompt: Why might an app persist decoded model data itself rather than relying only on URLCache for offline support?

options.text: URLCache guarantees indefinite retention of every response, making extra persistence redundant
URLCache cannot be used alongside async URLSession APIs
Persisting model data is only relevant for apps that don't use JSON
URLCache stores raw HTTP payloads with no retention guarantee, while explicit persistence gives structured, queryable, and reliably available offline data

quiz.explanation: Application-level persistence provides durable, structured offline data that the app controls directly, addressing gaps in URLCache's non-guaranteed, unstructured caching of raw responses.

slides.title: What UserDefaults is for
slides.body: `UserDefaults` is a lightweight key-value store backed by a plist, intended for small amounts of simple settings and preferences, like a theme choice, a feature flag, or whether onboarding was completed. It is not designed for large datasets or sensitive data; everything in it is stored unencrypted and loaded into memory as a whole.

slides.title: Reading and writing values
slides.body: UserDefaults supports property-list-compatible types directly, strings, numbers, booleans, dates, arrays, and dictionaries of those, without needing Codable, though you can store Codable data by encoding it to Data first. Writes are cheap for small values but UserDefaults isn't transactional, so it's a poor fit for data you need strong consistency guarantees around.
slides.example:
UserDefaults.standard.set(true, forKey: "hasCompletedOnboarding")
let done = UserDefaults.standard.bool(forKey: "hasCompletedOnboarding")

slides.title: @AppStorage in SwiftUI
slides.body: SwiftUI's `@AppStorage` property wrapper reads and writes a UserDefaults value directly and automatically invalidates the view when it changes, making it a convenient way to bind simple settings straight into view state without manually observing UserDefaults notifications.

slides.title: What UserDefaults should NOT be used for
slides.body: UserDefaults should never store sensitive data like tokens, passwords, or personal information, since it's unencrypted and readable by anyone with access to the device's file system on a jailbroken device; that data belongs in the Keychain. It's also a poor choice for large or structured datasets that need querying, sorting, or relationships, which is what Core Data or SwiftData are built for.

quiz.prompt: What kind of data is UserDefaults best suited for?

options.text: Small, simple settings and preferences like a theme choice or a completed-onboarding flag
Large relational datasets with complex queries
Sensitive credentials like authentication tokens
Binary media files like videos and large images

quiz.explanation: UserDefaults is designed as a lightweight key-value store for small configuration and preference values, not for large datasets, relational data, or sensitive information.

quiz.prompt: Why is UserDefaults an inappropriate place to store an authentication token?

options.text: UserDefaults cannot store String values
UserDefaults is unencrypted, so anything stored there is exposed if the device's file system is accessed; sensitive data belongs in the Keychain instead
UserDefaults has a hard 10-item storage limit
Tokens are always too large to fit in a plist

quiz.explanation: UserDefaults data sits in an unencrypted plist, which is not appropriate for secrets; the Keychain provides the encrypted, access-controlled storage that credentials need.

quiz.prompt: What does SwiftUI's `@AppStorage` property wrapper do?

options.text: It creates a new Core Data persistent store automatically
It encrypts UserDefaults values automatically
It reads and writes a UserDefaults value directly and triggers a view update when that value changes
It syncs data across devices via iCloud automatically

quiz.explanation: @AppStorage is a thin, observable wrapper over UserDefaults, letting a simple setting drive SwiftUI view state without manual KVO or notification observing.

quiz.prompt: Why is UserDefaults a poor fit for storing a large, growing list of structured records, like thousands of downloaded articles?

options.text: UserDefaults can only store a single value total
UserDefaults cannot store arrays under any circumstances
UserDefaults automatically deletes data after 24 hours
UserDefaults loads its entire contents into memory and isn't designed for querying or partial updates, unlike Core Data or SwiftData

quiz.explanation: Since UserDefaults is meant for small key-value settings and is loaded wholesale, it doesn't scale well to large structured datasets that need efficient querying or partial updates the way a proper persistence framework does.

quiz.prompt: Can Codable data be stored in UserDefaults, and if so, how?

options.text: Yes, by encoding the Codable value to Data (e.g. via JSONEncoder) and storing that Data
No, UserDefaults only supports property-list types and can never store Codable data
Yes, but only if the type also conforms to NSObject
Yes, UserDefaults automatically detects and decodes any Codable type without encoding it first

quiz.explanation: UserDefaults natively supports plist types, so a Codable value is typically encoded to Data first (e.g. with JSONEncoder) and stored/retrieved as Data, decoding it back out on read.

slides.title: Persisting Codable models to disk
slides.body: For data too structured or large for UserDefaults but not requiring a full database, a common approach is encoding a Codable model to JSON (or another format) with `JSONEncoder` and writing it to a file in the app's Documents or Application Support directory. This is a simple, dependency-free way to persist a moderate amount of structured data, like a cached list of recently viewed items.

slides.title: Writing and reading a Codable file
slides.body: `FileManager` gives you access to standard directories like `.documentDirectory` or `.applicationSupportDirectory`, and `Data.write(to:)` / `Data(contentsOf:)` handle the actual disk I/O. Writing should generally happen off the main thread if the data is large, since file I/O is a blocking operation.

slides.title: Choosing Documents vs Application Support
slides.body: Files in `.documentDirectory` are meant for user-visible, user-generated content that might be exposed via iCloud Drive or the Files app, while `.applicationSupportDirectory` is meant for app-internal data the user doesn't directly manage. Using the wrong directory can lead to unexpected behavior, like internal cache files showing up in the Files app.

slides.title: Limitations of file-based Codable persistence
slides.body: This approach doesn't scale well to large datasets, since a read or write typically loads or serializes the entire file at once, and it doesn't support partial updates, relationships, or efficient querying the way a real database does. Once you outgrow 'a handful of structured objects that change infrequently,' it's usually time to move to Core Data or SwiftData.

quiz.prompt: When is encoding a Codable model to JSON and writing it directly to a file a reasonable persistence choice?

options.text: For any amount of data, no matter how large, since it always scales linearly
For a moderate amount of structured data that doesn't need complex querying, relationships, or frequent partial updates
Only for data that must be encrypted
Never; it's always better to use Core Data regardless of the data's size

quiz.explanation: File-based Codable persistence is well suited to simple, moderate-sized structured data with infrequent, whole-object updates; it's not designed for querying, relationships, or large-scale partial updates.

quiz.prompt: What's the difference between `.documentDirectory` and `.applicationSupportDirectory` in terms of intended use?

options.text: They are functionally identical with no meaningful difference
Application Support is only available on macOS, not iOS
Documents is meant for user-visible, user-generated content (potentially exposed via Files/iCloud Drive); Application Support is for internal app data the user doesn't manage directly
Documents cannot store JSON files

quiz.explanation: Apple's directory conventions distinguish user-facing content, appropriate for Documents, from internal app data that shouldn't clutter the user's view of their files, which belongs in Application Support.

quiz.prompt: Why should writing a large Codable-encoded file generally happen off the main thread?

options.text: JSONEncoder cannot run on the main thread under any circumstances
The main thread has a hard file-size write limit
It has no effect on performance either way
File I/O is a blocking, potentially slow operation that can stall the UI if performed synchronously on the main thread

quiz.explanation: Disk I/O, especially for larger files, can take a noticeable amount of time, and running it on the main thread blocks UI responsiveness, so it's best moved to a background context.

quiz.prompt: What's a key limitation of file-based Codable persistence compared to a database like Core Data or SwiftData?

options.text: A single change typically requires re-encoding and rewriting the entire file, with no efficient support for partial updates or querying
It cannot store arrays of objects
It requires an active network connection to read the file
Codable files can only be read once per app launch

quiz.explanation: Because the whole file is loaded and rewritten as a unit, this approach doesn't scale to frequent small updates or complex queries the way a proper database engine does.

quiz.prompt: A feature needs to persist thousands of records with frequent individual updates and the ability to query by multiple fields. Why would file-based Codable persistence be a poor fit here?

options.text: It would work fine and is the recommended approach for any dataset size
Each update would require rewriting the entire file, and there's no efficient query mechanism beyond loading everything into memory and filtering manually
Codable cannot encode more than 100 objects at once
File-based persistence is deprecated on iOS 17+

quiz.explanation: The whole-file read/write model and lack of indexed querying make this approach inefficient at scale; a database like SwiftData is built specifically for large, queryable, frequently-updated datasets.

slides.title: The Core Data object graph
slides.body: Core Data is an object graph and persistence framework built around a data model (defined in a `.xcdatamodeld` file) describing entities, attributes, and relationships, backed by a SQLite store by default. `NSManagedObject` subclasses represent individual records, and an `NSManagedObjectContext` tracks changes to them in memory before they're saved to the persistent store.

slides.title: Contexts and saving
slides.body: Changes to managed objects (inserts, updates, deletes) live in memory within a context until you call `context.save()`, which writes them to the persistent store; if you never save, the changes are lost. Core Data apps commonly use a main-thread context for UI-bound data and a background context for heavier import or processing work, since a context is not thread-safe and must only be used on the queue it was created for.

slides.title: Fetching with NSFetchRequest
slides.body: Querying Core Data uses `NSFetchRequest`, which supports predicates (via `NSPredicate`) for filtering and sort descriptors for ordering, executed against a specific managed object context. `NSFetchedResultsController` builds on this to efficiently drive a table or collection view, observing changes and computing the minimal diff needed to update the UI.

slides.title: Why Core Data has a learning curve
slides.body: Core Data's power comes with real complexity: understanding context threading rules, merge policies for conflicting concurrent edits, and the `.xcdatamodeld` migration story for evolving your schema over app versions all take real investment to use correctly. This complexity is part of why SwiftData, built on similar underlying concepts, was introduced to offer a simpler, more Swift-native API for iOS 17+ apps.

quiz.prompt: What role does an `NSManagedObjectContext` play in Core Data?

options.text: It defines the visual layout of a Core Data-backed screen
It is a networking layer used to sync Core Data with a remote server
It tracks in-memory changes to managed objects and is responsible for saving them to the persistent store
It replaces the need for a data model file

quiz.explanation: A context acts as a scratchpad tracking inserted, updated, and deleted managed objects; those changes only reach the persistent store when the context is explicitly saved.

quiz.prompt: What happens to changes made to a managed object if the context is never saved?

options.text: They are automatically saved the next time the app launches
Core Data saves automatically every 60 seconds regardless of explicit save calls
The app crashes immediately upon any unsaved change
They are lost; changes only persist to the store once context.save() is called

quiz.explanation: Core Data changes live only in the context's memory until an explicit save; without calling save(), those changes never reach the persistent store and are discarded when the context is deallocated.

quiz.prompt: Why is it important not to use the same NSManagedObjectContext concurrently from multiple threads?

options.text: Contexts are not thread-safe; each context is meant to be used only on the queue (thread) it was created for
Core Data automatically serializes all access, so this is never actually a concern
Multi-threaded access is fine as long as the model has fewer than 10 entities
It only matters for contexts backed by an in-memory store

quiz.explanation: NSManagedObjectContext instances are confined to a specific queue; accessing one from the wrong thread violates Core Data's threading contract and can cause crashes or data corruption.

quiz.prompt: What does `NSFetchedResultsController` help with?

options.text: Encrypting Core Data's SQLite store
Efficiently driving a table or collection view from a fetch request, observing changes and computing minimal UI diffs
Migrating between different .xcdatamodeld schema versions
Establishing a network connection to a remote Core Data server

quiz.explanation: NSFetchedResultsController wraps a fetch request and tracks changes to its results, making it well suited to keeping a list-style UI in sync with the underlying Core Data store efficiently.

quiz.prompt: Why was SwiftData introduced despite Core Data already being capable and mature?

options.text: Core Data was fully deprecated and removed starting in iOS 17
SwiftData replaces the need for any data model definition whatsoever
SwiftData offers a simpler, more Swift-native API on similar underlying concepts, reducing some of Core Data's inherent complexity (context threading, migrations, boilerplate)
SwiftData is unrelated to Core Data and uses an entirely different storage engine

quiz.explanation: SwiftData builds on Core Data's proven foundation but exposes it through a much more ergonomic, macro-based Swift API, addressing some of the learning curve and boilerplate that made Core Data harder to approach.

slides.title: Defining a model with @Model
slides.body: SwiftData turns a plain Swift class into a persisted model just by adding the `@Model` macro, which generates the storage and change-tracking machinery Core Data required you to configure through an .xcdatamodeld file. This is the modern, iOS 17+ way to add lightweight, type-safe persistence without leaving the Swift type system.

slides.title: ModelContainer and ModelContext
slides.body: A `ModelContainer` owns the underlying storage (comparable to Core Data's persistent container), and a `ModelContext` is where you insert, delete, and track changes to model instances, roughly analogous to a managed object context. In a SwiftUI app, `.modelContainer(for:)` on the app or a scene sets this up and makes a context available to views via the `@Environment(\.modelContext)` key.

slides.title: Querying with @Query
slides.body: The `@Query` property wrapper declaratively fetches model instances directly into a SwiftUI view, optionally with a predicate and sort order, and automatically keeps the view updated as the underlying data changes, no NSFetchedResultsController wiring required. This tightly couples the data layer to SwiftUI in a way that removes a lot of the observation boilerplate Core Data needed.

slides.title: SwiftData relationships and when to still consider Core Data
slides.body: SwiftData supports relationships between `@Model` types declaratively (using `@Relationship` for more advanced configuration like delete rules), covering much of what Core Data relationships offered with far less setup. For apps with very advanced requirements, like complex multi-store configurations or existing large Core Data schemas with custom migration logic, staying on or interoperating with Core Data may still make sense, but for new iOS 17+ projects SwiftData is generally the default choice.

quiz.prompt: What does adding `@Model` to a Swift class do?

options.text: It makes the class conform to Codable automatically and nothing else
It marks the class as immutable
It is required for any class used in SwiftUI
It turns the class into a persisted SwiftData model, generating the storage and change-tracking machinery automatically

quiz.explanation: @Model is SwiftData's macro-based mechanism for making a plain Swift class persistable, replacing the need to hand-configure an .xcdatamodeld file the way Core Data required.

quiz.prompt: What is the SwiftData equivalent of Core Data's NSManagedObjectContext?

options.text: ModelContext
ModelContainer
@Query
PersistentStore

quiz.explanation: ModelContext is where you insert, delete, and track changes to @Model instances, playing the role NSManagedObjectContext played in Core Data; ModelContainer is closer to the persistent container.

quiz.prompt: What does the `@Query` property wrapper do in a SwiftUI view?

options.text: It sends a network request to fetch remote data
It declaratively fetches SwiftData model instances (with optional predicate/sort) and keeps the view automatically updated as the data changes
It only works for read-only, non-persisted structs
It requires manually setting up an NSFetchedResultsController underneath

quiz.explanation: @Query integrates SwiftData fetching directly into SwiftUI's declarative model, automatically re-rendering the view when the underlying queried data changes, without manual observer wiring.

quiz.prompt: For a new iOS 17+ project without unusual legacy requirements, which persistence framework does Apple generally position as the default modern choice?

options.text: Core Data, since SwiftData is purely experimental
UserDefaults, since it's simplest to set up
SwiftData, since it offers a simpler Swift-native API built on similar underlying concepts to Core Data
Neither; raw SQLite is always preferred

quiz.explanation: SwiftData is Apple's modern, Swift-native persistence framework for iOS 17+, intended to be the default choice for new projects, with Core Data remaining relevant mainly for legacy or highly specialized needs.

quiz.prompt: How does a SwiftUI view typically gain access to the current ModelContext?

options.text: By calling ModelContext() directly inside the view's body every time it renders
ModelContext is a global singleton with no setup required
It must be passed manually through every initializer in the view hierarchy
Via `@Environment(\.modelContext)` after the app or scene sets up `.modelContainer(for:)`

quiz.explanation: Setting `.modelContainer(for:)` on the app or scene configures the container and makes its context available through the environment, so views read it with @Environment(\.modelContext).

slides.title: Why sensitive data needs the Keychain
slides.body: The Keychain is the system-provided secure storage for small, sensitive pieces of data, passwords, tokens, and cryptographic keys, encrypted at rest and protected by the device's security infrastructure. Unlike UserDefaults, Keychain items can be configured to survive app deletion, be excluded from backups, or require biometric authentication to access.

slides.title: The raw Keychain API and why wrappers exist
slides.body: Apple's native Keychain API (`SecItemAdd`, `SecItemCopyMatching`, `SecItemUpdate`, `SecItemDelete`) is a C-based API built around dictionaries of query parameters, which is verbose and easy to get subtly wrong. Many teams write a small typed wrapper, or use a well-vetted open-source one, around these calls to get a simple `save`/`load`/`delete` interface for strings or Data.
slides.example:
let query: [String: Any] = [
    kSecClass as String: kSecClassGenericPassword,
    kSecAttrAccount as String: "authToken",
    kSecValueData as String: tokenData
]
SecItemAdd(query as CFDictionary, nil)

slides.title: Accessibility levels
slides.body: Keychain items have an accessibility attribute (like `kSecAttrAccessibleAfterFirstUnlock` or `kSecAttrAccessibleWhenUnlockedThisDeviceOnly`) that controls when the item can be read, for example, only while the device is unlocked, or only after the first unlock since boot, which matters for background processes that need access before the user has unlocked the device. Choosing an overly permissive accessibility level for sensitive data increases the exposure window unnecessarily.

slides.title: What belongs in the Keychain vs elsewhere
slides.body: Authentication tokens, passwords, and API secrets belong in the Keychain; general app settings and non-sensitive preferences belong in UserDefaults; and structured application data belongs in SwiftData, Core Data, or files. Mixing these up, like storing a refresh token in UserDefaults for convenience, is a common but avoidable security mistake in production apps.

quiz.prompt: What kind of data is the Keychain specifically designed to store?

options.text: Small, sensitive data such as passwords, tokens, and cryptographic keys, encrypted at rest
Large media files like videos
Bulk structured application data with complex relationships
Non-sensitive user preferences like a theme setting

quiz.explanation: The Keychain is purpose-built for securely storing small sensitive secrets, leveraging device-level encryption and access control that general-purpose storage like UserDefaults doesn't provide.

quiz.prompt: Why do many teams build a small wrapper around Apple's native Keychain API instead of calling SecItemAdd/SecItemCopyMatching directly everywhere?

options.text: The native API is deprecated and no longer functions
The native API is a verbose, C-based, dictionary-driven interface that's easy to misuse, so a typed wrapper simplifies it to a save/load/delete interface
Wrappers are required by Apple's App Store review guidelines
The native API cannot store String values, only raw bytes

quiz.explanation: The raw Keychain API's dictionary-of-CFTypes design is powerful but error-prone to use correctly and repetitively at every call site, which is why a thin wrapper is common practice.

quiz.prompt: What does a Keychain item's accessibility attribute (like kSecAttrAccessibleWhenUnlockedThisDeviceOnly) control?

options.text: Whether the item is visible in the Settings app
How large the stored value is allowed to be
When the item can be read, such as only while the device is unlocked, and whether it can be restored on a different device
Whether the item can be queried using NSPredicate

quiz.explanation: Accessibility attributes govern the conditions under which the OS will let the app read the item, which matters for balancing convenience (e.g. background access) against minimizing exposure of sensitive data.

quiz.prompt: Why is storing a refresh token in UserDefaults considered a security mistake even though it's technically possible?

options.text: UserDefaults cannot store strings longer than 10 characters
It's not actually a mistake; UserDefaults and Keychain are equally secure
UserDefaults automatically deletes tokens after 5 minutes
UserDefaults is unencrypted, exposing the token more than the Keychain's encrypted, access-controlled storage would

quiz.explanation: Because UserDefaults data isn't encrypted the way Keychain items are, storing a sensitive credential there increases the risk of exposure compared to using the storage mechanism designed for secrets.

quiz.prompt: Which storage choice is most appropriate for a user's non-sensitive 'preferred temperature unit' setting?

options.text: UserDefaults (or @AppStorage), since it's a small, non-sensitive preference value
Keychain, since all user-specific data should be encrypted
SwiftData, since every persisted value needs a full model schema
It must be stored only in memory and re-entered every launch

quiz.explanation: A simple, non-sensitive preference is exactly the use case UserDefaults/@AppStorage is designed for; reserving Keychain for actual secrets keeps the right tool matched to the right kind of data.

slides.title: Matching the tool to the data
slides.body: Choosing a persistence layer is a matter of matching the data's characteristics, size, sensitivity, query needs, update frequency, to the tool built for that job: UserDefaults for small settings, Keychain for secrets, file-based Codable persistence for modest structured data, and SwiftData/Core Data for larger, queryable, relational datasets. Defaulting to the same tool for everything, regardless of fit, tends to cause pain as the app grows.

slides.title: A practical decision framework
slides.body: A useful set of questions: is it sensitive (Keychain)? Is it a single small setting (UserDefaults/@AppStorage)? Does it need relationships, complex queries, or frequent partial updates at meaningful scale (SwiftData)? Otherwise, is it just a moderate amount of structured data that changes as a whole (Codable + file)? Working through these in order usually converges on the right layer quickly.

slides.title: Mixing layers within one app
slides.body: Most real apps use several persistence layers side by side: @AppStorage for a handful of UI preferences, Keychain for the session token, and SwiftData for the app's core structured content. There's nothing wrong with this combination, each layer is doing the job it's best suited for, as long as the boundaries between them are deliberate rather than accidental.

slides.title: Migrating between layers as needs grow
slides.body: It's common for a feature to start simple, a Codable file cache for a small list, and outgrow that as the dataset or query needs grow, at which point migrating to SwiftData becomes worthwhile. Recognizing the signals early (frequent partial updates, complex filtering, dataset size climbing into the thousands) helps you migrate before the simpler approach becomes a real performance or maintainability problem.

quiz.prompt: Which persistence layer is the right default choice for storing a user's authentication token?

options.text: UserDefaults, for simplicity
Keychain, because it provides encrypted, access-controlled storage appropriate for secrets
A plain Codable JSON file in Documents
SwiftData, since it's the most modern framework

quiz.explanation: Regardless of how modern or convenient other frameworks are, sensitive credentials specifically need the Keychain's encryption and access control, not general-purpose persistence.

quiz.prompt: A feature needs to store a single Boolean flag indicating whether the user has seen a particular tutorial. What's the most appropriate storage choice?

options.text: SwiftData with a dedicated @Model type
Keychain, since all persisted booleans should be encrypted
UserDefaults (or @AppStorage), since it's a single small, non-sensitive setting
A custom SQLite database

quiz.explanation: A single simple flag is exactly the lightweight use case UserDefaults/@AppStorage is designed for; reaching for a full database or encrypted storage would be unnecessary overhead.

quiz.prompt: What signals suggest a feature has outgrown a simple Codable-file persistence approach and should migrate to SwiftData?

options.text: The feature now has exactly one more property than before
The team simply prefers newer APIs regardless of actual need
The app has been updated to a new version number
The dataset has grown large, needs frequent partial updates, or requires complex querying/filtering that whole-file read/write can't support efficiently

quiz.explanation: The practical signals are scale and access pattern: large datasets, frequent partial updates, and query needs are exactly what a proper persistence framework like SwiftData is designed to handle efficiently, unlike whole-file rewrites.

quiz.prompt: Is it a problem for a single app to use UserDefaults, Keychain, and SwiftData simultaneously for different kinds of data?

options.text: No, using each layer for the kind of data it's best suited for (preferences, secrets, structured content) is a normal and reasonable design
Yes, an app should always standardize on exactly one persistence mechanism
Yes, because SwiftData cannot coexist with UserDefaults in the same app
No, but only if the app targets iOS 16 or earlier

quiz.explanation: Mixing persistence layers deliberately, matching each to its appropriate data type, is standard practice; the goal is intentional boundaries, not forcing everything through a single mechanism.

quiz.prompt: A junior engineer proposes storing the entire app's structured content catalog (tens of thousands of records, frequently filtered and updated) as a single large Codable JSON file. What's the main concern?

options.text: Codable cannot encode more than a few dozen objects
Every update would require re-encoding and rewriting the whole file, and there's no efficient way to query or filter without loading everything into memory
JSON files cannot exceed 1KB in size on iOS
There is no concern; this is the recommended approach at any scale

quiz.explanation: At that scale and update frequency, whole-file read/write becomes a real performance and memory problem, and the lack of indexed querying makes filtering expensive; this is precisely the scenario SwiftData is built for.

quiz.prompt: What kind of data is UserDefaults designed for?

options.text: Encrypted secrets like tokens
Large relational datasets
Small, simple settings and preferences
Binary video files

quiz.explanation: UserDefaults is a lightweight plist-backed key-value store meant for small configuration values, not secrets, large datasets, or media.

quiz.prompt: What does SwiftUI's @AppStorage do?

options.text: Encrypts data before saving it to disk
Creates a SwiftData ModelContainer
Persists data to iCloud automatically
Reads and writes a UserDefaults value and updates the view automatically when it changes

quiz.explanation: @AppStorage is a thin, observable wrapper around UserDefaults for simple settings bound directly into SwiftUI view state.

quiz.prompt: Why is a Codable-model-to-file approach a poor fit for a large dataset with frequent partial updates?

options.text: Each update typically requires re-encoding and rewriting the entire file, with no efficient querying support
Codable cannot handle nested objects
Files larger than 1MB cannot be written on iOS
It actually scales perfectly well regardless of size

quiz.explanation: The whole-file read/write model makes frequent small updates and complex queries inefficient compared to a real database engine.

quiz.prompt: In Core Data, what happens to changes on a managed object if the context is never saved?

options.text: They persist automatically in the background
They are lost, since changes only reach the persistent store via an explicit context.save()
Core Data throws a compile-time error

quiz.prompt: Why must a given NSManagedObjectContext only be used on the thread/queue it was created for?

options.text: Core Data automatically synchronizes context access across all threads
It's only a performance guideline, not a hard requirement
Contexts are not thread-safe, and cross-thread access can cause crashes or data corruption
This restriction only applies to contexts backed by an in-memory store

quiz.prompt: What does the `@Model` macro do in SwiftData?

options.text: Marks a class as unavailable for SwiftUI previews
Converts a struct into a class automatically
Registers the type with URLSession for networking
Turns a plain Swift class into a persisted model, generating the necessary storage and tracking machinery

quiz.explanation: @Model is the core SwiftData mechanism that makes a Swift class persistable without manually defining a Core Data-style schema file.

quiz.prompt: What does @Query provide in a SwiftUI view using SwiftData?

quiz.prompt: Why should an authentication token be stored in the Keychain rather than UserDefaults?

options.text: UserDefaults cannot store string values
The Keychain provides encrypted, access-controlled storage appropriate for secrets, while UserDefaults is unencrypted
Tokens are too large to fit in UserDefaults

quiz.prompt: What does a Keychain item's accessibility attribute (e.g. kSecAttrAccessibleAfterFirstUnlock) control?

options.text: The maximum size of the stored value
Whether the item appears in Spotlight search
When the item can be read by the app, such as only after the device has been unlocked once since boot
Whether the item syncs across the user's other devices by default

quiz.explanation: Accessibility attributes determine under what device-lock conditions the OS permits reading the item, balancing convenience against exposure risk.

quiz.prompt: A team needs to store: (1) a dark-mode toggle, (2) a session token, and (3) a catalog of thousands of frequently-queried articles. What's the appropriate layer for each?

options.text: All three in SwiftData, since it's the most modern framework

@AppStorage/UserDefaults for the toggle, Keychain for the token, SwiftData for the article catalog

quiz.explanation: Each kind of data maps to the tool built for it: simple preferences to UserDefaults, secrets to Keychain, and large queryable structured data to SwiftData — mixing layers deliberately is the normal, recommended approach.

slides.title: What Instruments is for
slides.body: Instruments is Xcode's profiling tool for measuring an app's real runtime behavior, CPU usage, memory allocations, time spent per method, disk and network activity, using dedicated 'instruments' (templates) rather than guessing from reading source code. Profiling with real data is essential because performance intuition is frequently wrong about where the actual bottleneck lives.

slides.title: Key instrument templates
slides.body: The Time Profiler samples the call stack periodically to show where CPU time is actually being spent, the Allocations instrument tracks memory usage and object lifetimes, and the Leaks instrument specifically flags memory that's no longer reachable but never freed. Choosing the right instrument for the symptom you're chasing (slow scrolling vs. growing memory vs. a suspected leak) makes the investigation far more targeted.

slides.title: Reading a Time Profiler trace
slides.body: The Time Profiler's call tree shows which functions consumed the most CPU time, and enabling 'Separate by Thread' is important for distinguishing main-thread work (which affects UI responsiveness) from background work (which usually doesn't). Sorting by 'Self Weight' highlights the specific function doing the heavy lifting, rather than just the top-level function that happened to call it.

slides.title: Profiling in a Release-like configuration
slides.body: Profiling a Debug build can give misleading results, since Debug builds skip compiler optimizations and include extra runtime checks that inflate timings unrealistically. Using Xcode's Profile action (Cmd+I), which builds with Release-like optimizations by default, gives numbers that are much closer to what real users will experience.

Instruments modifies the app's source code automatically to fix issues

quiz.explanation: Performance intuition is frequently wrong; measuring real execution with Instruments grounds optimization decisions in actual data rather than assumptions.

The thread with the fewest samples

quiz.explanation: Self Weight isolates time spent directly in a function's own body, excluding time attributed to its callees, which pinpoints the actual code doing the heavy work rather than just a high-level caller.

slides.title: Why the main thread is special
slides.body: The main thread is responsible for UI rendering, layout, and handling user input, and iOS targets a smooth frame rate (commonly 60 or up to 120 Hz on ProMotion devices), giving the main thread only a matter of milliseconds per frame. Any work that blocks the main thread for longer than that budget causes dropped frames, visible as stutter or an unresponsive UI (jank).

slides.title: Common sources of accidental main-thread work
slides.body: Synchronous file I/O, JSON decoding of large payloads, image decoding, and even seemingly innocuous computed properties that do real work in a SwiftUI view's `body`, are common culprits for accidentally blocking the main thread. Because these often 'work fine' with small test data, they can slip through code review and only show up as jank with production-scale data.

slides.title: Moving work off the main thread
slides.body: The fix is usually to perform the expensive work in a background Task and only hop back to the main actor with the final, already-computed result, rather than doing the computation itself inside MainActor-isolated code. This keeps the main thread free to keep handling input and drawing frames while the heavy lifting happens elsewhere.

slides.title: Spotting main-thread work in Instruments
slides.body: In a Time Profiler trace filtered to the main thread, any function consuming a large 'Self Weight' or 'Total Weight' during a period of visible jank is a strong candidate for offloading. Correlating the trace timeline with when a stutter was actually observed (e.g. during a scroll or a screen transition) helps confirm you're looking at the right span of time.

quiz.explanation: Since the main thread drives rendering and UI updates, exceeding the per-frame time budget causes the system to miss a frame, which is visible as dropped frames or jank.

quiz.explanation: SwiftUI evaluates body on the main thread, potentially on every re-render, so any non-trivial computation placed there directly competes with the frame budget needed for smooth UI.

quiz.explanation: Moving the actual expensive work to a background context and keeping only the final, lightweight state update on the main actor preserves UI responsiveness.

quiz.explanation: Correlating high main-thread CPU consumption with the actual moment of observed jank is what confirms a function is the real cause, rather than unrelated background activity.

Production builds decode JSON more slowly than Debug builds by design

quiz.explanation: The same code can perform fine with a handful of test records but become expensive with a realistically large production payload, which is why performance issues often only surface under production-scale data.

slides.title: How SwiftUI decides what to redraw
slides.body: SwiftUI re-evaluates a view's `body` when its observed state changes, then diffs the new view tree against the old one to determine what actually needs to be redrawn on screen; identity (whether SwiftUI considers two views 'the same' across updates) drives whether it animates a transition or treats it as an entirely new view instance with reset state.

slides.title: Structural vs explicit identity
slides.body: For most views, identity is structural, determined by the view's position and type in the view tree, so SwiftUI can tell two `Text` views apart implicitly. In a `ForEach`, though, identity must be explicit via `Identifiable` or an `id:` parameter, and using an unstable id (like an array index for a mutating list) causes SwiftUI to misattribute state or animate incorrectly when items are inserted or removed.
slides.example:
ForEach(items, id: \.id) { item in ItemRow(item: item) } // stable identity
// vs. using an array index as id: breaks on insert/remove/reorder

slides.title: Over-observation causes unnecessary re-renders
slides.body: A view re-renders whenever ANY property it reads from an observed object changes, so a view that reads an entire large model object, even if it only displays one field, re-renders on every unrelated change to that object. Narrowing what a view actually observes (reading only the specific properties it needs, or splitting a large model into smaller pieces) reduces unnecessary re-renders.

slides.title: The Observation framework's fine-grained tracking
slides.body: The `@Observable` macro (Observation framework, iOS 17+) tracks property-level access rather than the old `ObservableObject`/`@Published` model, which invalidated a view on ANY published property change regardless of whether the view actually read that property. This means views using `@Observable` models naturally re-render less often, since SwiftUI only invalidates a view for the specific properties it actually accessed during the last body evaluation.

quiz.explanation: SwiftUI needs a consistent identity per logical item to correctly preserve or discard view state and animate transitions; an index-based id shifts meaning whenever the list changes shape, breaking that correspondence.

quiz.explanation: ObservableObject's invalidation is coarse-grained: it fires on any @Published change, so a view that reads the whole object re-renders even for unrelated property changes it doesn't actually display.

quiz.prompt: How does the `@Observable` macro (Observation framework) improve on ObservableObject's re-render behavior?

quiz.explanation: @Observable enables fine-grained dependency tracking: SwiftUI knows exactly which properties a view's body accessed and only invalidates that view when one of those specific properties changes.
