slides.title: Why raw image size matters
slides.body: An oversized image, larger in pixel dimensions than it will ever be displayed at, wastes memory and decode time proportional to its full resolution, not its display size, since decoding happens at the image's native dimensions before any downscaling for display. Shipping assets at an appropriate resolution (matching the actual display size at the device's scale factor) avoids this waste from the start.

slides.title: Downsampling large images before display
slides.body: For images loaded at runtime (e.g. from the network or the photo library) that may be much larger than needed, downsampling with `ImageIO` (via `CGImageSourceCreateThumbnailAtIndex` with `kCGImageSourceCreateThumbnailFromImageAlways` and a `kCGImageSourceThumbnailMaxPixelSize`) decodes directly at a smaller size, avoiding the memory spike of decoding the full-resolution image just to shrink it afterward.

slides.title: Asset catalogs and compression formats
slides.body: Using Asset Catalogs lets Xcode deliver only the appropriately-scaled variant per device via App Thinning, and choosing an efficient format, HEIC for photographic content, or vector PDF/SVG for icons that need to scale cleanly, reduces both app size and decode cost compared to using oversized or poorly-compressed PNGs everywhere.

slides.title: Caching decoded images to avoid repeated work
slides.body: Decoding the same image repeatedly, like every time a cell scrolls back into view, wastes CPU; caching the decoded `UIImage`/`CGImage` in memory (with a bounded cache like `NSCache` that responds to memory pressure) avoids redundant decode work while still letting the system reclaim memory when needed.
slides.example:
let cache = NSCache<NSString, UIImage>()
cache.countLimit = 100 // NSCache automatically evicts under memory pressure

options.text: SwiftUI automatically compresses any image to its display size before decoding

This is only a concern for PNG files, not JPEG or HEIC

quiz.explanation: The decode cost and memory footprint scale with the image's actual pixel dimensions, so simply displaying it smaller with layout constraints doesn't reduce that underlying cost.

options.text: It decodes the image directly at the smaller target size, avoiding the memory spike of first decoding at full resolution and then downscaling
It applies a watermark to the image automatically

quiz.explanation: Downsampling via ImageIO decodes straight to the requested size, sidestepping the temporary full-resolution decode that a naive load-then-resize approach would incur.

options.text: It automatically translates image alt text into multiple languages

quiz.explanation: HEIC's compression is generally more efficient for photo-like content than PNG, which is a lossless format better suited to graphics with sharp edges or few colors, like icons.

quiz.explanation: NSCache is designed specifically for this kind of memory-sensitive caching: it participates in the system's memory pressure handling and evicts entries automatically, unlike a Dictionary which just grows unbounded.

slides.title: Why launch time matters and how it's measured
slides.body: Slow launch is one of the first performance impressions a user forms, and Apple's guidance targets getting to an interactive first screen quickly, historically citing under 400ms pre-main time as a goal. Launch time splits into 'pre-main' time (dynamic linking, loading libraries and frameworks) and 'post-main' time (your app's own startup code, including the first view's setup), each with different causes and fixes.

slides.title: Reducing pre-main time
slides.body: Pre-main time grows with the number of dynamic libraries and frameworks the app links against, since each one must be located and loaded before your code runs at all; consolidating dependencies, preferring static linking for small frameworks, and avoiding unnecessary third-party libraries all reduce this. Xcode's Organizer and the App Launch instrument can show a breakdown of where pre-main time is going.

slides.title: Reducing post-main time
slides.body: Post-main time is dominated by whatever your app does before it can show a usable first screen: heavy work in `application(_:didFinishLaunchingWithOptions:)` or `App.init()`, synchronous disk reads, or eagerly initializing subsystems the first screen doesn't actually need yet. Deferring non-critical setup (analytics initialization, prefetching unrelated data) until after the first frame is drawn is one of the highest-leverage launch time fixes.

slides.title: Measuring launch time in practice
slides.body: The App Launch instrument in Instruments breaks a real launch down into phases and flags the specific initializers or symbols taking the most time, which is far more precise than guessing from `applicationDidFinishLaunching` alone. Measuring on a real, representative (ideally older/slower) device matters, since launch time on the newest simulator or device can look artificially fast.
slides.example:
// App Launch instrument phase breakdown (illustrative):
// Static init: 40ms | Dynamic linking: 90ms | didFinishLaunching: 210ms | First frame: 60ms

quiz.explanation: Faster hardware can hide real launch time regressions; testing on representative, potentially older devices gives a more accurate picture of what real users experience.

quiz.explanation: The App Launch instrument gives concrete, measured data about where time is actually going during a real launch, which is far more actionable than inspecting code and guessing.

slides.title: Retain cycles and ARC
slides.body: Swift uses Automatic Reference Counting (ARC), where an object is deallocated once its strong reference count drops to zero; a retain cycle happens when two or more objects hold strong references to each other (directly or via a closure), so neither's count ever reaches zero and both leak. Closures are a particularly common source, since a closure captures `self` strongly by default unless told otherwise.

slides.title: Breaking cycles with weak and unowned
slides.body: Marking a captured reference `[weak self]` in a closure, or a delegate property `weak var`, breaks the strong reference cycle by not incrementing the reference count; `unowned` does the same but crashes if accessed after the referenced object has been deallocated, so it should only be used when the reference's lifetime is guaranteed to outlive the access.

slides.title: Using the Leaks and Allocations instruments
slides.body: The Leaks instrument specifically flags memory that has become unreachable but was never freed, a true leak, while the Allocations instrument shows overall memory growth over time and can capture generation snapshots to compare what's grown between two points, useful for finding retained objects that aren't technically 'leaked' by ARC's definition but are held longer than intended.

slides.title: Memory graph debugger in Xcode
slides.body: Xcode's Memory Graph Debugger (the icon in the debug bar during a live debug session) visualizes the live object graph and highlights suspected leaks with a purple exclamation icon, letting you inspect exactly which objects are holding a strong reference to a supposedly-deallocated instance. This is often faster for diagnosing a specific suspected leak than running a full Instruments trace.

quiz.prompt: What causes a retain cycle between two Swift objects under ARC?

options.text: Both objects conform to the same protocol
Two or more objects hold strong references to each other, so neither's reference count ever reaches zero and neither gets deallocated
One object is a class and the other is a struct
The objects were both created on a background thread

quiz.explanation: ARC deallocates an object once its strong reference count hits zero; if two objects mutually hold strong references (directly or through a closure), that count never reaches zero for either, and both leak.

quiz.prompt: Why does capturing `self` in a closure stored as a property (like a completion handler) commonly cause a retain cycle?

options.text: Closures always capture self weakly by default
Closures cannot capture self under any circumstances
By default, a closure captures self strongly, and if that closure is itself stored as a strong property on self, self and the closure end up strongly referencing each other
This only happens in Objective-C, never in Swift

quiz.explanation: The default strong capture, combined with the closure being retained by self (e.g. as a stored property), creates the classic self-to-closure-to-self strong reference loop.

quiz.prompt: What's the key risk of using `unowned` instead of `weak` for a captured reference?

options.text: unowned references cannot be captured in closures at all
unowned always causes a retain cycle, defeating its purpose
unowned references are slower than weak references at runtime
Accessing an unowned reference after the referenced object has already been deallocated causes a crash, unlike weak which becomes nil safely

quiz.explanation: unowned assumes the referenced object will always outlive the access point; if that assumption is wrong and the object has already deallocated, accessing it crashes, whereas weak degrades gracefully to nil.

quiz.prompt: What does the Leaks instrument specifically detect, as distinct from general memory growth?

options.text: Memory that has become unreachable (no live references point to it, or only cyclical ones) but was never freed
Any increase in memory usage over time, regardless of cause
Only memory allocated on the main thread
Only memory used by system frameworks, not app code

quiz.explanation: Leaks specifically identifies memory ARC can no longer reach through any live reference path but that still hasn't been deallocated, which is the technical definition of a true leak, as opposed to memory that's just being held longer than ideal but is still reachable.

quiz.prompt: What does Xcode's Memory Graph Debugger help you see that's especially useful for diagnosing a specific suspected leak?

quiz.explanation: By visualizing actual strong reference chains between live objects, the Memory Graph Debugger lets you pinpoint exactly what's retaining an object that should have already been deallocated.

slides.title: The App and Scene protocols
slides.body: The SwiftUI App lifecycle replaces the old AppDelegate/SceneDelegate boilerplate with a declarative `App` protocol conformance as the entry point, and a `Scene` (most commonly `WindowGroup`) describing the app's UI structure. `@main` marks the type conforming to `App` as the program's entry point, and its `body` returns the scene content shown when the app launches.

slides.title: Observing scene phase changes
slides.body: The `@Environment(\.scenePhase)` value reports whether the current scene is `.active`, `.inactive`, or `.background`, and observing it with `.onChange(of:)` is the SwiftUI-native replacement for AppDelegate methods like `applicationDidBecomeActive` or `applicationDidEnterBackground`. This lets you react to lifecycle transitions without needing a UIKit delegate at all.

slides.title: Reacting to phase transitions
slides.body: A common pattern is pausing timers, saving in-progress state, or stopping location updates when the scene phase moves to `.background`, and resuming or refreshing data when it returns to `.active`. Because SwiftUI evaluates this declaratively, the same `.onChange(of: scenePhase)` modifier works whether the transition came from the user backgrounding the app or from a system interruption like an incoming call.

slides.title: Bridging to UIApplicationDelegate when needed
slides.body: Some system integrations, like push notification registration callbacks or certain URL scheme handling, still require `UIApplicationDelegate` methods; SwiftUI's `@UIApplicationDelegateAdaptor` lets you plug a traditional AppDelegate class into an otherwise SwiftUI-lifecycle app to receive those callbacks. This is the standard way to access UIKit-only hooks without abandoning the SwiftUI App/Scene structure entirely.

slides.title: Why background time is limited
slides.body: When an app moves to the background, iOS gives it only a short window of extra runtime (historically around 30 seconds via a background task) before suspending it, in order to preserve battery life and free resources for the foreground app. Understanding this constraint is essential: any 'finish this critical work before we're suspended' logic has to fit within that budget or use a purpose-built background API instead.

slides.title: Requesting extra time with a background task
slides.body: `UIApplication.shared.beginBackgroundTask(withName:expirationHandler:)` (or the structured `withBackgroundTask` in modern APIs) requests a short grace period to finish in-flight work, like completing a network upload, and the expiration handler is your last chance to clean up if the work doesn't finish before time runs out. Every `beginBackgroundTask` call must be matched with `endBackgroundTask` or the app is penalized for holding background time unnecessarily.

slides.title: BGTaskScheduler for deferred and periodic work
slides.body: For work that doesn't need to happen immediately, like periodic content refresh or app maintenance, the `BackgroundTasks` framework's `BGTaskScheduler` lets you register a `BGAppRefreshTask` or `BGProcessingTask` that the system runs at its own discretion based on factors like battery level, network conditions, and usage patterns. The app registers a handler for a task identifier declared in Info.plist and requests scheduling, but the OS decides exactly when (or whether) to actually run it.

slides.title: Background modes require declared capabilities
slides.body: True ongoing background execution, like continuous audio playback, background location updates, or VoIP, requires declaring the corresponding Background Modes capability in the app's configuration, and each mode comes with its own API and App Store review expectations. Declaring a background mode you don't genuinely need, or misusing one, is a common cause of App Store rejection.

quiz.explanation: BGAppRefreshTask is designed exactly for this kind of periodic, system-scheduled refresh work where exact timing isn't required and the OS optimizes for battery and resource usage.

slides.title: Why state restoration matters
slides.body: iOS can terminate a backgrounded app at any time to reclaim memory for the foreground app, and when the user later relaunches it, a good app restores the user to roughly where they left off (the same screen, scroll position, or in-progress input) rather than dumping them back at the root. This preserves continuity and avoids the app feeling like it 'forgot' what the user was doing.

slides.title: SwiftUI's Scene-based restoration with @SceneStorage
slides.body: `@SceneStorage` persists small pieces of UI state, like a selected tab index or a navigation path, tied to a specific scene instance, and the system automatically restores that value when the scene is recreated after termination. It's intended for lightweight UI state, not for substantial application data, which belongs in a real persistence layer instead.

slides.title: UIKit's NSUserActivity-based state restoration
slides.body: In UIKit, state restoration traditionally uses `NSUserActivity` to capture what the user was doing (encoded as a dictionary of relevant identifiers, like a specific document or record being viewed) and restores that activity when the scene reconnects, rather than serializing the entire view controller hierarchy. This activity-based approach is also what powers Handoff between a user's devices.

slides.title: What NOT to restore
slides.body: State restoration should reconstruct navigational and UI context (which screen, which item), not attempt to fully replay every transient piece of state, like an in-flight network request or animation state, which should just restart fresh. Trying to restore too much can actually make the experience feel worse if restored state is stale or inconsistent with current data.

quiz.explanation: The system may terminate suspended apps under memory pressure to give resources to the foreground app, which is exactly why state restoration matters for a good relaunch experience.

slides.title: Requesting permission and registering
slides.body: Before an app can receive remote push notifications, it must request authorization via `UNUserNotificationCenter.current().requestAuthorization(options:)` and, once granted, call `UIApplication.shared.registerForRemoteNotifications()`, which asynchronously provides a unique device token through the AppDelegate callback `didRegisterForRemoteNotificationsWithDeviceToken`. That token is what your backend uses to address push notifications to this specific device installation via APNs (Apple Push Notification service).

slides.title: The notification payload and delivery paths
slides.body: A remote notification payload can be a standard alert (title/body shown by the system) or a 'silent' background push (`content-available: 1` with no visible alert) that wakes the app briefly to fetch fresh data before the user even opens it. Handling both cases correctly requires implementing the right delegate methods and respecting their time constraints, since background pushes get a very limited execution window.

slides.title: UNUserNotificationCenterDelegate
slides.body: Implementing `UNUserNotificationCenterDelegate` lets you control how a notification is presented while the app is in the foreground (via `willPresent`, where you decide whether to show a banner/sound even though the app is already active) and respond when the user taps a notification (via `didReceive response:`), such as navigating to the relevant screen.

slides.title: Deep linking from a notification tap
slides.body: A well-designed notification handling flow extracts routing information from the notification's payload (like a specific post ID) in `didReceive response:` and translates it into in-app navigation, so tapping a notification takes the user directly to the relevant content rather than just opening the app to its default screen. This routing logic is often shared with universal link handling, since both need to map an external payload to an in-app destination.

quiz.explanation: Authorization must be explicitly requested from the user, and registration with APNs produces the device token your backend needs to target that specific installation.

slides.title: Suspension vs. termination
slides.body: When a user backgrounds an app, it's typically suspended (frozen in memory, consuming no CPU) rather than immediately terminated; termination happens later, silently, when the system needs to reclaim memory, or when the user force-quits the app from the app switcher. Because termination from a suspended state happens without warning the app first, you can't rely on any 'about to terminate' callback firing reliably in that case.

slides.title: Why work should be saved proactively, not just on willTerminate
slides.body: `applicationWillTerminate` (or its SwiftUI scenePhase equivalent) is only called in limited circumstances, notably not when the app is silently killed from a suspended background state, so relying on it as your only save point is unsafe. The reliable pattern is to persist important state as it changes, or at the latest when the app transitions to `.background`, rather than waiting for a termination signal that may never come.

slides.title: Responding to memory warnings
slides.body: `didReceiveMemoryWarning` (UIKit) or the equivalent low-memory notification signals that the system is under memory pressure and may terminate the app if it doesn't free some memory soon; a well-behaved app responds by releasing caches, discarded images, or other reconstructable data, while preserving essential state that can't be easily regenerated.

slides.title: Designing for unexpected termination
slides.body: Because termination can happen at any time without a guaranteed callback, especially from a suspended background state, the safest architecture treats every state transition to background (via scenePhase or applicationDidEnterBackground) as the reliable save point, not a last-resort termination handler. This mirrors the general lesson that in mobile development, 'save early and often' beats relying on a graceful shutdown sequence.

slides.title: Multiple scenes, one app process
slides.body: On iPadOS (and macOS via Catalyst/Mac apps), a single app process can host multiple independent scene instances simultaneously, for example two separate windows showing different documents, each represented by its own `UIScene`/SwiftUI scene instance with its own view hierarchy and navigation state. This is a meaningful shift from the one-window-per-app assumption that held throughout most of iOS's history.

slides.title: Per-scene state, not per-app state
slides.body: Because each scene instance can represent a different piece of content, state that's specific to what's currently being viewed, like the selected document or navigation path, needs to live at the scene level (e.g. via `@SceneStorage` or scene-scoped model objects), not in app-wide singletons that would incorrectly be shared across every open window.
slides.example:
// wrong: a single app-wide singleton can't represent two different open documents
// right: scene-scoped state, e.g. via @SceneStorage or a scene-specific model owned by that scene's root view

slides.title: Handling a new scene's connection options
slides.body: When the system creates a new scene, for example because the user chose 'New Window' or tapped a notification that should open in a fresh window, `UIScene.ConnectionOptions` (or SwiftUI's `onOpenURL`/scene-level handling) carries context about how and why that scene was created, like a URL to open or a user activity to continue. Using this context to configure the new scene's initial content is what makes multi-window flows feel intentional rather than generic.

slides.title: Designing view models for multi-scene safety
slides.body: A view model or shared service that assumes it's the only instance of 'the app' in memory, such as one holding a single currently-selected item as global mutable state, breaks under multi-window use since two scenes could stomp on each other's selection. Designing state ownership explicitly, deciding what's genuinely global (like an auth session) versus what belongs to a single scene (like which item is currently open) is central to supporting multitasking correctly.
slides.example:
// global (shared across scenes): AuthSession
// scene-scoped (one per window): DocumentEditorViewModel(document: openDocument)

slides.title: Caching as an architectural decision
slides.body: Caching trades staleness for speed, and that trade is never free: every cache needs an invalidation policy, a storage budget, and an owner who understands when the cached value is allowed to be wrong. Senior engineers choose the cache layer (in-memory, on-disk, HTTP) based on how expensive the data is to refetch and how tolerant the feature is of staleness. A cache without an eviction and invalidation story is just a bug that hasn't happened yet.

slides.title: Cursor-based vs. offset-based pagination
slides.body: Offset-based pagination (page=3&size=20) is simple but breaks under concurrent writes: if rows are inserted or deleted between requests, items shift and the client sees duplicates or gaps. Cursor-based pagination anchors each request to an opaque token derived from the last item seen, so it stays correct even as the underlying dataset mutates.
slides.example:
GET /feed?cursor=eyJpZCI6MTIzfQ&limit=20
// server decodes cursor -> last id 123, returns next 20 items after it

slides.title: Offline-first as a default posture
slides.body: Offline-first architecture treats the network as an unreliable, high-latency dependency rather than the source of truth: the local database is authoritative for what the UI renders, and a background sync engine reconciles it with the server opportunistically. This makes the app feel instant and keeps it usable on flaky connections, but it pushes real complexity into conflict resolution and sync-state tracking.

slides.title: Matching cache lifetime to data volatility
slides.body: Not all data deserves the same staleness budget: a user's display name can be cached for hours, a stock price or seat-availability count should barely be cached at all, and a paginated feed sits somewhere in between with a short TTL plus pull-to-refresh. Segmenting caching policy by data type, instead of applying one blanket TTL app-wide, is what keeps the app both fast and correct.

quiz.prompt: A social feed screen needs to support infinite scroll on a dataset that is frequently modified by other users in real time. Which pagination approach is most appropriate?

options.text: Cursor-based pagination, since it stays consistent even as rows are inserted or removed between requests
Loading the entire dataset once and paginating client-side
Offset-based pagination with a client-side cache to paper over duplicates
Offset-based pagination, since it is simpler to implement and debug

quiz.explanation: Cursor-based pagination anchors each page to the last seen item rather than a numeric position, so concurrent inserts/deletes don't shift results into duplicates or gaps.

quiz.prompt: What is the primary risk of introducing a cache without a defined invalidation policy?

options.text: It will use slightly more memory than expected
The app will show stale or incorrect data with no mechanism to know when to refresh it
It will make the app's build time longer
It will violate App Store review guidelines

quiz.explanation: A cache is only safe when there is an explicit answer to 'when does this become wrong,' whether that's a TTL, an event, or an explicit invalidation call — without one, staleness bugs are inevitable and hard to trace.

quiz.prompt: In an offline-first architecture, what should the UI layer read from?

options.text: In-memory state only, discarding data once the view disappears
The network response directly, falling back to cache only on failure
The local database, which is treated as the source of truth and updated by a background sync process
Whichever of network or cache responds first, using the faster result

quiz.explanation: Offline-first flips the usual assumption: the local store is authoritative for rendering, and a sync engine reconciles it with the server in the background, which is what keeps the UI responsive regardless of connectivity.

quiz.prompt: A junior engineer proposes caching every network response for 24 hours 'to be safe and fast.' What is the strongest objection to this blanket policy?

options.text: Caching should never be used in a well-designed app
Caching responses violates most REST API license agreements
24 hours is an arbitrary number and should be exactly 12 hours instead
Different data has different staleness tolerance, so a single TTL will either serve unacceptably stale data for volatile endpoints or waste cache capacity on rarely-changing ones

quiz.explanation: Staleness tolerance varies by data type — a blanket TTL is a proxy for actually thinking about which data can be stale for how long, and applying one policy everywhere either breaks correctness or wastes the cache's value.

quiz.prompt: Which scenario is the best fit for event-driven cache invalidation rather than a simple TTL?

options.text: A user's own profile data that the app itself can mutate (e.g., after they edit their bio) and should reflect immediately
A weather forecast that updates on the server every few hours regardless of client actions
An onboarding tutorial's static copy text
A static list of country codes bundled with the app

quiz.explanation: When the client itself is the source of a mutation, it can proactively invalidate or update the cache the moment the change succeeds, giving correctness a TTL alone can't guarantee for self-caused changes.

slides.title: What makes a contract good
slides.body: A good API contract is explicit about types, required vs. optional fields, and error shapes, and it hides server-side implementation details the client shouldn't depend on. The contract is the thing both teams can change their internals around without breaking each other, so ambiguity in it (an 'it depends' field, an undocumented enum) becomes a recurring source of production bugs.

slides.title: Designing contracts to evolve without breaking
slides.body: Additive, backward-compatible changes — new optional fields, new enum cases handled with a default case, new endpoints — let clients and servers deploy independently. Renaming or removing a field, or narrowing what a field can contain, is a breaking change and needs a version bump or a deprecation window, not a silent edit.

slides.title: Consumer-driven contract testing
slides.body: Rather than trusting that a documented schema stays true, consumer-driven contract tests let the client team encode their actual expectations (which fields they read, in what shape) as a test suite the server runs in CI. This catches breaking changes at the source, before they ship, instead of at runtime in a client that's already in the App Store.

slides.title: Errors are part of the contract too
slides.body: A well-designed API returns structured, machine-readable error bodies (a stable error code plus a human-readable message) rather than relying on HTTP status codes alone, since 400 vs 422 vs 409 can't express 'this coupon expired' vs 'this coupon was already used.' Clients should be able to branch on the error code, not string-match the message.

quiz.prompt: A backend team wants to change the type of an existing JSON field from a string to a nested object to support new functionality. What is the senior-engineer-approved way to ship this?

options.text: Change the field in place since JSON is loosely typed and clients should adapt
Add a new field with the new shape (or bump the API version) and deprecate the old field on a timeline, rather than mutating the existing field's type
Ship the change directly to production and notify the mobile team afterward
Avoid the change entirely since API contracts should never change once shipped

quiz.explanation: Changing a field's type in place breaks every client currently decoding it as the old type; additive changes or a versioned migration path let clients update on their own schedule.

quiz.prompt: Why is relying solely on HTTP status codes (e.g., 400) insufficient for conveying business-logic errors like 'this coupon has already been redeemed'?

options.text: Clients are not allowed to read HTTP status codes on iOS
HTTP status codes are deprecated in modern APIs
Status codes express a category of failure, not the specific business reason, so clients can't reliably branch on 'expired' vs 'already used' vs 'invalid' without a structured error code
Status codes cannot be returned over HTTPS

quiz.explanation: A single 400 can mean many different business failures; a structured error code in the response body gives the client something specific and stable to branch on, while the message stays for humans.

quiz.prompt: What is the main advantage of consumer-driven contract tests over relying purely on shared documentation?

options.text: They make the API faster at runtime
They replace the need for versioning APIs
They eliminate the need for a backend team entirely
They encode what clients actually depend on as executable tests the server runs in CI, catching breaking changes before release instead of relying on docs staying accurate

quiz.explanation: Documentation drifts from reality; contract tests are executable and run automatically, so a server change that breaks a real client expectation fails CI immediately rather than surfacing as a production incident.

quiz.prompt: A mobile client decodes a `status` enum from the server. The server team plans to add a new case next quarter. What client-side design avoids a crash or broken UI when that happens?

options.text: Decode the enum with an `unknown`/default fallback case so unrecognized values degrade gracefully instead of failing to decode
Ask the server team to never add new enum cases
Re-submit the app to the App Store every time the server adds a case
Force-unwrap the enum since the server contract guarantees only known cases will ever be sent

quiz.explanation: Treating server-controlled enums as open sets with a default/unknown case is a standard forward-compatibility technique — it lets the server evolve independently without forcing a synchronized client release.

quiz.prompt: Two teams are integrating a new endpoint. The backend engineer says 'the docs are up to date, just build against those.' What is the strongest risk with skipping any form of contract verification?

options.text: Documentation review takes longer than writing tests
Docs can silently drift from the actual server behavior, and without an automated check, that drift is discovered in production rather than in CI
This approach makes the API slower
It violates App Store guidelines to build against documentation

quiz.explanation: Documentation is a claim, not a guarantee; without something automated tying the docs to the live implementation, integration bugs from drift surface as runtime failures rather than caught pre-release.

slides.title: Pull, push, and hybrid sync models
slides.body: Pull-based sync (client polls or refreshes on demand) is simple and client-controlled but can be stale or wasteful; push-based sync (server-sent events, silent push, websockets) is timely but adds infrastructure and battery cost. Most production systems use a hybrid: push as a low-latency 'something changed' signal, followed by a pull to fetch the authoritative state.

slides.title: Conflict resolution strategies
slides.body: When the same record is edited offline on two devices, the sync layer needs an explicit merge policy: last-write-wins (simplest, can silently drop a user's edits), field-level merging (merge non-conflicting fields, flag conflicting ones), or CRDT-style structures that are mathematically guaranteed to converge. The right choice depends on how costly a silently-lost edit is to the user.
slides.example:
// Last-write-wins by server timestamp
if localEdit.updatedAt > remote.updatedAt { push(localEdit) } else { adopt(remote) }

slides.title: Idempotency in sync operations
slides.body: Sync operations are retried after timeouts, app kills, and network drops, so every mutating sync request needs to be safe to apply twice — typically via a client-generated idempotency key the server deduplicates on. Without idempotency, a retried 'create order' after a timeout can create two orders even though the first one actually succeeded server-side.

slides.title: Handling partial failures in a sync batch
slides.body: When a sync batch of 50 pending local changes is sent and 3 fail server-side validation, the sync engine needs a policy for the other 47: apply-and-report-failures is usually right, so one bad record doesn't block everything else from syncing. The failed items should be marked and surfaced to the user or retried individually, never silently dropped.

quiz.prompt: A note-taking app allows offline editing on multiple devices. The same note is edited on a phone (offline) and an iPad (offline) before either syncs. What is the risk of using pure last-write-wins by timestamp?

options.text: It only works for numeric fields, not text
It is computationally too expensive for mobile devices
One device's edits can silently overwrite the other's, permanently losing content the user typed, with no indication anything was lost
It requires a CRDT library that doesn't exist for iOS

quiz.explanation: Last-write-wins is simple but has no concept of merging — it picks one version and discards the other, which for free-text content means silent, irrecoverable data loss for whichever edit lost.

quiz.prompt: Why should a 'submit order' sync request include a client-generated idempotency key?

options.text: It is required by Swift's Codable protocol
It removes the need for authentication on the request
It makes the JSON payload smaller
It lets the server recognize and deduplicate a retried request (e.g., after a timeout) so the same action isn't applied twice

quiz.explanation: Retries are inevitable in mobile networking; an idempotency key lets the server tell 'this is the same request retried' from 'this is a new request,' preventing duplicate side effects like double-charging or duplicate orders.

quiz.prompt: A sync batch of 50 local changes is sent to the server; 3 fail validation. What is the best client behavior?

options.text: Apply the 47 successful changes and retain only the 3 failed ones for retry or user-facing resolution
Silently discard the 3 failures and mark the whole batch as synced
Stop syncing entirely until the user manually intervenes on all 50 items
Roll back all 50 changes locally since the batch didn't fully succeed

quiz.explanation: Treating the batch as atomic-or-nothing needlessly blocks unrelated successful changes; isolating the failures lets the majority sync while giving a clear, scoped path to resolve the problem records.

quiz.prompt: What is the main tradeoff of a pure push-based sync architecture (server pushes every change immediately) versus a hybrid push-then-pull model?

options.text: Push-only is always slower than polling
Push-only requires trusting the push payload as complete and current state, whereas push-as-signal-then-pull tolerates dropped or out-of-order push messages by re-fetching authoritative state
Push-only cannot be implemented on iOS due to platform restrictions
Push-only uses less battery in all cases

quiz.explanation: Push delivery isn't guaranteed or ordered; using push only as a 'something changed, go fetch' trigger and then pulling authoritative state is more resilient to dropped or reordered notifications than trusting the pushed payload itself.

quiz.prompt: A team is deciding between last-write-wins and a field-level merge strategy for a shared shopping cart. What consideration should drive that choice?

options.text: Last-write-wins is deprecated and should never be used
Which strategy is easier to explain in a design doc
How costly a silently dropped edit is to the user — a shopping cart where items disappear is worse than a display-name conflict, so higher-cost domains justify more complex merge logic
Field-level merging is always strictly better and should always be used

quiz.explanation: Merge strategy complexity should be proportional to the cost of getting it wrong; a shopping cart silently dropping items is a real product problem, which justifies the added complexity of field-level merging over simple last-write-wins.

slides.title: Testability is architecture, not test-writing
slides.body: A system is testable when its components can be exercised in isolation, with dependencies swapped for fakes, without touching the network, disk, or wall-clock time. This is a property of how boundaries and dependencies are structured — protocols, injected dependencies, pure functions — not something you can bolt on with more test-writing effort after the fact.

slides.title: Designing seams for fakes
slides.body: A 'seam' is a place in the code where behavior can be substituted without editing the class itself — typically a protocol-typed dependency injected through an initializer. Every direct call to `URLSession.shared`, `Date()`, or a singleton is a place a test can't control, so senior design work is largely about deciding which of those need a seam.

slides.title: The test pyramid at the system level
slides.body: A healthy system has many fast, isolated unit tests, a smaller number of integration tests that verify components wired together correctly, and very few end-to-end tests that exercise the whole stack, because E2E tests are slow, flaky, and expensive to maintain. When the ratio inverts — heavy reliance on E2E — the whole suite becomes slow and untrustworthy, and engineers stop trusting or running it.

slides.title: Deterministic tests for asynchronous systems
slides.body: Async code (network calls, timers, debouncing) is the most common source of flaky tests; the fix is to inject the sources of nondeterminism — a clock, a scheduler, a dispatch queue — so tests can control time and ordering explicitly rather than sleeping and hoping.

quiz.prompt: A codebase has 90% test coverage but the test suite takes 40 minutes and is flaky. What is the most likely underlying design issue?

options.text: Coverage percentage is not a real metric
The tests are written in the wrong testing framework
The team wrote too many tests and should delete some
Coverage was achieved with slow, heavily-integrated tests (e.g., many E2E tests hitting real networking or timing) instead of a healthy pyramid of fast, isolated unit tests

quiz.explanation: High coverage says nothing about test shape; a suite dominated by slow, flaky, heavily-integrated tests instead of fast isolated units produces exactly this symptom — coverage without confidence or speed.

quiz.prompt: Why is direct use of `URLSession.shared` inside a view model considered a testability problem?

options.text: It hardcodes a concrete, network-dependent implementation with no seam to substitute a fake in tests, forcing tests to hit the real network or skip that code path
It causes memory leaks in all cases
It cannot be called from Swift concurrency
URLSession.shared is deprecated in modern iOS

quiz.explanation: Testability requires a seam — typically a protocol — where a fake can be substituted; a hardcoded concrete dependency like `URLSession.shared` removes that option and couples tests to real network behavior.

quiz.prompt: A test for a debounced search feature currently uses `sleep(0.5)` to wait for the debounce timer, and occasionally fails in CI. What is the better long-term fix?

options.text: Increase the sleep duration to 2 seconds
Inject a controllable scheduler/clock so the test can deterministically advance virtual time instead of racing against real wall-clock time
Remove the test since flaky tests provide no value
Run the test suite serially instead of in parallel

quiz.explanation: Sleeping and hoping is inherently racy against real time; injecting a fake scheduler lets the test advance time deterministically and removes the flakiness at its source rather than papering over it.

quiz.prompt: What is the main risk of a system where end-to-end tests are the primary form of test coverage?

options.text: They require App Store approval to run
End-to-end tests are too easy to write
They are slow and prone to unrelated failures (network, environment, timing), so the suite becomes expensive to run and engineers lose trust in — and start ignoring — its failures
End-to-end tests cannot detect any real bugs

quiz.explanation: E2E tests exercise the whole stack, which means many unrelated things can make them fail; when they dominate the suite, failures become noisy and slow, and teams start skipping or ignoring the very tests meant to catch regressions.

quiz.prompt: A senior engineer reviewing a new module's design flags that a core class directly instantiates its database and network dependencies inside its initializer. What is the most accurate description of the problem?

options.text: The class will run slower at runtime due to more allocations
The class cannot be compiled without those dependencies present
The class violates Swift naming conventions
The class has no seams for dependency substitution, making it impossible to unit test in isolation without touching real infrastructure

quiz.explanation: Concrete dependencies instantiated internally, rather than injected as protocols, remove the seam a test would need to substitute fakes — this is a design-level testability defect, not a style nitpick.

slides.title: The real cost of a dependency
slides.body: Adding a third-party library costs more than its bytes and build time: it's an ongoing commitment to track its security patches, API churn, maintenance status, and license terms for as long as the app ships. A dependency that saves two days of work now but goes unmaintained in a year can cost far more than it saved.

slides.title: A checklist before adopting a library
slides.body: Before pulling in a dependency, a senior engineer checks: is it actively maintained (recent commits, responsive issue tracker), what's its license, how large is its footprint, does it have transitive dependencies of its own, and — critically — could the team build the needed subset in well under the time it'd take to vet and integrate the library properly?
slides.example:
Checklist before adding a library:
- Last commit < 6 months ago?
- License compatible with commercial shipping?
- Bus factor > 1 maintainer?
- Does it pull in its own dependency tree?

slides.title: Wrapping third-party code behind your own abstraction
slides.body: Calling a third-party API directly from dozens of call sites across the codebase couples the whole app to that vendor's API shape; wrapping it behind a small protocol your team owns means swapping vendors, mocking it in tests, or dropping it entirely later touches one file instead of dozens.

slides.title: Build vs. buy
slides.body: Building in-house makes sense when the capability is close to the app's core differentiator or when available libraries are poorly maintained, oversized, or license-incompatible; buying (or using an open-source library) makes sense for well-solved, non-differentiating problems like JSON parsing or crash reporting, where reinventing it is pure opportunity cost.
slides.example:
Buy: a stable, widely-used networking or analytics SDK.
Build: your app's core recommendation algorithm — the thing you're actually differentiated on.

quiz.prompt: A team is evaluating a popular third-party image-loading library. It hasn't had a commit in 18 months and has several open, unanswered issues about crashes on the latest iOS version. What should most heavily factor into the decision?

options.text: Its maintenance status — an unmaintained library with unresolved crash reports is a growing liability regardless of past popularity
Whether the library's logo matches the app's brand colors
How many total lines of code the library contains
The number of GitHub stars it has, which indicates community trust

quiz.explanation: Popularity is a lagging indicator; an unmaintained library with known, unresolved crashes is an active risk that will likely need to be forked, patched, or replaced — the maintenance signal matters more than historical adoption.

quiz.prompt: Why is it good practice to wrap a third-party SDK behind an internal protocol rather than calling its API directly from many call sites?

options.text: It makes the app bundle smaller
It isolates the vendor's API shape behind an abstraction your team controls, so swapping vendors, testing with a fake, or removing the SDK later requires changing one place instead of every call site
It is required by Apple's App Store review guidelines
It automatically improves the SDK's performance

quiz.explanation: A thin ownership layer around a dependency contains the blast radius of vendor changes, deprecations, or a future swap to a single wrapper, rather than every call site across the app.

quiz.prompt: A junior engineer wants to add a small library (200 lines) to handle simple string formatting that the team could write in about an hour. What is the most defensible senior judgment here?

options.text: Add the library but never read its source code
Always prefer a library over in-house code since it's been tested by more people
For a small, well-understood, non-differentiating problem, writing the hour of code in-house is likely better than taking on a new dependency's long-term maintenance and vetting cost
Reject all third-party libraries categorically regardless of the task

quiz.explanation: For small, well-scoped, non-core problems, the ongoing cost of tracking a new dependency (updates, licensing, transitive risk) can easily exceed the one-time cost of writing and owning a small amount of code directly.

quiz.prompt: What is a 'transitive dependency' risk that a checklist for adopting a new library should account for?

options.text: The library might not compile on Linux
The library's transitive dependencies are always removed automatically by Swift Package Manager
The library might use too much RAM at launch
The library may itself depend on other third-party packages, each adding its own maintenance, security, and licensing risk that the team inherits indirectly

quiz.explanation: Adopting a library also silently adopts everything it depends on; those nested dependencies carry their own maintenance and license risk that the evaluating team may not have directly vetted.

quiz.prompt: A team is deciding whether to build their own crash-reporting pipeline or adopt an established, well-maintained third-party SDK. Which reasoning best supports 'buy' in this case?

options.text: Crash reporting is a well-solved, non-differentiating problem, so using a mature, widely-adopted SDK avoids years of reinventing edge-case handling the team gains no competitive advantage from
Third-party SDKs are always faster than anything built in-house
Building in-house is against App Store policy
Crash reporting is central to the app's competitive differentiation, so it must be built in-house

quiz.explanation: Build-vs-buy should track how close a capability is to the product's actual differentiation; crash reporting is infrastructure, not differentiation, so leaning on a mature SDK is the better use of engineering time.

slides.title: Start from requirements, not from code
slides.body: Before sketching any classes or view models, a senior engineer pins down the actual requirements: what must work offline, what's the acceptable staleness, what happens on failure, and who consumes this data besides the current screen. Skipping this and jumping straight to implementation is how features end up re-architected mid-build.

slides.title: Sketch the data flow before the UI
slides.body: Drawing where data originates, how it's cached, and how it reaches the view — before writing any SwiftUI — surfaces architectural questions (single source of truth? Who owns retries?) while they're still cheap to change, rather than after the UI is built around a flawed data model.
slides.example:
Server -> SyncEngine -> Local DB (source of truth) -> Repository -> ViewModel -> View
(UI never talks to the network directly)

slides.title: Identify failure modes early
slides.body: For every step in the data flow, ask what happens when it fails: no network, a 500 from the server, a decode error, a write conflict. Deciding these behaviors during design — not discovering them from a crash report post-launch — is what separates a robust feature from one that merely works in the happy path.

slides.title: Worked example: an offline-capable checkout queue
slides.body: For a checkout feature that must work with spotty connectivity: orders are written to a local queue immediately (instant UI feedback), a background sync engine submits them with idempotency keys, failures are retried with backoff and surfaced to the user after N attempts, and the UI subscribes to local queue state rather than a network call — so the walkthrough ties caching, sync, idempotency, and testability together into one coherent design.
slides.example:
1. User taps 'Place order' -> written to local OrderQueue (status: pending)
2. SyncEngine drains queue with idempotency key per order
3. On success: status -> confirmed. On failure after 3 retries: status -> needsAttention
4. UI observes OrderQueue directly, never blocks on network

quiz.prompt: Before writing any code for a new offline-capable feature, what should a senior engineer establish first?

options.text: The exact SwiftUI view hierarchy
The requirements around staleness tolerance, offline behavior, and failure handling, since these drive the data flow and architecture decisions that come after
The unit test file names
The App Store screenshot copy

quiz.explanation: Architecture decisions like caching, sync strategy, and error handling all follow from requirements; starting with UI code before those are settled tends to produce a design that has to be reworked once real constraints surface.

quiz.prompt: In a well-designed checkout queue feature, why should the UI subscribe to local queue state rather than directly awaiting a network call when the user taps 'Place order'?

options.text: It is required for App Store approval
Direct network calls are not supported in SwiftUI
Subscribing to local state gives instant feedback regardless of connectivity and decouples the UI from the timing and reliability of the network, consistent with an offline-first design
It reduces the app's binary size

quiz.explanation: Writing to a local queue first and letting a background sync engine handle submission means the UI responds instantly and consistently, whether the network is present or not — a core offline-first pattern.

quiz.prompt: During end-to-end feature design, a reviewer asks 'what happens if the server returns a 500 during sync?' The engineer hadn't considered this. What does this gap indicate?

options.text: 500 errors are the server team's problem exclusively
The feature should be cancelled
The reviewer is being overly pedantic about an edge case that doesn't matter
A failure mode wasn't identified during design, which is exactly the kind of gap that should be caught before implementation rather than discovered via a crash report later

quiz.explanation: Enumerating failure modes (network loss, server errors, decode failures, conflicts) is a core part of system design; catching a missing case in review is the process working as intended, not pedantry.

quiz.prompt: Why does the worked checkout example use a client-generated idempotency key per order during sync?

options.text: To ensure that if a submission is retried after a timeout, the server can recognize it as the same order rather than creating a duplicate
Idempotency keys are required by Swift's Codable protocol
To encrypt the order data
To make the order JSON payload smaller

quiz.explanation: Retries are expected in a queue-based sync system; an idempotency key is what allows a safely-retried submission to avoid creating duplicate orders server-side.

quiz.prompt: A team designing a new feature end-to-end skips the 'sketch the data flow' step and goes straight to building UI, planning to 'wire up the backend later.' What is the most likely consequence?

options.text: The feature will ship faster with no downside

Architectural assumptions get baked into the UI layer (e.g., assuming a single network call rather than a cached, syncing local store), often forcing a costly rework once real data-flow requirements surface
This approach is best practice for MVPs and has no real risk
SwiftUI cannot be used without a backend already built

quiz.explanation: Data flow and ownership (source of truth, sync, retries) shape the UI's assumptions; deferring that design tends to bake in assumptions that don't hold once real constraints (offline, conflicts, retries) are addressed, forcing rework.

slides.title: Build times as an organizational problem
slides.body: In a single monolithic target, changing one file forces the whole app to recompile and relink, and as the codebase grows this tax is paid by every engineer, on every build, all day. Splitting into modules lets the build system recompile only what actually changed and its dependents, which is often the single biggest lever on developer velocity at scale.

slides.title: Modules as ownership boundaries
slides.body: A module boundary is a natural place to attach a CODEOWNERS entry, a team, and an API review process — it turns 'everyone can touch anything' into 'this team owns this surface and reviews changes to its public API.' This is what makes large multi-team codebases scale without every change requiring cross-team coordination.

slides.title: Modularity forces better testability
slides.body: A module can only depend on another module's public API, so anything a module needs to be testable — clear seams, injectable dependencies — has to be exposed deliberately rather than reached into via `internal` access from a neighboring file in the same target. The compiler enforces the boundary that architecture diagrams only suggest.

slides.title: The cost side of modularization
slides.body: Modularizing isn't free: it adds indirection, cross-module API design overhead, and a temptation to over-fragment into modules too small to justify their own package boundary. The right granularity groups code that changes together and is owned by the same team — modularizing prematurely, before those boundaries are clear, usually costs more than it saves.
slides.example:
Bad: a `Utilities` module with 40 unrelated helpers, touched by every team, constantly causing merge conflicts.
Better: cohesive modules like `Networking`, `Payments`, `DesignSystem`.

quiz.prompt: In a large monolithic app target, why does modularization typically improve day-to-day build times?

options.text: It removes the need for Swift's type checker
It reduces the total number of lines of code in the app
The build system can recompile only the module that changed and its dependents, instead of relinking the entire app for every change
Modules are compiled using a faster compiler than a single target

quiz.explanation: Module boundaries let incremental builds skip unaffected code entirely; in a single target, the whole app is one compilation unit for linking purposes, so small changes can trigger large rebuilds.

quiz.prompt: How do module boundaries support team ownership in a large codebase?

options.text: They remove the need for code review entirely
They are only useful for open-source projects
They automatically assign bugs to the correct team
They give each team a clear, enforceable surface (their module's public API) to own and review changes to, rather than requiring coordination across the whole codebase for every change

quiz.explanation: A module maps naturally to a CODEOWNERS entry and a review process — it's the mechanism that lets a team be accountable for and gate changes to a specific area without every PR needing whole-codebase sign-off.

quiz.prompt: Why does splitting code into modules tend to force better testability, beyond team discipline alone?

options.text: The compiler enforces that only a module's declared public API is visible to consumers, so anything another module needs (e.g., a way to inject a fake) must be deliberately exposed rather than reached into informally
XCTest only works inside Swift packages
Modules run their tests in parallel by default
Modules automatically generate unit tests

quiz.explanation: In a single target, `internal` access lets any file reach into any other file's implementation details; a module boundary is compiler-enforced, so seams for testing have to be intentionally designed into the public API.

quiz.prompt: A team creates a `Utilities` module containing 40 unrelated helper functions used by every other team, and it becomes a constant source of merge conflicts and cross-team review bottlenecks. What is the underlying modularization mistake?

options.text: The module has too few files to justify its own target
Grouping unrelated code that doesn't change together or share an owner defeats the purpose of a module boundary — it should be cohesive and ideally have one clear owning team
The module's name is too generic
Utility functions should never be extracted into their own module under any circumstances

quiz.explanation: Effective modules group code that changes together and is owned together; a grab-bag of unrelated helpers touched by everyone recreates the coordination problem modularization is meant to solve.

quiz.prompt: A senior engineer is asked whether a brand-new, still-rapidly-changing feature should be split into its own module immediately. What is the most defensible position?

options.text: The decision should be made by whichever engineer writes the most code in that area
Always modularize immediately since it's cheaper to do early
It's often better to wait until the feature's boundaries and ownership stabilize, since premature modularization adds cross-module API overhead before it's clear what that API should even look like
Modularization should never be applied to feature code, only to shared infrastructure

quiz.explanation: Modularizing before a feature's shape is settled means repeatedly redesigning a public API that's still churning; it's often better to let boundaries stabilize first and extract the module once the shape and ownership are clear.

slides.title: SPM as the standard tool for internal modularization
slides.body: Swift Package Manager isn't just for pulling in third-party dependencies — local Swift packages are the standard way to split an app's own codebase into independently buildable, independently testable modules, each with its own `Package.swift` declaring its public API surface and dependencies explicitly.

slides.title: Local packages and target graphs
slides.body: A local package can define multiple targets (e.g., a library target plus its own test target), and the app project depends on the package rather than embedding its source directly. Xcode resolves and builds the dependency graph declared in `Package.swift`, so a module's dependencies are explicit and machine-checked, not just a convention documented somewhere.

slides.title: Access control enforces the public API
slides.body: Within a Swift package, `public` (or `package` for cross-module-but-same-package visibility) is what other modules can see; everything else defaults to `internal` and is invisible outside the module. This means the package's declared public API isn't just documentation — the compiler rejects any attempt to reach past it.

slides.title: Structuring for parallel build and test
slides.body: Because each local package is a separate compilation unit, Xcode and CI can build and test unaffected packages in parallel and skip ones that haven't changed, so a well-factored module graph directly shortens both local iteration time and CI wall-clock time — not just organizational clarity.
slides.example:
$ swift test --filter PaymentsTests
// runs only Payments' tests, without rebuilding unrelated modules

quiz.prompt: What is the primary role of local Swift packages in a large app codebase, beyond pulling in third-party dependencies?

options.text: They replace the need for Xcode project files entirely in all cases
They are required for App Store submission
They are only useful for distributing code publicly on GitHub
They split the app's own code into independently buildable, independently testable modules with explicit, declared dependencies between them

quiz.explanation: SPM's local package support is the standard mechanism for internal modularization — declaring targets, dependencies, and public APIs explicitly rather than relying on convention within one big target.

quiz.prompt: In a `Package.swift` manifest, what does declaring `dependencies: ["Networking"]` on a `Payments` target enforce?

options.text: That Payments can access Networking's public API, and this dependency edge is explicit and checked by the build system rather than an informal convention
That Payments and Networking must share the same test target
That Networking's internal implementation details become visible to Payments
That Networking must be written before Payments chronologically

quiz.explanation: SPM dependency declarations make the module graph explicit and machine-enforced — Payments gets access to Networking's public API specifically, not its internals, and the edge is visible to tooling, not just documentation.

quiz.prompt: Within a Swift package's module, what happens to a type or function that is not marked `public` (or `package`)?

options.text: It is still accessible to any other module that imports the package
It defaults to `internal` visibility and is invisible to any code outside that module, meaning the module's declared public API is compiler-enforced, not just documented
It is automatically deleted from the compiled binary
It becomes accessible only in DEBUG builds

quiz.explanation: Swift's default access level is `internal`; without `public` (or `package`), a symbol simply isn't visible outside its module, which is what makes a package's public API surface a hard boundary rather than a convention.

quiz.prompt: Why does splitting an app into well-factored local Swift packages typically speed up CI, beyond the developer-experience benefits?

options.text: CI systems charge less for projects using SPM
SPM packages compile with a fundamentally different, faster compiler
Each package is a separate compilation unit, so CI can skip rebuilding and retesting packages that haven't changed and can build/test unaffected ones in parallel
SPM automatically disables tests for packages older than 30 days

quiz.explanation: Because packages are independent compilation units with an explicit dependency graph, tooling can determine what actually needs rebuilding/retesting and parallelize the rest — a direct mechanical benefit, not just organizational.

quiz.prompt: A team wants a type to be visible across several modules within the same Swift package, but not exposed to external consumers of the package as a whole. Which access level fits this need?

options.text: `fileprivate`
`open`
`private`
`package`

quiz.explanation: The `package` access level (introduced for exactly this case) allows visibility across targets within the same package without exposing the symbol as part of the package's public, externally-consumable API.

slides.title: Design the API, not the implementation, first
slides.body: A module's public API should be designed from the consumer's perspective — what does a caller need to accomplish, with what inputs and outputs — before worrying about internal implementation. An API that leaks implementation details (e.g., exposing a Core Data `NSManagedObject` across a module boundary) couples consumers to internals that should be free to change.

slides.title: Minimal surface area
slides.body: Every `public` symbol is a promise to every consumer, forever (or until a breaking version bump) — so the right default is `internal`, and something is made `public` only when a real external consumer needs it. A module with 200 public symbols is much harder to evolve than one with 15 carefully chosen ones.

slides.title: Returning protocols vs. concrete types
slides.body: Exposing a protocol instead of a concrete type at a module boundary lets the implementing module change its internal type freely and lets consumers substitute fakes in tests; but overusing protocols for types that will only ever have one implementation adds indirection without real benefit, so this is a judgment call per boundary, not a blanket rule.

slides.title: Documenting intent, not just signatures
slides.body: A public API's doc comments should explain what the function is for and any non-obvious contract (does it throw on empty input? is it safe to call concurrently?) — a bare signature tells a consumer the types but not the behavior they can rely on, which is exactly what breaks when the implementation changes 'safely' according to its own tests but not according to the contract callers assumed.

quiz.prompt: A `Payments` module exposes its internal Core Data `NSManagedObject` subclass directly as part of its public API. What is the main problem with this design?

options.text: It couples every consumer of Payments to a Core Data implementation detail, so changing the persistence layer later becomes a breaking change for every module that depends on it
It makes the Payments module compile more slowly
It is not possible to mark NSManagedObject subclasses as public
NSManagedObject cannot be used in Swift packages

quiz.explanation: Exposing an internal persistence type at the module boundary leaks implementation details that consumers shouldn't depend on; a plain public struct/DTO would let the persistence layer change freely without breaking consumers.

quiz.prompt: Why is 'default to internal, promote to public only when needed' good practice for a module's API design?

options.text: Public symbols compile faster than internal ones
Every public symbol is a long-term commitment to consumers, so keeping the public surface minimal keeps the module easier to evolve without breaking anyone
Internal symbols are automatically documented by Xcode
Apple requires modules to have fewer than 20 public symbols

quiz.explanation: A large public surface means more things that count as breaking changes when the module evolves; minimizing it to what's actually needed externally keeps the module free to refactor internally.

quiz.prompt: When is exposing a protocol rather than a concrete type at a module boundary most justified?

options.text: Only when the type has more than 10 properties
Always — protocols should be used for every public type regardless of context
When consumers need to substitute a fake implementation in tests, or when the implementing module wants the freedom to change its concrete type without breaking the public contract
Never — concrete types are always preferable for module boundaries

quiz.explanation: Protocol boundaries are valuable specifically when substitutability (testing) or implementation flexibility is needed; applying them uniformly to types that will only ever have one implementation adds indirection without real benefit.

quiz.prompt: A public function's signature is `func submitPayment(order: Order, key: String) async throws -> PaymentResult` with no doc comment. What risk does the missing documentation create for consumers?

options.text: Xcode will refuse to autocomplete the function
The function's access level defaults to internal without documentation
The function will not compile without a doc comment

Consumers can't tell non-obvious behavioral contracts (e.g., whether it's safe to call twice with the same key) from the signature alone, so they may rely on undocumented behavior that later changes 'safely' from the implementer's point of view but breaks callers

quiz.explanation: A signature conveys types, not behavioral guarantees like idempotency or thread-safety; without documenting those contracts, consumers either guess or read the implementation, and either way a later internal change can silently break them.

quiz.prompt: A module currently has 200 public symbols, many unused outside the module itself. What is the recommended senior approach to cleaning this up?

options.text: Audit which symbols have real external consumers, narrow the rest back to internal, and treat this as an intentional API-surface reduction, communicating it as a change to consumers
Delete all 200 symbols immediately without checking usage
Add even more public symbols so the API feels comprehensive
Leave it as-is since removing public symbols is never worth the effort

quiz.explanation: An oversized public API accrued without discipline should be pruned deliberately — checking real usage first, since some pruning is a breaking change for any external consumer that does depend on a symbol.

slides.title: Why circular dependencies break modularization
slides.body: A circular dependency (Module A depends on B, and B depends on A) is something Swift's build system flatly rejects between separate targets — it can't determine a build order — so it's not just a design smell, it's a hard compile-time error once two things are actually split into modules.

slides.title: The usual root cause: a missing abstraction
slides.body: Circular dependencies almost always mean two modules need to talk to each other, and the fix is to introduce a third module (or protocol) that both depend on, so the relationship becomes a one-directional dependency on a shared abstraction instead of a direct cycle.

slides.title: Dependency direction should follow stability
slides.body: Lower-level, more stable modules (networking, design system, core models) should be depended upon, not do the depending; higher-level, more frequently-changing feature modules should sit at the top of the graph. When a stable module starts depending on a volatile feature module, that's usually the sign of an inverted, cycle-prone dependency direction.

slides.title: Catching cycles before they're designed in
slides.body: Cycles are far cheaper to prevent at design time — by sketching the intended module graph and checking it's a DAG before writing code — than to untangle after two teams have built features assuming they can freely reference each other. Some teams enforce this with a lightweight dependency-graph lint in CI.
slides.example:
# Simple CI check: fail if `swift package show-dependencies`
# reveals an unexpected edge between two modules

quiz.prompt: Module `Feed` depends on `Profile` for a user card view, and `Profile` depends on `Feed` for a post count. What happens when these are split into separate Swift package targets?

options.text: Swift will silently pick a build order and it will compile as normal
The build fails, because Swift Package Manager cannot resolve a build order for a circular target dependency
Only the second module built will have compile errors
The app will build but crash at runtime

quiz.explanation: SPM (and most module systems) require a directed acyclic dependency graph; a genuine cycle between two targets is a hard error because there's no valid order to build them in.

quiz.prompt: What is the most common underlying fix for a circular dependency between two feature modules?

options.text: Rename one of the modules so the cycle is no longer detected
Merge the two modules back into a single target permanently
Extract the shared functionality both modules need into a third, lower-level module (or protocol) that both depend on, turning the cycle into a one-directional dependency on a shared abstraction
Use `@testable import` to bypass the cycle

quiz.explanation: Cycles usually indicate a missing shared abstraction; extracting the common piece into its own module and having both original modules depend on it (rather than each other) resolves the cycle structurally.

quiz.prompt: In a healthy module graph, which direction should dependencies generally flow?

options.text: Dependency direction doesn't matter as long as there are no cycles
All modules should depend equally on all other modules
From low-level, stable modules (networking, design system) toward high-level, frequently-changing feature modules
From high-level, frequently-changing feature modules toward low-level, stable modules — stable modules should be depended upon, not do the depending

quiz.explanation: Stable, foundational modules changing less often should sit low in the graph and be depended upon; when a stable module starts depending on a volatile feature module, that inversion is a common precursor to future cycles.

quiz.prompt: Why is it valuable to sketch the intended module dependency graph before implementation, rather than discovering the shape organically as features are built?

options.text: It's much cheaper to catch and fix a cyclic or inverted dependency on paper than after two teams have already built features assuming they can freely reference each other
It eliminates the need for any future refactoring
It automatically generates the Package.swift file
Sketching a graph is required by Xcode before creating a package

quiz.explanation: Untangling a real cycle after the fact requires renegotiating APIs and possibly re-architecting both modules; catching the shape at design time costs a diagram, not a rewrite.

quiz.prompt: A CI job runs `swift package show-dependencies` and fails the build if an unexpected edge appears between two modules. What is the primary value of this check?

options.text: It replaces the need for code review
It catches accidental new dependency edges (which can introduce cycles or inversions) automatically, before they're merged, rather than relying on engineers to notice manually
It speeds up the build by skipping dependency resolution
It is required for App Store submission

quiz.explanation: Automating a dependency-graph check turns 'we hope nobody adds an unintended edge' into an enforced constraint, catching architectural drift at PR time instead of after it's baked into the codebase.

slides.title: The dependency inversion principle at the module level
slides.body: Dependency inversion means a high-level module (business logic) should depend on an abstraction, and a low-level module (a concrete implementation, e.g., networking) should also depend on — implement — that same abstraction, rather than the high-level module depending directly on the low-level one's concrete types. This is what breaks the 'core depends on infrastructure' coupling that makes core logic hard to test or swap.

slides.title: Where the protocol should live
slides.body: In practice, the abstraction (protocol) is usually owned by the high-level/core module, and the low-level implementation module depends on the core module to conform to it — not the other way around. This means core business logic has zero compile-time dependency on networking, persistence, or any specific vendor.

slides.title: Composition happens at the edge
slides.body: Since core logic only knows about the protocol, something has to wire the concrete implementation in — typically the app target itself, or a small composition-root module, at startup. This keeps the wiring decision (which implementation to use — real, mocked, staged) in one place instead of scattered across the codebase.

slides.title: What inversion buys you across a module boundary
slides.body: With inversion in place, the core module can be unit tested with a fake `OrderRepository` with zero networking code involved, a new backend or caching layer can be swapped in by writing a new conformance without touching core logic, and the core module's build doesn't even need to link against networking — all direct consequences of the dependency pointing the right way.

quiz.prompt: In a properly inverted architecture, which module should typically own (define) the `OrderRepository` protocol?

options.text: Whichever module was created first in the project
The Networking module, since it implements the repository
The core/business-logic module that needs to fetch orders, since it defines the abstraction it depends on and the concrete implementation conforms to it
A separate `Protocols` module that only contains protocol definitions

quiz.explanation: Dependency inversion places the abstraction with the high-level module that needs it; the low-level implementation module then depends on the core module to conform to that protocol, keeping the dependency arrow pointing toward core.

quiz.prompt: What is the main practical benefit of a core business-logic module having zero compile-time dependency on the concrete Networking module?

options.text: It removes the need for the Networking module entirely
It automatically encrypts network traffic
It makes the app's binary smaller
The core module can be unit tested with fakes with no real networking code involved, and it can build and evolve independently of networking implementation changes
