quiz.explanation: Once core logic depends only on a protocol, tests can supply an in-memory fake with no real I/O, and swapping or upgrading the concrete networking implementation never requires touching or rebuilding core logic.

quiz.prompt: Where should the decision of 'which concrete `OrderRepository` implementation to use — real, staged, or mocked' typically be made in an inverted architecture?

options.text: At the composition root (e.g., app startup or a small composition module), which is the one place responsible for wiring concrete implementations to the abstractions core code depends on
Inside every view model that needs an OrderRepository
It should be decided independently by each unit test
Inside the core module itself, hardcoded

quiz.explanation: Centralizing this wiring at a composition root keeps the decision in one place, rather than having it scattered — or worse, hardcoded into business logic that should stay implementation-agnostic.

quiz.prompt: A team has a `Core` module directly importing `Networking` and calling `URLSession`-based classes throughout its business logic. What architectural problem does this represent?

options.text: Core is missing unit tests, which is unrelated to its imports
The dependency points the wrong way — high-level business logic depends on a low-level, volatile implementation detail, coupling core logic to networking and making it hard to test or swap
This is actually the correct, standard architecture and needs no change
Networking modules should never be imported by any other module under any circumstances

quiz.explanation: This is the inversion principle violated directly: the stable, high-value core logic is coupled to a concrete low-level detail, which is exactly the coupling dependency inversion is meant to eliminate by introducing a protocol boundary.

quiz.prompt: Why might a team choose to introduce a protocol for `OrderRepository` even though, today, there is only one real implementation (the live backend)?

options.text: It is purely stylistic and has no functional benefit
Protocols are required by Swift for all types
It enables substituting a fake for tests now and gives room to add a second implementation (e.g., an offline-cache-backed one) later without changing core logic's dependencies
It makes the app compile faster in all cases

quiz.explanation: Even with a single current implementation, the protocol boundary is what makes core logic testable in isolation today and keeps the door open for a second implementation (caching, offline, staging) without touching core code later.

slides.title: Internal APIs need discipline too, even without semantic versioning
slides.body: Internal modules within one app usually don't need strict semver, since all consumers ship together — but that doesn't mean 'break anything, anytime' is fine. A module's public API is still a contract other teams build against, and an unannounced breaking change still causes build failures and lost trust, just discovered at compile time instead of via a version number.

slides.title: Deprecation before removal
slides.body: The standard pattern for evolving a public API without surprising consumers is: add the new API alongside the old one, mark the old one `@available(*, deprecated, message:...)` pointing at the replacement, give consumers a release or two to migrate, then remove it. This turns a hard break into a visible warning with a migration path.
slides.example:
@available(*, deprecated, message: "Use submitPayment(order:idempotencyKey:) instead")
public func submitPayment(order: Order) async throws -> PaymentResult

slides.title: Semantic versioning for genuinely shared/external packages
slides.body: For a package that's actually distributed to multiple independent consumers (e.g., a company-wide shared package used by several separately-releasing apps), real semantic versioning matters: MAJOR for breaking changes, MINOR for additive features, PATCH for fixes — since those consumers can't coordinate a synchronized migration the way one app's internal modules can.

slides.title: Communicating a breaking internal API change
slides.body: Even for an internal-only module, a breaking change to a widely-used public API should be announced ahead of time (a message in the team's channel, a note in the PR description, a migration guide for the common call patterns) rather than just landing — the module boundary doesn't remove the need for the social contract of not surprising other teams.
slides.example:
PR description: "BREAKING: OrderRepository.fetch(id:) now throws OrderError
 instead of returning nil. Migration: replace `if let order = ...`
 with `do { let order = try await ... }`. Rolling out over 2 sprints."

quiz.prompt: In a single app where all modules ship together, why does an internal module's public API still deserve some evolution discipline, even without formal semantic versioning?

options.text: Because Swift requires all internal modules to be semantically versioned
Internal modules are exempt from any API discipline since they never ship independently
Because App Store review checks internal module versions

Because other teams build against that public API as a real contract, and an unannounced breaking change still causes build failures and erodes trust, even though it's caught at compile time rather than by a version mismatch

quiz.explanation: Same-app shipping avoids the need for strict semver, but it doesn't remove the social contract: other teams depend on that API surface, and surprising them with a break is still costly even without a version number involved.

quiz.prompt: What is the purpose of marking an old API `@available(*, deprecated, message:...)` before removing it, rather than deleting it directly?

options.text: It gives consumers a visible compiler warning and a migration path, so they can move to the replacement on their own timeline before the old API is actually removed
It automatically migrates all call sites for you
It is required by the Swift language specification for all public APIs
It's purely cosmetic and has no functional effect

quiz.explanation: Deprecation is the mechanism that turns an abrupt break into an advance-notice warning with guidance, giving consuming teams time to migrate instead of hitting a sudden compile failure.

quiz.prompt: A company maintains a shared Swift package used independently by three separately-releasing apps across different teams. Why does strict semantic versioning matter more here than for modules used within a single app?

options.text: Semantic versioning is only relevant for open-source projects
These consumers release on independent schedules and can't coordinate a synchronized migration, so MAJOR/MINOR/PATCH distinctions let them safely decide when to take a breaking change
It makes the package's code run faster
It removes the need for the package to have tests

quiz.explanation: When consumers ship independently, they need a reliable signal (the version number) to know whether an update is safe to take automatically or requires planned migration work — that signal matters far less when everyone ships together.

quiz.prompt: A senior engineer plans to change `OrderRepository.fetch(id:)` from returning an optional to throwing a typed error. What is the most appropriate way to roll this out to other teams depending on it internally?

options.text: Wait for another team to discover the compile error and ask what happened
Merge the change directly since it's an internal module and no formal versioning is required
Announce the breaking change ahead of time with a migration guide, and ideally land it as an addition alongside the old signature with a deprecation window before removing the old one
Rename the module so other teams don't notice the change

quiz.explanation: Even internal-only breaking changes warrant advance communication and, where feasible, a deprecation window — this avoids blindsiding other teams with build failures and gives them a clear path to adapt.

quiz.prompt: Why is deleting an old public API immediately upon adding its replacement (rather than deprecating it for a period first) risky, even within a single app's modules?

options.text: It has no real risk since all modules ship together
It violates Swift's access control rules
Deleting old code is always a compile error in Swift
It forces every consuming team to migrate immediately and synchronously with the change, rather than on their own schedule, which can block unrelated work and create rushed, error-prone migrations

quiz.explanation: An immediate removal turns what could be a planned migration into a forced, synchronous one for every consumer, increasing the chance of rushed changes and blocked unrelated work across teams.

quiz.prompt: What is the primary build-time benefit of splitting a large monolithic app target into separate modules?

options.text: The build system can recompile only what changed and its dependents instead of relinking the entire app for every change
Modules eliminate the need for a build system entirely
It reduces the number of files in the project
Modules use a fundamentally faster Swift compiler

quiz.explanation: Module boundaries let incremental builds skip unaffected code; in one giant target, small changes can still trigger large relink costs across the whole app.

quiz.prompt: How do module boundaries support team ownership at scale?

options.text: They remove the need for any code review
Each module provides a clear, enforceable surface a team can own and gate changes to, avoiding the need for whole-codebase coordination on every change
They automatically resolve merge conflicts
They are relevant only for open-source projects

quiz.explanation: A module maps naturally onto a CODEOWNERS entry and review process, letting a team be accountable for a bounded surface instead of requiring cross-team sign-off on every change anywhere.

quiz.prompt: Why does modularization tend to force better testability, beyond team discipline?

options.text: Modules automatically achieve 100% coverage
Modules run tests in a special sandboxed mode

The compiler enforces that only the declared public API is visible across the boundary, forcing seams for testing (like injectable dependencies) to be deliberately exposed rather than reached into informally
XCTest requires modules to function at all

quiz.explanation: Where a single target allows informal `internal` access between files, a module boundary is compiler-enforced, so anything a consumer needs — including test seams — has to be part of the deliberate public API.

quiz.prompt: A `Utilities` module contains 40 unrelated helpers used by every team and is a constant source of merge conflicts. What modularization principle does this violate?

options.text: Utility code should never be reused across features
Modules must contain at least 50 files to be valid
Modules should be as large as possible
Modules should be cohesive and ideally owned by one team — grouping unrelated code that doesn't change together recreates the coordination problem modularization is meant to solve

quiz.explanation: A module should represent a cohesive area of change and ownership; a grab-bag of unrelated helpers touched by everyone undermines the isolation and ownership benefits modularization is meant to provide.

quiz.prompt: Within a Swift package's module, what happens to a symbol that is not explicitly marked `public` or `package`?

options.text: It defaults to `internal`, invisible outside its own module, making the module's public API compiler-enforced rather than just documented convention
It is stripped from the compiled binary entirely
It becomes available only in Release builds
It remains visible to any importer of the package

quiz.explanation: Swift's default `internal` access level means anything not explicitly exposed stays invisible outside its module — this is what makes a package's declared public API a hard, compiler-checked boundary.

quiz.prompt: Why is exposing an internal Core Data `NSManagedObject` subclass directly as part of a module's public API considered poor design?

options.text: NSManagedObject subclasses cannot be marked public in Swift
It couples every consumer to a persistence implementation detail, so changing the storage layer later becomes a breaking change for all dependents
It causes a compile error in Swift Package Manager
It is only a problem if the module has more than one consumer

quiz.explanation: Persistence types are implementation details; exposing them directly at a module boundary means any future change to how data is stored ripples out as a breaking change to every consumer, instead of being contained.

quiz.prompt: Module A depends on Module B, and Module B depends on Module A. What happens when these are compiled as separate Swift package targets?

options.text: The cycle is silently ignored in Release builds
The build succeeds by picking an arbitrary order
The build fails, since SPM requires a directed acyclic dependency graph and cannot resolve a build order for a true cycle
Only unit tests fail, not the main build

quiz.explanation: A genuine circular target dependency has no valid build order, so SPM (like most module systems) rejects it outright rather than resolving it heuristically.

quiz.prompt: What is the standard fix for a circular dependency discovered between two feature modules?

options.text: Alphabetize the module names so Xcode can determine build order
Disable one of the two modules' test targets
Permanently merge the two modules back into one target
Extract the shared functionality both need into a third, lower-level module (or protocol) that both depend on, replacing the cycle with one-directional dependencies on a shared abstraction

quiz.explanation: Cycles typically reveal a missing shared abstraction; extracting the common piece into its own module resolves the cycle structurally without permanently collapsing the two modules together.

quiz.prompt: In dependency inversion across a module boundary, which module should typically define the abstraction (protocol) that a low-level implementation module conforms to?

options.text: The high-level/core module that needs the capability, so its dependency points toward an abstraction it owns rather than toward a volatile concrete implementation
A separate, otherwise-unrelated `Protocols`-only module in all cases
Whichever module happens to be built first in CI
The low-level implementation module, since it knows the concrete details

quiz.explanation: Dependency inversion has the high-level module own the abstraction and the low-level module depend on the high-level module to conform to it — this keeps the dependency pointed toward the stable core, not the volatile implementation.

quiz.prompt: A team is about to change a widely-used internal module's public function from returning an optional to throwing a typed error. What is the most appropriate rollout approach?

options.text: Merge the change directly since internal modules don't require formal versioning
Add the new signature alongside the old one, deprecate the old one with a migration message, give consumers a window to migrate, then remove it — communicating the breaking change ahead of time
Rename the module so consumers don't notice
Wait for other teams to discover the compile failure and ask what changed

quiz.explanation: Even without semver, a breaking change to a widely-depended-on internal API deserves a deprecation path and advance communication so consuming teams can migrate on a reasonable timeline instead of being surprised by a break.

slides.title: Start with why, and with what 'done' means
slides.body: Before any migration work starts, the plan needs a concrete answer to why now (what's the cost of not migrating) and what done looks like (100% of screens? Just new feature work? A specific deprecated API fully removed?). Without a measurable end state, large migrations tend to run indefinitely, absorbing effort with no clear point of completion.

slides.title: Inventory before you plan
slides.body: A large migration (say, UIKit to SwiftUI) needs an honest inventory of the current surface area — how many screens, which ones are high-traffic vs. rarely touched, which have quirky platform-specific behavior that will be hard to replicate — before committing to a timeline. Skipping this step is how migration estimates turn out to be off by multiples.
slides.example:
Inventory example:
- 120 screens total, 18 handle >80% of traffic
- 6 screens use custom UIKit gesture recognizers with no direct SwiftUI equivalent
- 3 screens are legacy and slated for deletion, not migration

slides.title: Sequence by risk and value, not by ease
slides.body: It's tempting to migrate the easiest screens first to show quick progress, but the better sequencing usually front-loads the highest-risk or highest-uncertainty pieces (the ones most likely to reveal that the chosen approach doesn't work) so problems surface early, while there's still time and appetite to adjust the plan.

slides.title: A migration plan is a living document
slides.body: Even a well-researched migration plan will hit surprises — a SwiftUI performance cliff on a specific screen, a UIKit interop issue nobody anticipated. Treating the plan as a fixed contract rather than something revisited every few weeks against real progress is what turns a manageable migration into a stalled one that nobody trusts the timeline for anymore.
slides.example:
Weekly migration check-in: "Screen count migrated: 34/120.
 New finding: TableView with custom cell caching needs a bespoke
 SwiftUI equivalent — added 1 week to the estimate for that slice."

quiz.prompt: Why is it important for a migration plan to define a concrete 'done' state up front, such as 'all screens migrated' or 'all new feature work uses the new architecture'?

options.text: It guarantees the migration will finish faster
It is required by Apple for App Store submission
Without a measurable end state, large migrations tend to run indefinitely without a clear point of completion, making it hard to know when to stop investing effort or declare success
It has no real impact on the outcome, only on morale

quiz.explanation: An open-ended migration with no defined finish line tends to become permanent background work with unclear priority — a concrete done-state is what lets the team and stakeholders know when the investment is complete.

quiz.prompt: Before committing to a migration timeline, why should the team inventory the existing surface area (e.g., how many screens, which are high-traffic, which have unusual platform-specific behavior)?

options.text: It is only useful for UIKit-to-SwiftUI migrations specifically
It replaces the need for any further planning
Inventorying is a formality with no bearing on the estimate

Skipping this step is a common cause of estimates being off by multiples, since hidden complexity (quirky legacy behavior, edge-case screens) is exactly what an inventory surfaces before commitments are made

quiz.explanation: Migration estimates without an honest accounting of what actually exists — including the hard edge cases — routinely underestimate scope; the inventory is what surfaces that complexity while it's still cheap to plan around.

quiz.prompt: A team is sequencing a large migration and considers migrating the easiest, lowest-risk screens first to show quick progress. What is the main argument against this sequencing?

options.text: Front-loading the highest-risk or most uncertain pieces surfaces whether the chosen approach actually works while there's still time to adjust course, rather than discovering fundamental problems late after committing based on early 'easy win' momentum
Migrating easy screens first is always technically impossible
Risk-based sequencing takes the same amount of total time either way, so it doesn't matter
Easy screens should never be migrated at all

quiz.explanation: Sequencing by risk rather than ease means the plan's riskiest assumptions get tested early, when there's still room to change approach — deferring hard problems to the end risks discovering a blocking issue after most of the timeline is spent.

quiz.prompt: Midway through a UIKit-to-SwiftUI migration, the team discovers a serious performance issue on a specific screen type that wasn't anticipated in the original plan. What is the appropriate response?

options.text: Abandon the migration entirely since the original plan is now invalid
Revisit and update the migration plan based on this new information, since a migration plan should be treated as a living document adjusted against real progress rather than a fixed contract
Ignore the issue and continue exactly per the original plan and timeline
Reassign the issue to a different team without changing the plan

quiz.explanation: Migration plans are working hypotheses about a system that's only partially understood at the outset; treating the plan as fixed despite new evidence is what causes a manageable migration to stall or lose the team's trust in the timeline.

quiz.prompt: What is the risk of starting a large-scale migration without first answering 'why now' — i.e., without articulating the cost of not migrating?

options.text: It only matters for migrations initiated by non-engineering stakeholders
The migration will be technically impossible to execute
Without a clear cost/benefit case, the migration is more likely to get deprioritized under pressure or fail to secure the sustained resourcing large migrations require
It has no practical effect since engineers will do the work regardless

quiz.explanation: A migration without a clear articulated 'why now' struggles to justify sustained investment against competing priorities, making it an easy target for deprioritization the moment resourcing gets tight.

slides.title: The strangler-fig pattern
slides.body: Named after a vine that gradually envelops and replaces its host tree, the strangler-fig pattern replaces a legacy system incrementally by routing new functionality through the new implementation while the old one keeps serving what hasn't been migrated yet, until eventually nothing routes to the old path and it can be deleted. This avoids the classic big-bang rewrite failure mode where nothing ships until everything is done.

slides.title: Why big-bang rewrites tend to fail
slides.body: A big-bang rewrite freezes feature work on the old system (or forces double-implementation) for the whole migration duration, delivers zero incremental value until the very end, and bets the entire migration on one enormous, hard-to-validate cutover — any single blocking issue discovered late stalls everything at once.
slides.example:
A team spends 8 months rewriting checkout from scratch with
 no incremental release. In month 9, QA finds a critical gift-card
 edge case the rewrite never handled — the whole launch is blocked,
 and there's no partial win to fall back on.

slides.title: Routing at a seam
slides.body: The strangler-fig approach needs a seam to route through — a router, a feature flag, or a facade that decides per-request or per-screen whether to use the old or new path. Investing in that routing seam early is what makes the incremental migration possible at all; without it, teams end up doing a big-bang rewrite by accident.

slides.title: Knowing when to finish, not just start, incrementally
slides.body: The incremental approach still needs an explicit final step — removing the old path once nothing routes to it — or the migration lingers half-finished indefinitely, with both code paths maintained forever. Scheduling and tracking that removal (not just the initial cutovers) is part of the migration plan, not an afterthought.
slides.example:
Finish checklist: "0 requests routed to LegacyProfileViewController
 in the last 30 days -> delete LegacyProfileViewController.swift
 and the useNewProfile flag."

quiz.prompt: What is the core idea of the strangler-fig migration pattern?

options.text: Run the old and new systems in permanent parallel indefinitely with no plan to retire either
Migrate the UI layer only and never touch the underlying data layer
Rewrite the entire system in one large release to minimize the total migration timeline
Incrementally route new functionality through the new implementation while the old system keeps serving what hasn't migrated yet, eventually retiring the old system once nothing depends on it

quiz.explanation: The strangler-fig pattern is defined by gradual replacement at a routing seam, letting each piece migrate independently while the old system keeps working for what's left, until it can finally be deleted.

quiz.prompt: What is the primary risk of a big-bang rewrite compared to an incremental migration?

options.text: It delivers no incremental value until the very end and bets the entire migration on one large, hard-to-validate cutover, so any blocking issue discovered late stalls the whole effort
Big-bang rewrites cannot use Swift Package Manager
Big-bang rewrites are faster in every case
Big-bang rewrites are always technically infeasible on iOS

quiz.explanation: By deferring all value and validation to a single cutover, a big-bang rewrite concentrates risk instead of spreading it — a late-discovered problem threatens the entire migration rather than one incremental slice of it.

quiz.prompt: Why is a routing seam (e.g., a feature flag or facade deciding old vs. new implementation per screen) essential to a strangler-fig migration?

options.text: It is only needed for backend migrations, not client-side ones
Without an explicit place to decide which implementation handles a given case, teams end up doing a de facto big-bang rewrite instead of the intended incremental one
It removes the need for any testing during the migration
It is required by SwiftUI's view protocol

quiz.explanation: The incremental approach depends on being able to cut over piece by piece; that requires a concrete routing mechanism, and without one, migration work tends to collapse back into an all-at-once rewrite.

quiz.prompt: A team has been running a strangler-fig migration for a year. New screens use the new architecture, but the old implementation is still present and occasionally touched for legacy screens, with no plan to remove it. What is missing from their migration?

options.text: A rename of the legacy module to make it clearer
Nothing — this is the correct, complete end state of a strangler-fig migration

An explicit plan and timeline to finish routing everything to the new path and delete the old implementation, since leaving both paths permanently is a half-finished migration with ongoing double-maintenance cost
A rollback plan, which is irrelevant this late in the process

quiz.explanation: The strangler-fig pattern isn't complete until the old path is actually retired; without a scheduled final cutover and removal, the team pays the ongoing cost of maintaining two implementations indefinitely.

quiz.prompt: In a strangler-fig migration of a screen-by-screen UIKit-to-SwiftUI transition, what determines whether a given screen has 'finished' migrating?

options.text: Whether the screen's SwiftUI code has more lines than the original UIKit code
Whether the screen was migrated before any other screen
Whether the SwiftUI code compiles without warnings
Whether the routing seam sends 100% of traffic for that screen to the new implementation and the old implementation for that screen can be safely deleted

quiz.explanation: Migration completeness for a given piece is defined by the routing seam no longer needing the old path for it — once nothing routes to the legacy implementation, it's safe to delete, which is the actual finish line.

slides.title: Feature flags decouple deploy from release
slides.body: A feature flag lets code ship to production dark (inactive) and be turned on independently of the App Store release train — via a remote config toggle — which means a risky change can be enabled for 1% of users, watched, and rolled back instantly without shipping a new build.

slides.title: Flag types serve different purposes
slides.body: A release flag gates an in-progress feature until it's ready; an experiment flag drives an A/B test; an ops flag is a kill switch for something that might need emergency disabling; a permission flag gates by entitlement (e.g., beta users). Conflating these — using one flag type's lifecycle assumptions for another's purpose — causes confusion about who owns it and when it should be removed.

slides.title: Flags accumulate technical debt if not cleaned up
slides.body: Every live flag is a branch in the code and a combinatorial test burden — two flags means four code paths to reason about. A disciplined team tracks flag age and owner, and removes release flags (leaving only the winning code path) once a feature is fully rolled out, rather than letting stale flags accumulate indefinitely.

slides.title: Rolling out gradually, and watching the right signals
slides.body: A safe rollout ramps a flag from an internal cohort, to 1%, to 10%, to 100%, pausing at each stage to watch crash rate, key funnel metrics, and error logs specific to the change — not just 'did anything obviously break,' but the specific signals the new code path could plausibly affect.
slides.example:
Rollout ramp: internal -> 1% -> 10% -> 50% -> 100%,
watching checkout completion rate and payment error rate at each step

quiz.prompt: What is the primary advantage of gating a risky new implementation behind a feature flag rather than relying solely on the App Store release process?

options.text: It decouples code deployment from feature activation — the change can be enabled for a small cohort, monitored, and rolled back instantly via remote config, without needing a new App Store release to undo it
Feature flags are required for App Store approval
It eliminates the need for any QA testing
Feature flags make the code compile faster

quiz.explanation: Because a flag can be flipped remotely, a problem discovered after partial rollout can be mitigated in minutes rather than waiting for App Store review and user update adoption for a fixed build.

quiz.prompt: A team uses the same flag both to gate an in-progress migration feature and as a permanent emergency kill switch for that subsystem. What problem does conflating these two flag purposes cause?

options.text: It is technically impossible to implement in code

It creates confusion about the flag's intended lifecycle and ownership — a release flag is meant to be removed once rollout completes, while an ops kill switch is meant to be kept indefinitely, and conflating them makes it unclear when (or whether) to clean it up
It automatically doubles the app's binary size
It has no real downside as long as the flag works correctly

quiz.explanation: Different flag types carry different lifecycle expectations; treating a temporary release flag as if it were a permanent kill switch (or vice versa) leads to either premature removal of a needed safety valve or permanent accumulation of flags that should have been cleaned up.

quiz.prompt: Why do accumulated, never-removed feature flags represent a form of technical debt?

options.text: Flags cannot coexist with unit tests
Flags slow down the app's runtime performance measurably
Each live flag multiplies the number of code paths that must be reasoned about and tested, and stale flags whose feature has already fully shipped add this cost with no remaining benefit
Flags are deprecated by Apple and will eventually stop working

quiz.explanation: Two live flags imply four possible code paths in combination; once a feature has fully rolled out, the flag and its now-dead alternate path should be removed, or the team keeps paying a combinatorial complexity cost for no ongoing benefit.

quiz.prompt: During a gradual feature flag rollout (internal -> 1% -> 10% -> 100%), what should the team primarily watch for before advancing to the next stage?

options.text: Whether the App Store rating has changed that day
Whether competitor apps have shipped a similar feature
Whether the rollout percentage number looks round

Signals specific to what the new code path could plausibly affect — such as crash rate, relevant funnel metrics, and error logs tied to the change — not just a general sense that nothing seems obviously broken

quiz.explanation: A meaningful rollout gate watches metrics causally connected to the change (e.g., checkout completion rate for a checkout flow change), since generic 'nothing seems broken' checks can miss a real regression the specific metrics would catch.

quiz.prompt: A feature has been at 100% rollout for six months, and the original feature flag and its old code path are still present in the codebase. What should a senior engineer flag as a problem in review?

options.text: The flag has outlived its purpose as a release flag and should be removed, along with the now-dead old code path, to avoid ongoing combinatorial complexity with no remaining benefit
The flag should be renamed to reflect the new feature name
The flag should be converted into an experiment flag instead
Nothing — leaving the flag in place indefinitely is standard best practice

quiz.explanation: Once a release flag's rollout is complete and stable, keeping it (and the dead alternate path) around only adds maintenance and testing burden — cleanup is the expected final step of a flag-gated rollout, not optional.

slides.title: Two code paths is a deliberate, temporary state
slides.body: During any incremental migration, the old and new implementations coexist for a while by design — this isn't a mistake to feel bad about, but it is a cost (double the surface area to test, reason about, and fix bugs in) that should be minimized in duration, not treated as a comfortable steady state.

slides.title: Keeping both paths correct without duplicating logic
slides.body: Where possible, extract shared business logic (validation rules, calculations) into a common layer both the old and new UI/implementation call into, rather than reimplementing the same logic twice — a bug fix or rule change should ideally apply in one place, not need to be ported between two parallel implementations.

slides.title: Test both paths, but proportionally to traffic
slides.body: Both the old and new paths need test coverage for as long as they're both live and reachable, but effort should track real usage — a path serving 95% of traffic deserves more scrutiny than the 5% sliver still on the old implementation, and that ratio should shift as rollout progresses.

slides.title: Set an explicit expiration
slides.body: The team should track an expected removal date for the old path (tied to a rollout percentage or metric threshold, not just a vague 'eventually'), and revisit it in planning — an open-ended 'we'll keep both around for now' is how temporary migration scaffolding becomes permanent.
slides.example:
Ticket: "Remove LegacyCheckoutFlow once newCheckoutFlow has
 been at 100% for 4 consecutive weeks with no rollback. Target:
 review this ticket at the March 15 planning meeting."

quiz.prompt: During a migration, both the legacy and new implementations of a feature exist simultaneously. What is the correct framing of this state?

options.text: It's a mistake that should never happen and indicates poor planning
It's a deliberate but costly temporary state (doubled surface area for testing and bugs) that should be minimized in duration, not treated as an acceptable long-term steady state
It's the final, permanent architecture the team should aim for
It only matters for backend systems, not client apps

quiz.explanation: Running two implementations in parallel is a normal and often necessary part of incremental migration, but its cost means the team should actively work to shorten that window, not settle into it indefinitely.

quiz.prompt: Why is extracting shared business logic (e.g., checkout validation rules) into a common layer valuable while both an old and new UI implementation are live?

options.text: It automatically deletes the old code path once finished
It reduces the app's binary size
It ensures a bug fix or rule change applies in one place automatically, rather than needing to be manually ported and kept in sync between two separately-implemented versions of the same logic
It is required for SwiftUI and UIKit to coexist in the same app

quiz.explanation: Duplicated logic across two parallel paths is a correctness risk — a fix applied to only one implementation silently leaves the other one wrong; a shared layer keeps both paths consistent by construction.

quiz.prompt: A migration has old and new implementations both live, with the old path now serving only 5% of traffic. How should test and review effort be allocated between the two paths?

options.text: Entirely on the old path, since it's about to be removed
Entirely on the new path, abandoning any further testing of the old path immediately
Equally, regardless of traffic split, since both are technically still in production
Roughly proportional to real usage and risk — the 95%-traffic new path generally deserves more ongoing scrutiny, while the shrinking old path's investment should taper as its traffic does

quiz.explanation: Effort should track where the actual user impact is; a nearly-retired path with 5% traffic still needs enough coverage to be safe, but pouring equal ongoing investment into it as the dominant new path isn't the best use of limited time.

quiz.prompt: Six months after a migration began, the old code path is still live with no scheduled removal date, and 'we'll clean it up eventually' is the standing plan. What is the risk of this approach?

options.text: Without an explicit removal trigger (a rollout percentage, date, or metric threshold), the temporary scaffolding tends to become permanent, and the team keeps paying the ongoing cost of maintaining two implementations indefinitely
It will cause the app to fail App Store review
It only affects build time, not correctness
There is no real risk; open-ended cleanup is the standard practice for all migrations

quiz.explanation: Vague, undated cleanup plans routinely never happen because there's always something else prioritized; tying removal to a concrete, trackable trigger is what actually gets the old path retired instead of lingering indefinitely.

quiz.prompt: A team maintaining both old and new checkout implementations notices a rule change (a new tax calculation) only got applied to the new implementation, not the old one still serving 5% of traffic. What does this most directly illustrate?

options.text: That the old implementation should be deleted immediately regardless of its remaining traffic
The risk of duplicated business logic across two parallel paths — without a shared layer, a rule change can silently apply to only one implementation, leaving the other one incorrect
That tax calculation logic should never be duplicated under any migration strategy
That the new implementation has a bug and should be rolled back

quiz.explanation: This is exactly the failure mode shared logic extraction is meant to prevent — duplicated implementations can drift out of sync when a change is applied to only one of them, leaving the other silently wrong.

slides.title: Defining risk before you need it
slides.body: A migration's risk plan should be written before rollout starts, not improvised during an incident: what specific signals (crash rate delta, funnel drop, error rate spike) would trigger a pause or rollback, and what thresholds count as 'this is a problem' vs. 'this is normal noise.'

slides.title: Rollback needs to actually be possible
slides.body: A rollback plan is only real if the mechanism it depends on — flipping a remote feature flag, reverting a server-side routing rule — can act faster than the problem compounds; a rollback plan that requires shipping a new App Store build to fully revert is much weaker than one gated purely behind server-controlled configuration.
slides.example:
Weak: rollback requires a new App Store submission (days).
Strong: rollback is a remote config flip, effective within minutes for users online.

slides.title: Leading indicators vs. lagging indicators
slides.body: Crash rate and support ticket volume are lagging indicators — by the time they move, real users have already been affected. Where possible, a migration should also watch leading indicators (e.g., a spike in a specific error log, an increase in retry attempts) that can catch a problem before it shows up as a user-visible metric.

slides.title: Post-rollout risk doesn't disappear at 100%
slides.body: Reaching 100% rollout isn't the end of the risk window — the old path (and rollback capability) is often kept available for a defined grace period afterward specifically because some issues only surface at full scale or after enough elapsed time (e.g., a monthly billing cycle edge case).
slides.example:
Post-rollout plan: "Keep LegacyBilling and its rollback flag
 for 60 days after 100% rollout, since billing bugs often only
 surface at the next monthly invoice cycle."

quiz.prompt: Why should the specific metrics and thresholds that would trigger a migration rollback be defined before the rollout begins, rather than decided in the moment during an incident?

options.text: It guarantees no incidents will occur during rollout
It is required by Apple's App Store guidelines
Deciding thresholds calmly in advance avoids ambiguous, high-pressure judgment calls during an actual incident about whether an observed signal is 'real' or normal noise
It has no real benefit since thresholds always need to be adjusted anyway

quiz.explanation: Pre-defined trigger conditions remove the need to debate, under pressure and with incomplete information, whether a signal warrants rollback — that judgment is much easier to make well in advance, when it's not urgent.

quiz.prompt: A team's rollback plan for a risky migration requires shipping a new App Store build to fully revert the change. Why is this considered a weak rollback plan?

options.text: It is technically impossible to submit an app update quickly
Apple prohibits rollback-only App Store submissions
App Store submissions are always rejected on the first attempt
App Store review and user update adoption take days, so this rollback mechanism can't act fast enough to limit damage compared to a server-controlled toggle that takes effect within minutes

quiz.explanation: A rollback plan's value depends on how fast it can act relative to how fast the problem compounds; a mechanism gated behind app review and staged rollout adoption is far slower than a remote config change.

quiz.prompt: What distinguishes a 'leading indicator' from a 'lagging indicator' in the context of monitoring a migration rollout?

options.text: A leading indicator (e.g., a spike in a specific error log or retry rate) can signal a problem before it becomes user-visible, whereas a lagging indicator (e.g., crash rate, support tickets) only moves after real users have already been affected
Lagging indicators are collected before the rollout starts
There is no meaningful difference; both terms describe the same thing
Leading indicators are always more accurate than lagging indicators

quiz.explanation: Leading indicators are early warning signals closer to the root cause, giving a chance to act before user impact accumulates, while lagging indicators reflect harm that has already occurred by the time they move.

quiz.prompt: A migration has reached 100% rollout with no reported issues. What is the recommended next step regarding the old implementation and rollback capability?

options.text: Delete the old implementation and rollback mechanism immediately to reduce code complexity
Keep the old path and rollback capability available for a defined grace period, since some issues only surface at full scale or after specific elapsed-time conditions (e.g., a monthly billing cycle)
Nothing further is needed; 100% rollout means the risk window has fully closed
Immediately begin a second, unrelated migration using the same rollback mechanism

quiz.explanation: Full rollout doesn't eliminate risk instantly — certain classes of bugs only manifest at scale or after time-based triggers, so keeping a defined safety window (and the ability to roll back) before finally deleting the old path is the more cautious, correct approach.

quiz.prompt: A migration dashboard shows crash rate is flat, but the team also tracks a rising retry-attempt count on a specific network call tied to the new code path. Why might the retry count be the more important signal to act on first?

options.text: Because retry counts are the only metric App Store review checks
Retry counts are never a meaningful signal and can be safely ignored

It may be a leading indicator of an emerging problem — catching it before it escalates into a user-visible crash-rate increase, which is a lagging indicator that only moves after real damage has occurred
Because crash rate is always a less reliable metric than any other metric

quiz.explanation: Acting on leading indicators lets a team intervene before a problem compounds into visible user harm, whereas waiting for lagging indicators like crash rate to move means damage has already happened.

slides.title: Different audiences need different framings of the same plan
slides.body: An engineering team needs the technical sequencing, seams, and risk mitigations; a product or leadership audience needs the timeline, what changes for users (ideally nothing, visibly), and what tradeoffs were made (e.g., feature work slowing temporarily). Presenting the same deeply technical plan to both audiences either buries leadership in irrelevant detail or leaves engineers without the specifics they need to execute.

slides.title: Make the plan legible, not just correct
slides.body: A migration plan that only the author fully understands is a liability — if that engineer is out or leaves, the migration stalls. Writing the plan down with explicit phases, owners, and current status (not just in one person's head) is what lets other engineers pick up any piece of it without a lengthy handoff conversation.
slides.example:
Migration doc sections: Why now / Current state / Phases & owners /
Rollback plan / Current status (updated weekly) / How to help

slides.title: Give teams advance notice of what changes for them
slides.body: If a migration changes how other teams interact with a module (a new API, a deprecated pattern, a required test update), those teams need advance notice with enough lead time to plan around it — landing it unannounced turns colleagues into surprised blockers instead of informed collaborators.

slides.title: Status updates keep trust in the plan
slides.body: Large migrations lose credibility when they go quiet for months — regular, honest status updates (including 'we hit a snag and are behind schedule') keep stakeholders' trust in the plan even when things aren't going perfectly, whereas silence followed by a missed deadline erodes trust far more than transparent bad news would have.
slides.example:
Weekly Slack update: "Migration status: 60/120 screens done,
 on track for Q3. Hit a snag with custom gesture recognizers on 3
 screens — adding 1 week, still within our buffer."

quiz.prompt: Why should a migration plan be presented differently to a leadership/product audience versus an engineering audience?

options.text: The technical plan and the leadership summary must always be word-for-word identical documents
Leadership audiences only care about the exact line count of code changed
Leadership audiences should never be told about migrations at all

Each audience needs different information to act on — engineers need technical sequencing and risk mitigations to execute, while leadership needs timeline, user impact, and tradeoffs to make resourcing and prioritization decisions — and conflating the two either buries one audience in irrelevant detail or starves the other of what they need

quiz.explanation: Effective communication tailors depth and framing to what the audience needs to act on; a single one-size-fits-all presentation typically fails one of the two audiences.

quiz.prompt: Why is it risky for a large migration's plan and current status to exist only in the lead engineer's head rather than written down?

options.text: If that engineer is unavailable or leaves, the migration stalls because nobody else has the context to pick up any part of it without a lengthy handoff
It has no real risk as long as the engineer is skilled
Written plans automatically execute themselves
Written plans are required by Apple for App Store submission

quiz.explanation: An unwritten plan creates a single point of failure — the migration's continuity depends entirely on one person's availability, which a written, legible plan with owners and status removes.

quiz.prompt: A migration will require another team to adopt a new API and deprecate an old pattern they currently use. What is the appropriate way to introduce this change to that team?

options.text: Land the change and let the other team discover it via a compile error or deprecation warning
Give them advance notice with enough lead time to plan the migration work into their own schedule, rather than surprising them with an unannounced requirement
Avoid informing them since it's not their migration to worry about
Wait until they file a complaint before explaining the change

quiz.explanation: Changes that affect another team's work should be communicated as a heads-up with lead time, turning them into informed collaborators who can plan around it rather than surprised blockers reacting after the fact.

quiz.prompt: A migration has gone quiet for three months with no status updates, and now the team announces it's significantly behind schedule. What would have better preserved stakeholder trust?

options.text: Renaming the migration so the delay isn't associated with the original announcement
Waiting even longer before announcing, until the migration is fully back on track

Regular, honest status updates throughout — including acknowledging setbacks as they happen — since transparent bad news generally damages trust far less than silence followed by a surprise missed deadline
Never having started the migration in the first place

quiz.explanation: Trust in a long-running plan is maintained through consistent, honest visibility into progress and setbacks; going silent and then delivering a surprise miss is what actually erodes confidence, not the setback itself.

quiz.prompt: A migration lead is preparing two different documents: one for the engineering team and one for a leadership review. What is the key difference that should exist between them?

options.text: The leadership version should omit any mention of risk or delay to avoid concerning stakeholders
The engineering version should be shorter than the leadership version
There should be no difference; leadership should read the exact same technical document engineers use

The leadership version should translate technical sequencing into timeline, user impact, and tradeoffs relevant to prioritization decisions, while the engineering version keeps the technical detail needed to execute

quiz.explanation: Each audience needs the plan translated into what they can act on — engineers need execution detail, leadership needs decision-relevant framing — rather than a single undifferentiated document serving neither well.

quiz.prompt: Why is it important for a migration plan to define a concrete 'done' state before work begins?

options.text: Without a measurable end state, large migrations tend to run indefinitely with no clear point at which effort can stop or success can be declared
It guarantees the migration completes on schedule
It has no real bearing on the outcome, only on team morale
It is required for the migration to compile

quiz.explanation: An undefined end state is how migrations become permanent background work — a concrete definition of done is what lets the team and stakeholders recognize completion and stop investing further.

quiz.prompt: What is the core mechanism of the strangler-fig migration pattern?

options.text: Rewriting the entire system in one release for a single cutover
Incrementally routing new functionality through the new implementation while the old system keeps serving what hasn't migrated yet, until the old system can eventually be retired
Running old and new systems in permanent, indefinite parallel with no plan to retire either
Migrating only the backend and leaving all client code unchanged

quiz.explanation: Strangler-fig migration is defined by gradual, routed replacement — each piece migrates independently while the rest keeps functioning on the old path, avoiding the all-or-nothing risk of a big-bang rewrite.

quiz.prompt: What is the primary risk of a big-bang rewrite compared to an incremental migration?

options.text: Big-bang rewrites are always cheaper in total engineering time
Big-bang rewrites cannot be tested at all
It delivers no incremental value until the very end and concentrates all risk into one large, hard-to-validate cutover, so a late-discovered blocking issue threatens the entire effort
Big-bang rewrites are prohibited by Swift Package Manager

quiz.explanation: By deferring value and validation entirely to a single cutover, a big-bang rewrite spends the whole migration budget before finding out whether the approach actually works.

quiz.prompt: What is the main advantage of gating a risky change behind a feature flag rather than relying solely on an App Store release to control exposure?

options.text: Feature flags are mandatory for App Store approval
It removes the need for any monitoring during rollout
Feature flags make the underlying code run faster
It decouples activation from deployment — the change can be enabled for a small cohort, monitored, and rolled back via remote config within minutes, without needing a new build to undo it

quiz.explanation: A flag's value is the speed and granularity of control it gives after the code is already shipped dark — enabling gradual exposure and near-instant rollback that a build-based release cycle can't match.

quiz.prompt: Why do stale, never-removed feature flags accumulate technical debt over time?

options.text: Each live flag multiplies the number of code paths to reason about and test, and once a feature is fully rolled out, the flag and its dead alternate path add this cost with no remaining benefit
Flags are deprecated by Apple and stop functioning after a fixed time
Flags prevent unit tests from compiling
Flags measurably degrade the app's runtime performance

quiz.explanation: Combinatorial complexity grows with each live flag; once rollout is complete, keeping the flag and its now-unused path only adds ongoing maintenance burden without further purpose.

quiz.prompt: While both an old and new implementation of a feature are live during migration, why is extracting shared business logic into a common layer valuable?

options.text: It reduces the app's binary size measurably
It ensures a bug fix or rule change applies once, rather than needing to be manually kept in sync across two separately-implemented versions of the same logic
It is required for the two implementations to coexist in the same app target
It automatically removes the old implementation once finished

quiz.explanation: Duplicated business logic across two parallel paths risks the two silently diverging; sharing the logic keeps both consistent by construction instead of relying on engineers to manually port every change.

quiz.prompt: Why should a migration's rollback trigger thresholds (which metrics, what values) be defined before rollout begins rather than decided during an incident?

options.text: It has no practical benefit since thresholds always change later anyway
It is required by Apple's App Store guidelines
Deciding calmly in advance avoids ambiguous, high-pressure judgment calls under incident conditions about whether an observed signal actually warrants rollback
It guarantees the rollout will have zero incidents

quiz.explanation: Pre-committing to thresholds removes the need to debate, under time pressure and incomplete information, whether a given signal is a real problem — that judgment is far easier to make calmly in advance.

quiz.prompt: A rollback plan for a risky migration depends on shipping a new App Store build to fully revert. Why is this a weaker rollback mechanism than a server-controlled feature flag?

options.text: It is technically impossible to submit an emergency app update
Apple prohibits using App Store releases for rollback purposes
App Store submissions are always rejected initially
App Store review and staged update adoption take days, far slower than a remote toggle that can take effect within minutes, limiting how quickly damage can be contained

quiz.explanation: A rollback mechanism's usefulness depends on its speed relative to how fast a problem compounds; build-and-review-gated rollback is far slower than a server-side configuration change.

quiz.prompt: A migration will require another team to adopt a new API and retire a pattern they currently depend on. What is the best way to introduce this change to that team?

options.text: Give them advance notice with enough lead time to plan the required work into their own schedule
Avoid telling them since it's not directly their migration
Wait for them to file a complaint before explaining the change
Land the change and let them discover it via a compile error or deprecation warning

quiz.explanation: Advance, proactive communication turns an affected team into an informed collaborator who can plan around the change, rather than a surprised blocker reacting to an unannounced break.

quiz.prompt: A large migration has gone quiet for three months with no status updates before an announcement that it's significantly behind schedule. What would have better preserved stakeholder trust throughout?

options.text: Waiting even longer to announce, until things are fully back on track
Regular, honest status updates throughout — including acknowledging setbacks as they occur — since transparent bad news generally damages trust far less than silence followed by a surprise miss
Never announcing the migration's existence at all
Renaming the migration effort to distance it from the delay

quiz.explanation: Ongoing visibility, including honest bad news, sustains stakeholder confidence in a long-running plan; it's the silence followed by a surprise that actually erodes trust, not the setback itself.

slides.title: Correctness first, but not only
slides.body: A review should verify the code actually does what it claims — edge cases, error paths, off-by-ones, concurrency issues — since a beautifully structured change that's subtly wrong is still a bug. But stopping at correctness misses design and readability problems that won't show up as a test failure today but will cost real time in six months.

slides.title: Design: does this fit the system, not just compile
slides.body: Beyond 'does this work,' a design-level review asks whether the change belongs where it is, whether it introduces a new pattern where an existing one already solves the problem, and whether it couples things that shouldn't be coupled. This is the level of review that prevents architectural drift one PR at a time.
slides.example:
Comment: "This adds a second way to fetch the user profile,
 bypassing the existing UserRepository. Can we route through
 that instead so caching/auth stay consistent?"

slides.title: Readability is a correctness proxy for the next reader
slides.body: Code that's hard to follow is code the next engineer — possibly the same author in six months — will misunderstand and modify incorrectly. Flagging unclear naming, tangled control flow, or a function doing three unrelated things isn't pedantry; it's reducing the probability of a future bug caused by misreading the current one.

slides.title: Calibrate depth to the change's blast radius
slides.body: A one-line copy change and a change to the payment retry logic don't deserve the same depth of scrutiny — reviewing everything with maximum rigor wastes time on low-risk changes and, worse, trains reviewers to skim, which is exactly when a high-risk change slips through under-reviewed.
slides.example:
A localized string tweak: skim for typos, approve in under a
 minute. A change to retry/backoff logic in the payment SDK: read
 every branch, check tests for the failure paths, ask about idempotency.

quiz.prompt: A PR passes all tests and does what the ticket describes, but introduces a second, parallel way to fetch user profile data that bypasses the existing shared repository. What should a thorough review flag?

options.text: The PR should be rejected solely for not adding more tests
Nothing — passing tests and matching the ticket is sufficient for approval
The design-level issue: the new code path bypasses the existing abstraction, risking inconsistent caching or auth behavior, even though it happens to work and pass tests today
Only the variable naming, since that's the sole legitimate scope of review

quiz.explanation: Correctness alone doesn't catch design problems — a change that works today but introduces a duplicate, inconsistent path around an existing abstraction is exactly the kind of issue that compounds into architectural drift if left unflagged.

quiz.prompt: Why is readability considered a legitimate, substantive review concern rather than mere style preference?

options.text: Readability only matters for code written by junior engineers
Apple's App Store review explicitly checks code readability
Unreadable code always fails to compile
Code that's hard to follow increases the odds that a future reader misunderstands it and introduces a bug while modifying it, so readability functions as a proxy for future correctness

quiz.explanation: Readability isn't cosmetic — it directly affects how likely the next person (possibly the original author, later) is to correctly understand and safely modify the code, making it a real risk factor, not just taste.

quiz.prompt: A reviewer spends 45 minutes doing a deep architectural review of a one-line typo fix in a comment, with the same rigor as a payment-processing change. What is the problem with this approach?

options.text: Review depth should scale with a change's actual risk and blast radius; applying maximum scrutiny uniformly wastes time on low-risk changes and can train reviewers to skim overall, which is dangerous for genuinely high-risk changes
45 minutes is always too long for any code review
Comment changes cannot introduce bugs, so they need no review
Typo fixes should never be reviewed at all

quiz.explanation: Calibrating review depth to risk is what keeps reviews sustainable and effective — treating every change identically either wastes effort on trivial ones or, through reviewer fatigue, under-scrutinizes the changes that actually matter.

quiz.prompt: During review of concurrent code, what should a senior reviewer specifically check beyond whether the happy-path tests pass?

options.text: Whether the PR description is grammatically correct
Whether the code correctly handles race conditions, cancellation, and ordering guarantees, since these often aren't exercised by typical happy-path tests but cause real production bugs
Whether the function names start with a verb
Whether the PR was opened before or after lunch

quiz.explanation: Concurrency bugs are notorious for passing straightforward tests while harboring race conditions or ordering issues that only manifest under specific timing — this is exactly the kind of correctness issue a careful review needs to actively look for, not assume away.

quiz.prompt: A reviewer notices a function that is technically correct but has a confusing name, tangled nested conditionals, and mixes three unrelated responsibilities. The author argues 'it works, so it's fine.' What is the strongest response?

options.text: Ignore the issue since Swift has no style requirements
Agree and approve, since correctness is the only thing code review should ever evaluate
Readability issues like this increase the odds a future reader misunderstands and incorrectly modifies the code, so flagging them is a legitimate, substantive part of review, not pedantry
Reject the PR outright without explaining why, since 'it works' isn't an acceptable justification for anything

quiz.explanation: Readability functions as a proxy for future correctness — code that works today but is hard to follow raises the odds of an incorrect modification later, which is exactly why it deserves review attention beyond 'does it work now.'

slides.title: Comment on the code, not the coder
slides.body: "This function does too much" invites a discussion about the code; "you always write functions that do too much" attacks the person and invites defensiveness instead of a fix. Framing feedback around the artifact, not a pattern of personal failing, keeps the conversation productive and is simply more accurate — you're reviewing this PR, not auditing someone's character.

slides.title: Be specific enough to act on
slides.body: "This could be cleaner" gives the author nothing to do; a good comment names the specific problem and, ideally, a concrete direction — what's wrong, why it matters, and what a better version might look like — without necessarily prescribing the exact code to paste in.
slides.example:
Weak: "This is confusing."
Actionable: "This function mixes network fetching and
 view-model state updates. Splitting the fetch into its own
 method would make the state-update logic easier to unit test."

slides.title: Distinguish must-fix from nice-to-have
slides.body: Not every comment carries the same weight, and burying a blocking correctness issue among ten stylistic nitpicks makes it easy to miss. Many teams use a lightweight convention (e.g., prefixing optional suggestions with 'nit:') so the author can immediately tell what's required before merge versus what's optional polish.

slides.title: Kindness and rigor aren't in tension
slides.body: Being kind doesn't mean softening real problems into vague, unhelpful comments — a reviewer who says "looks good!" on a change with a real bug to avoid an awkward conversation isn't being kind, they're deferring the cost (and making it worse) to whoever hits the bug in production. The kind version of hard feedback is direct, specific, and focused on the work.
slides.example:
Not kind: "LGTM!" (on a PR with a real race condition).
Actually kind: "Found a real issue: this closure can run after
 the view is dismissed, causing a crash. Want to pair on a fix?"

quiz.prompt: Which review comment is the most actionable and effective example of feedback?

options.text: "You always write functions that do too much."
"Not a fan of this approach."
"This code is messy, please fix it."
"This function mixes network fetching and state updates — splitting the fetch into its own method would make the state-update logic independently testable."

quiz.explanation: This comment names the specific problem (mixed responsibilities), explains why it matters (testability), and points toward a concrete direction, giving the author something they can actually act on.

quiz.prompt: A reviewer writes: "You always structure your PRs like this and it's hard to review." What is the main problem with this feedback?

options.text: It frames the issue as a personal pattern/character trait rather than commenting on the specific code in this PR, which tends to trigger defensiveness rather than a productive fix
It should have been given in person rather than in writing
It fails to use technical terminology
It is too short to be useful

quiz.explanation: Feedback aimed at the person rather than the artifact reads as a character judgment, which is both less accurate (you're reviewing this PR) and more likely to produce defensiveness than a specific, code-focused comment would.

quiz.prompt: Why do some teams adopt a convention like prefixing optional suggestions with 'nit:' in code review comments?

options.text: It is required by most linters

It distinguishes must-fix issues from optional polish, so a blocking correctness or design comment doesn't get lost among stylistic suggestions and the author knows what's actually required before merging
It makes the review process faster to complete automatically
It removes the need for the author to read any comments carefully

quiz.explanation: Without signaling severity, a genuinely blocking issue can be buried among nitpicks; a lightweight convention like 'nit:' lets the author immediately triage what must be addressed versus what's optional.

quiz.prompt: A reviewer notices a real correctness bug in a PR but approves it with just "LGTM!" to avoid an uncomfortable conversation with the author. How should this be evaluated?

options.text: It is fine because most bugs are caught by QA anyway
This is the correct, kind approach since it avoids conflict
This isn't actually kind — it defers the cost of the bug to whoever encounters it in production, and true kindness here means giving direct, specific, code-focused feedback about the real issue
It is acceptable as long as the author is a senior engineer

quiz.explanation: Withholding real feedback to avoid short-term discomfort isn't kindness — it trades a manageable, private conversation now for a costlier, more visible problem later; direct and specific feedback focused on the code is the actual kind option.

quiz.prompt: A reviewer wants to flag ten small comments on a PR, one of which is a genuine blocking correctness bug. What technique helps ensure the blocking issue doesn't get lost among the others?

options.text: Split the PR into ten separate PRs, one per comment
List all ten comments in a random order with no distinction between them
Omit the correctness bug from the written review and mention it verbally instead
Signal severity explicitly, for example by clearly marking optional suggestions as non-blocking (e.g., 'nit:') so the blocking issue stands out from the nine minor ones

quiz.explanation: Explicitly distinguishing blocking issues from optional polish keeps the important signal from being buried in volume, letting the author immediately see what actually needs to change before merge.

slides.title: Architecture issues compound; style nitpicks don't
slides.body: A misplaced responsibility or a leaky abstraction gets built on top of by the next PR and the one after that, making it progressively more expensive to fix — a stylistic inconsistency (spacing, naming convention) stays a fixed, small cost no matter how long it's left. Review time should be weighted toward the issues that get more expensive over time.

slides.title: Recognizing an architecture-level comment vs. a nitpick
slides.body: "This couples the view layer directly to Core Data" is architectural — it affects how easily the system can change later. "I'd have named this `items` instead of `list`" is a nitpick — it affects nothing beyond this file's immediate readability. Both can be valid comments, but they're not the same weight and shouldn't be reviewed, or responded to, as if they were.
slides.example:
Architectural: "This view directly imports CoreData —
 should it go through the repository so we can swap persistence
 later without touching UI code?"
Nitpick: "nit: prefer `items` over `list` here."

slides.title: Automate the nitpicks away
slides.body: Formatting, import ordering, and many naming conventions can be enforced by a linter or formatter run in CI, which removes them from human review entirely — freeing reviewer attention for the things tooling genuinely can't catch, like whether this is the right abstraction.

slides.title: When a nitpick is actually hiding an architecture question
slides.body: Sometimes a seemingly small comment ("why is this logic in the view instead of the view model?") is really an architecture question in disguise — the size of the comment doesn't always match the size of the underlying issue, so it's worth asking, before dismissing something as a nitpick, whether it's actually pointing at a structural problem.
slides.example:
"nit: why is this logic here?" turns out to reveal the view
 directly performs network calls — what looked like a one-line
 question was actually flagging a missing repository layer.

quiz.prompt: Why should architecture-level review comments generally be weighted more heavily than pure style nitpicks?

options.text: Architectural issues (misplaced responsibilities, leaky abstractions) compound as more code is built on top of them, becoming progressively more expensive to fix, while a style inconsistency stays a fixed, small cost regardless of how long it persists
Style nitpicks are never valid review feedback
Architecture comments are required by Apple's Human Interface Guidelines
Architecture comments are always longer to write

quiz.explanation: The cost of an architectural flaw grows over time as more code depends on the flawed structure, whereas a naming or spacing inconsistency doesn't get more expensive the longer it exists — which is why review attention should be weighted accordingly.

quiz.prompt: What is the best way to remove most style and formatting nitpicks from human code review entirely?

options.text: Ask reviewers to stop mentioning style issues even if noticed
Enforce formatting, import ordering, and naming conventions via a linter/formatter run automatically in CI, so those issues never reach a human reviewer in the first place
Only allow senior engineers to comment on style
Disable code review for small PRs

quiz.explanation: Automating enforceable style rules frees reviewer attention entirely for issues tooling can't catch — like whether an abstraction is the right one — rather than relying on humans to manually flag things a linter could catch instantly.

quiz.prompt: A reviewer leaves a short comment: "Why is this validation logic in the view instead of the view model?" A teammate dismisses it as "just a nitpick." What is the more accurate read of this comment?

options.text: It's automatically a nitpick because it doesn't mention a specific bug
It genuinely is just a stylistic nitpick and can be safely ignored
Despite being brief, it's actually raising an architectural question about responsibility placement, which can matter more than its short length suggests and shouldn't be dismissed by size alone
It should be dismissed because it's phrased as a question rather than a directive

quiz.explanation: Comment length isn't a reliable signal of severity — a short question about where logic belongs is often pointing at a genuine architectural concern (separation of concerns, testability) that deserves real consideration, not automatic dismissal.

quiz.prompt: A PR both introduces a genuine coupling problem (a service layer directly manipulating UIKit views) and has inconsistent indentation in one file. How should a reviewer prioritize these in feedback?

options.text: Only mention the indentation issue since it's easier to fix quickly
Reject the PR solely for the indentation issue since consistency matters most
Treat both as equally important and address them in the same tone and urgency

Flag the coupling issue as the substantive, likely-blocking concern, and treat the indentation issue as a minor, non-blocking nitpick (ideally something a formatter should catch automatically going forward)

quiz.explanation: The coupling problem has real architectural consequences and should be treated as the priority concern; the formatting issue is a minor, easily fixed, and ideally tooling-catchable nitpick that shouldn't be given equal weight.

quiz.prompt: A team spends most of its code review discussion time debating tab-width and brace placement, with architectural issues rarely discussed. What change would most improve the team's review effectiveness?

options.text: Adopt an automated formatter/linter enforced in CI to remove style debates from human review, freeing discussion time for design and architecture questions that tooling can't evaluate
Require every PR to include a full architecture diagram regardless of size
Increase the minimum number of reviewers required per PR
Ban all discussion of code style permanently, even informally

quiz.explanation: Automating what tooling can reliably enforce redirects human attention toward the judgment calls that actually need it — architecture and design — rather than spending scarce review time re-litigating style.

slides.title: What actually warrants a block
slides.body: A block (requesting changes before merge) is appropriate for correctness bugs, security issues, or design decisions that would be expensive to undo once other code depends on them — not for stylistic disagreement or a suggestion the author could reasonably take or leave. Reserving blocks for things that truly need to be fixed before merge keeps the signal meaningful.

slides.title: Approve-with-comments respects author judgment
slides.body: For genuinely optional suggestions — a preference, an alternative approach that isn't clearly better, a question for the author's own judgment — approving while leaving comments lets the PR merge without forcing the author into a re-review cycle for something that was never going to block release.
slides.example:
"Approving — one thought: have you considered extracting this
 into a computed property? Not blocking, just a suggestion if you
 want to tidy it up later."

slides.title: Over-blocking trains authors to fear review
slides.body: A reviewer who blocks on everything, including matters of pure preference, teaches authors to dread review and, over time, to either avoid that reviewer or pre-emptively over-engineer PRs defensively — the blocking mechanism loses its power to signal 'this genuinely needs to change' when it's used indiscriminately.

slides.title: Under-blocking on real issues is its own failure
slides.body: Conversely, approving a PR with a real correctness or security issue because the reviewer didn't want to seem difficult trades a short-term social cost for a real production risk — the bar for blocking should be calibrated to actual risk, not to reviewer comfort or a desire to move quickly.
slides.example:
Under-blocking: approving a PR with an unhandled force-unwrap
 on user input because "it'll probably be fine" — six weeks later
 it crashes in production for a subset of users.

quiz.prompt: A reviewer sees a PR with a debatable naming choice they'd have made differently, but the current naming is clear and consistent with the surrounding code. What's the appropriate action?

options.text: Block the PR (request changes) until the naming matches the reviewer's preference
Approve the PR, optionally leaving a non-blocking comment noting the alternative naming as a suggestion, since this is a matter of preference rather than a real problem
Leave no comment at all since preferences shouldn't be voiced in review
Escalate the naming disagreement to engineering leadership

quiz.explanation: Blocking should be reserved for issues that genuinely need fixing before merge; a debatable but reasonable naming choice is a good candidate for approve-with-comments, respecting the author's judgment on non-critical matters.

quiz.prompt: What is the main risk of a reviewer who habitually blocks PRs over matters of pure stylistic preference, in addition to real issues?

options.text: It is required by most engineering style guides
It has no real downside since it ensures maximal code quality
