options.text: It directly addresses the fact that junior engineers often have less social capital and context to rebuild trust on their own, providing an explicit signal of continuity during a period when informal cues that usually convey this are disrupted.
It replaces the need for the new manager to build their own relationship with those engineers.
It has no measurable effect on psychological safety during organizational change.
It is primarily useful for the distinguished engineer's own visibility rather than for the junior engineers involved.

quiz.explanation: Junior engineers typically have less accumulated social capital to fall back on, so explicit, proactive reassurance fills the gap left by disrupted informal trust signals during a period of change.

quiz.prompt: What is a common mistake organizations make when reorganizing teams, with respect to culture?

options.text: Over-communicating context and norms that used to be implicit in the old team structure.
Giving new teams explicit space to establish their own working agreements.
Assuming that culture, norms, and trust will automatically carry over into the new team configuration without deliberate effort to rebuild them.
Naming explicitly which norms and standards mattered in the old configuration.

quiz.explanation: The common failure is assuming culture transfers automatically with the org chart — without deliberate effort to name norms, rebuild trust, and give new teams room to establish agreements, culture erodes quietly.

quiz.prompt: What concrete action can a distinguished engineer take during organizational change to help preserve technical standards, even without formal management authority?

options.text: Wait passively for the new organizational structure to stabilize before taking any action.
Visibly model the standards they want preserved from day one in the new structure, rather than waiting for those standards to feel established on their own.
Avoid engaging with the reorg process entirely to stay neutral.
Assume junior engineers will raise any concerns about safety or standards on their own initiative.

quiz.explanation: Visibly modeling desired standards from the very start of a new configuration establishes the real expectation immediately, rather than leaving it to chance or waiting for informal culture to re-form on its own.

quiz.prompt: A company's values doc emphasizes quality, but promotion is based almost entirely on shipping speed with no engineer ever promoted for quality improvements. What does this predict?

options.text: The values document will shape behavior regardless of the incentive mismatch.
Engineers will prioritize quality because it's written down.
Engineers will read the real culture from what's actually rewarded — shipping speed — regardless of the stated values.
This mismatch has no practical effect on engineering behavior.

quiz.explanation: Engineers infer real priorities from what's actually rewarded — promotion criteria — not from stated values, so a mismatch undermines the values in practice.

quiz.prompt: A 60-person engineering org still relies on a single Slack channel for all major technical decisions, and decisions are now routinely missed. What does this indicate?

options.text: A practice that worked when everyone shared context has hit a scale threshold requiring structured documentation to replace informal awareness.
The org should shrink back down to make the old practice work again.
Nothing needs to change; the practice will start working again naturally.
The Slack channel practice was always a flawed idea.

quiz.explanation: Practices built on shared informal context work only up to a certain scale; beyond it, structured documentation needs to substitute for awareness that no longer happens naturally.

quiz.prompt: A junior engineer stays silent about a suspected race condition during review because a past concern was met with public dismissal. The bug later causes an incident. What does this illustrate?

options.text: This is unrelated to psychological safety.
The junior engineer is solely responsible for the incident.
Public dismissal is an effective way to maintain high standards.
Low psychological safety has a direct, measurable cost on engineering quality by suppressing valid technical concerns.

quiz.explanation: This is a direct example of psychological safety's effect on quality — a valid concern was suppressed by a past negative experience, and the predicted failure occurred.

quiz.prompt: A postmortem concludes 'Engineer X made a mistake' and stops there. What's missing from a blameless postmortem perspective?

options.text: Nothing; this is a complete and sufficient postmortem.
An analysis of why the system allowed the mistake to happen and what pressures contributed, which is what would actually produce a fix preventing recurrence.
A recommendation to discipline Engineer X.
A statement that no further investigation is needed.

quiz.explanation: Blameless postmortems look for the systemic and contextual factors behind an incident; stopping at individual blame skips the analysis that would actually prevent recurrence.

quiz.prompt: A hiring panel uses the same coding-focused loop for staff candidates as for senior candidates, just with harder problems. What is this likely to miss?

options.text: The multiplier effect that differentiates staff-plus engineers — their ability to improve systems and people around them across boundaries they don't control — since coding exercises don't test for that.
Nothing; harder coding problems are sufficient for any level.
It will systematically overqualify candidates for the staff role.
It accurately tests everything relevant to the staff role.

quiz.explanation: Staff-plus differentiation is about multiplier effect and cross-boundary influence, not raw individual execution, which a harder senior-style interview doesn't test.

quiz.prompt: After a reorg, an engineer who used to raise concerns comfortably becomes hesitant under a new manager they've never worked with. What does this most likely reflect?

options.text: The engineer has become less competent.
This is unrelated to the reorg.
Psychological safety was built in a specific trust relationship that didn't automatically transfer to the new structure.
The engineer is being deliberately obstructive.

quiz.explanation: Psychological safety is relational and built over time; a new reporting relationship starts without that accumulated trust unless deliberately rebuilt.

quiz.prompt: A senior engineer blocks a PR for a week over a cosmetic style disagreement while an urgent security fix sits unreviewed. What does this illustrate?

options.text: Correct application of technical excellence.
Style should always take priority over shipping speed.
Both PRs are handled with equally appropriate priority.
Perfectionism mislabeled as excellence — real excellence would prioritize the urgent fix.

quiz.explanation: Genuine technical excellence prioritizes real risk and impact; blocking on cosmetic issues while urgent risk goes unaddressed damages both velocity and actual quality.

quiz.prompt: After one incident from insufficient design review, a VP mandates a heavyweight, multi-approver design-doc process for every team company-wide immediately. What's the risk?

options.text: Over-processing: a broad, heavyweight solution applied to what may be a narrower problem, slowing teams who weren't part of the original failure.
There is no risk since more process is always better after an incident.
The mandate is guaranteed to have no negative effects.
This is the only way to prevent similar incidents in the future.

quiz.explanation: Reacting to a single incident with a broad mandate risks imposing ongoing cost on teams that weren't part of the original failure, rather than solving the actual scoped problem.

quiz.prompt: An engineer who caused an outage while following documented procedure in good faith is publicly thanked for their honest, detailed account during the postmortem. What's the primary purpose of this?

options.text: To avoid any technical follow-up actions.
To make blamelessness credible through demonstrated practice, showing engineers honest disclosure is genuinely safe.
To ensure the engineer is never asked about it again.
To shift responsibility onto the reviewing team.

quiz.explanation: Blamelessness is only credible when demonstrated in practice; publicly recognizing honest disclosure teaches the org the process is safe to use honestly.

quiz.prompt: A leveling committee finds they tend to level up candidates who present with high confidence, even when their answers don't clearly demonstrate staff-level judgment. What does this illustrate?

options.text: Confidence is a reliable indicator of technical judgment at any level.
The committee's overall bar is too low.
A proxy bias: mistaking seniority-coded communication style for actual technical judgment, which can distort leveling independent of real impact.
This has no bearing on leveling accuracy.

quiz.explanation: Confident presentation style is an unreliable but common proxy for technical judgment, and relying on it risks leveling decisions disconnected from real impact.

questions.prompt: What is the safest way to unwrap an optional when you want to exit the current function immediately if it's nil?

options.text: Force unwrap with !
try! optional
guard let value = optional else { return }
if value = optional {}

questions.explanation: guard let safely unwraps the optional and requires the else branch to exit the current scope if it's nil, avoiding a crash.

questions.prompt: What is the key practical difference between assigning a struct instance and assigning a class instance to a new variable?

options.text: The struct assignment produces an independent copy; the class assignment produces another reference to the same shared instance
There is no difference
Classes are always copied, structs are always shared
Only classes support assignment

questions.explanation: Structs have value semantics (copied on assignment) while classes have reference semantics (shared via pointer).

questions.prompt: What must a type provide to conform to a protocol?

options.text: A final keyword
Implementations for every requirement the protocol declares
A subclass relationship
Nothing, conformance is automatic

questions.explanation: Protocol conformance requires implementing every method, property, and initialiser the protocol declares.

questions.prompt: What is a key benefit of moving formatting and state logic out of a view controller and into a ViewModel?

options.text: The ViewModel has no dependency on UI framework types, so it can be unit tested in isolation
It makes the code slower
It's only a stylistic preference with no practical benefit
It removes the need for a Model layer entirely

questions.explanation: A UI-framework-agnostic ViewModel can be instantiated and tested directly, without any UIKit or SwiftUI dependency.

questions.prompt: Why does injecting dependencies as protocols (rather than concrete types) improve testability?

options.text: It removes the need to write tests
Protocols can't be used in production code
It doesn't affect testability
Tests can substitute a fake or mock conforming to the protocol instead of using the real implementation

questions.explanation: A protocol-typed dependency lets a test supply a controllable fake in place of the real implementation, such as a real network call.

questions.prompt: What causes a retain cycle between a class instance and a closure it stores as a property?

options.text: Closures can't be stored as properties
ARC automatically prevents this scenario
The closure captures self weakly by default
The instance strongly holds the closure, and the closure captures self strongly by default, so each keeps the other alive

questions.explanation: Both directions of the strong reference (instance to closure, closure to self) must exist simultaneously for the reference counts to never reach zero.

questions.prompt: Why must a weak reference always be an optional type?

options.text: Optional weak references are faster
Because the runtime sets it to nil automatically once the instance it refers to is deallocated
Weak references can't be initialized
It's an arbitrary Swift restriction

questions.explanation: Since a weak reference can become nil at any point when its instance is deallocated, it must be declared as an optional.

questions.prompt: Why does @State work correctly across a SwiftUI view struct being recreated on every re-render?

options.text: @State properties are recomputed identically each time by coincidence
@State stores its value in separate, persistent storage tied to the view's identity, outside the struct itself
The view struct is never actually recreated
SwiftUI views are classes, not structs

questions.explanation: @State keeps its underlying value in SwiftUI-managed storage independent of the view struct, so it survives the struct's frequent recreation.

questions.prompt: What is a key advantage of @Observable over the older ObservableObject/@Published pattern?

options.text: There is no meaningful difference between them
@Observable tracks changes per-property, so a view only re-renders for the specific properties its body actually reads
@Observable only works with structs
@Observable requires marking every property @Published

questions.explanation: Field-level tracking in @Observable avoids the broad re-renders caused by ObservableObject's single combined change signal.

questions.prompt: Why is Swift's throws/try mechanism considered explicit compared to unchecked exceptions in other languages?

options.text: Because throws has no effect on how a function is called
Because every throwing call and throws-marked function signature is visible directly in the source code
Because Swift doesn't actually support error propagation across functions
Because Swift automatically catches every error without any code

questions.explanation: The try keyword at call sites and throws in function signatures make every point where an error can occur or propagate visible in the code.

questions.prompt: A view model needs to fetch a user and their posts concurrently, then combine both results. Which approach best expresses this with structured concurrency?

options.text: async let for both calls, then await both together once their values are needed
Two sequential await calls, one after the other
Two separate Task.detached calls with no coordination
DispatchGroup with a completion handler

questions.explanation: async let starts both operations concurrently as structured child tasks and lets you join on both results together, which is the idiomatic modern approach for a fixed, known set of concurrent operations.

questions.prompt: Why does marking a view model class `@MainActor` help prevent a common category of SwiftUI bugs?

options.text: It makes all of its methods run faster
It isolates its state to the main actor, so the compiler enforces that UI-driving state is only mutated on the main thread
It disables Swift's concurrency checking entirely for that type
It automatically makes the class conform to Codable

questions.explanation: SwiftUI requires state driving the UI to be touched from the main thread; @MainActor turns that requirement into a compile-time-enforced guarantee rather than a convention that can be forgotten.

questions.prompt: What's the main practical difference between a stub and a mock in unit testing?

options.text: Stubs can only be used with Swift Testing, never XCTest
Mocks are always faster to execute than stubs
A mock also records how it was invoked so tests can assert on interactions, while a stub just returns fixed data
There is no practical difference between the two terms

questions.explanation: The distinguishing feature of a mock is call-tracking for interaction verification, beyond a stub's simpler role of just returning canned data.

questions.prompt: Why is 100% code coverage a poor primary goal for a test suite?

options.text: It's mathematically impossible to achieve in Swift
Coverage tools are not available for iOS projects
High coverage always slows down the app's runtime performance
Coverage measures whether code executed, not whether the test meaningfully verified behavior, so chasing the number can reward low-value tests

questions.explanation: A test can execute a line without asserting anything meaningful about it, so coverage percentage alone doesn't guarantee the suite actually catches regressions.

questions.prompt: After a successful (non-throwing) async URLSession call, why is it still necessary to check the HTTP status code?

options.text: Because the call only throws for transport-level failures; a server error like 404 or 500 still returns a valid response with a non-2xx status
Because status codes only matter for POST requests
It isn't necessary; absence of a thrown error always means success
Because URLSession never actually throws under any circumstances

questions.explanation: URLSession's error throwing covers connectivity/transport failures, not the server's own response status, so the status code must be inspected separately to detect application-level failures.

questions.prompt: Why would a client refresh an expired access token via a single coordinated task (e.g. an actor) rather than letting every failed concurrent request trigger its own refresh?

options.text: To make refresh calls run faster in parallel
To avoid redundant or racing refresh attempts that could waste limited refresh tokens or produce inconsistent authentication state
Coordinated refresh is required by Apple's networking APIs
It has no real benefit over independent refreshes

questions.explanation: Centralizing refresh through a single in-flight task prevents multiple concurrent requests from each kicking off separate, potentially conflicting token refresh attempts.

questions.prompt: For a new iOS 17+ app without unusual legacy requirements, why is SwiftData generally recommended over UserDefaults for storing a large, queryable catalog of structured records?

options.text: UserDefaults cannot store arrays under any circumstances
SwiftData is required for the app to compile on iOS 17+
UserDefaults is meant for small settings and loads its entire contents into memory, while SwiftData is built for large, queryable, relational structured data
There is no practical difference between the two for this use case

questions.explanation: UserDefaults' design targets small key-value preferences, not large structured datasets; SwiftData is purpose-built for exactly this kind of queryable, relational persistence.

questions.prompt: Why should a sensitive authentication token be stored in the Keychain rather than UserDefaults or a plain Codable file?

options.text: Tokens are too large to fit in UserDefaults or a file
Keychain is simply the newest API and should always be preferred
There's no real security difference between these storage options
The Keychain provides encrypted, access-controlled storage appropriate for secrets, unlike the unencrypted plist/file storage of the alternatives

questions.explanation: Keychain items are encrypted and access-controlled at the OS level, which is specifically what credentials and other secrets need; UserDefaults and plain files offer no such protection.

questions.prompt: Why can expensive work inside a SwiftUI view's computed properties or `body` cause visible UI stutter?

options.text: body is evaluated on the main thread, so heavy inline computation there directly consumes the limited per-frame time budget
SwiftUI always evaluates body on a background thread, so this should never cause stutter
Computed properties are forbidden inside SwiftUI views
It only affects apps running on the simulator, not real devices

questions.explanation: Since view rendering happens on the main thread with a tight per-frame time budget, any non-trivial computation placed directly in body competes with that budget and can cause dropped frames.

questions.prompt: Why is it unsafe to rely solely on `applicationWillTerminate` (or its SwiftUI equivalent) as the only place important state gets saved?

options.text: It fires too often, hurting performance
It is not reliably called when the app is silently terminated from a suspended background state, a very common termination path
It has been removed starting in iOS 17
It only applies to apps using Core Data

questions.explanation: Because termination from suspension frequently happens without any callback to the app, relying only on a termination handler risks silently losing unsaved state; saving proactively (e.g. on backgrounding) is the reliable pattern.

questions.prompt: A feed screen with millions of frequently-mutating rows needs infinite scroll. Which pagination strategy avoids duplicate or missing items as the dataset changes concurrently?

options.text: Cursor-based pagination anchored to the last item seen
Loading the entire dataset into memory once
Randomly sampling rows for each page
Offset-based pagination with a larger page size

questions.explanation: Cursor-based pagination is stable under concurrent mutation because it anchors each page to a specific item rather than a numeric position that shifts as rows are inserted or removed.

questions.prompt: Why should a module's public API default to minimal surface area, promoting symbols to `public` only when a real external consumer needs them?

options.text: Public symbols compile more slowly than internal ones
Every public symbol is a long-term commitment to consumers, so a minimal surface keeps the module free to evolve internally without breaking dependents
Internal symbols cannot be tested
Apple limits the number of public symbols a module may declare

questions.explanation: A large public API surface means more things count as breaking changes when the module evolves; keeping it minimal preserves the freedom to refactor internals safely.

questions.prompt: What is the core idea of the strangler-fig migration pattern, and why is it generally preferred over a big-bang rewrite?

options.text: Migrate only the UI layer and leave all underlying data logic untouched
Rewrite everything in one release for a single, well-tested cutover

Incrementally route new functionality through the new implementation while the old system keeps serving what hasn't migrated yet, avoiding the risk of betting everything on one large, hard-to-validate cutover
Run old and new systems in permanent parallel indefinitely with no plan to retire either

questions.explanation: Strangler-fig migration spreads risk and delivers incremental value throughout the process, unlike a big-bang rewrite, which defers all value and validation to a single high-stakes cutover.

questions.prompt: A PR passes all tests and matches its ticket, but introduces a second, parallel way to fetch data that bypasses an existing shared repository. What should a thorough code review flag?

options.text: Only variable naming, since that is the sole legitimate scope of review
The PR should be rejected solely for lacking additional tests
Nothing, since passing tests and matching the ticket is sufficient for approval
The design-level issue that the new path bypasses the existing abstraction, risking inconsistent behavior even though it currently works and passes tests

questions.explanation: Passing tests only verifies correctness on the paths exercised; a working-but-duplicated path around an existing abstraction is a design problem that compounds into architectural drift if left unaddressed.

questions.prompt: Why does the quality of a new engineer's first few weeks of onboarding matter beyond immediate comfort?

options.text: Early wins and clarity build momentum and confidence that compound over following months, while a rough, unsupported start can set someone back well past onboarding itself
It has no measurable effect on team performance
It matters only for engineers hired directly out of school
It only affects short-term morale with no lasting consequence

questions.explanation: Onboarding quality is high-leverage precisely because its effects compound over time — a strong or weak start shapes confidence and trajectory well beyond the first weeks.

questions.prompt: Module A depends on Module B, and Module B depends on Module A. What happens when these are compiled as separate Swift package targets, and what does this indicate about the design?

options.text: The build succeeds by arbitrarily picking an order; this is a normal, healthy pattern
The build fails, since a true cycle has no valid build order — this typically signals a missing shared abstraction that both modules actually depend on
Only unit tests fail; the main app target compiles fine
The cycle is silently ignored in Release configuration

questions.explanation: A genuine circular dependency has no valid build order and is rejected outright; the usual fix is extracting the shared functionality into a third module both can depend on instead of depending on each other.

questions.prompt: What is the primary advantage of gating a risky change behind a feature flag rather than relying solely on an App Store release to control its exposure?

options.text: It removes the need for any monitoring during rollout
Feature flags make the underlying code execute faster
It decouples activation from deployment — the change can be enabled for a small cohort, monitored, and rolled back via remote config within minutes, without needing a new build to undo it
Feature flags are mandatory for App Store approval

questions.explanation: A flag's value is the speed and granularity of control after code is already shipped dark — near-instant rollback and gradual exposure that a build-and-review release cycle cannot match.

questions.prompt: A reviewer notices a genuine security issue (an access token logged in plaintext) but approves the PR anyway to avoid seeming overly critical. How should this decision be evaluated?

options.text: This is acceptable since security issues are solely another team's responsibility
This is fine as long as it is mentioned informally at some later point
This is good judgment, since preserving team harmony matters most
This is a failure of the review responsibility — the bar for blocking should track actual risk, and a real security issue clearly warrants blocking regardless of social comfort

questions.explanation: Blocking exists specifically for issues like this; letting social discomfort override a genuine security concern trades a short, manageable conversation now for a real production risk later.

questions.prompt: In a properly inverted architecture, which module should typically own (define) an abstraction like an `OrderRepository` protocol that a low-level networking module implements?

options.text: The core/business-logic module that needs the capability, so the dependency arrow points toward an abstraction it owns rather than toward a volatile, low-level implementation
A separate, unrelated `Protocols`-only module in every case
Whichever module happens to be compiled first in the build graph
The Networking module, since it implements the repository's behavior

questions.explanation: Dependency inversion places the abstraction with the high-level module and has the low-level module depend on the high-level module to conform to it, keeping the dependency pointed toward the stable core rather than a volatile implementation detail.

questions.prompt: A mentor delegates a design decision to a mentee but then insists the mentee's solution match exactly what the mentor would have chosen, rejecting a different-but-valid approach. What does this reveal about the delegation?

options.text: That the mentor is holding the mentee to an appropriately high standard
That this isn't genuine delegation — insisting on one specific outcome after delegating the decision is really just dictating the same outcome through an extra step
That the mentee's approach was definitely technically incorrect
That code review should be skipped for delegated tasks

questions.explanation: Real delegation means tolerating a genuinely different, equally valid path to the outcome; requiring convergence on the mentor's own preferred solution defeats the purpose of delegating the decision in the first place.
